docs.title: Tack
docs.text:
Tack is a Python framework for data-parallel computing on CPUs and GPUs. You write a kernel as an ordinary Python function with one parallel loop, and Tack compiles it when you call it, for the CPU (through LLVM), Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA, AMD HIP or Intel Level Zero. Arrays live on a device, kernels run where their arrays are, and the same kernel source runs on every backend, within each backend's capabilities: Metal has no f64, for example, and the CPU has no workgroup primitives.

Tack comes in two packages, and the second is built on the first:

  • Tack core (tack-core, the tack module): the kernel language, arrays and devices, parallel algorithms and communication between devices and MPI ranks. It is general purpose: simulations, data processing, analysis, anything you would write as loops over arrays.
  • Tack vis (tack-vis, tack.dataset and tack.interop): datasets and scientific visualization -- meshes, point clouds, fields and the filters over them -- written as Tack kernels, with VTK, MFEM and Warp interop.
import tack, numpy as np

tack.set_default_device("cpu")          # or metal, cuda, hip, level_zero

@tack.kernel
def vector_add(x, y, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):   # the outermost loop maps to thread parallelism
        out[i] = x[i] + y[i]

n = 1_000_000
x = tack.empty((n,))
y = tack.empty((n,))
out = tack.empty((n,))
tack.copyto(x, np.arange(n, dtype=np.float32))
tack.copyto(y, np.ones(n, dtype=np.float32))

vector_add(x, y, out)
print(out.numpy()[:4])         # [1. 2. 3. 4.]

Only the tack.set_default_device() line changes between backends:

CPUMetalCUDAHIPLevel Zero 

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
LLVM IR through llvmlite, dispatched with ctypes. Threads are used only when a measurement says they pay — see Backends.

tack.set_default_device("metal")
MSL compiled by the Metal API. Buffers are shared memory on Apple silicon, so host and device see the same allocation.

tack.set_default_device("cuda")
CUDA C through NVRTC to PTX, launched with cuLaunchKernel.

tack.set_default_device("hip")
HIP C through hipRTC. The code generator is the CUDA one with a different #include — device syntax is shared.

tack.set_default_device("level_zero")
OpenCL C compiled to SPIR-V by libocloc, launched through Level Zero.

docs.title: Tack core
docs.text:
A kernel call goes from Python source to native code in one step: Tack reads the function's source, lowers it to its own intermediate representation, specializes it for the argument types, generates the backend's code and compiles it. The compiled kernel is kept in memory and on disk, so later calls, and later processes, skip the compilation. Around that compiler, the core has these parts:

Part What it gives you Read The kernel language @tack.kernel with one parallel loop; @tack.func device functions; control flow, math, and integer and floating-point arithmetic with defined semantics on every backend; vectors and matrices; atomics; workgroups (shared memory, barriers, block reductions) on GPUs Kernels, Control Flow and Math, Device Functions, Vectors and Matrices, Advanced Features Templates @tack.device_class objects: data and methods that a kernel takes as an argument and compiles in, composed of other templates, so one kernel serves many data structures Templates Arrays typed arrays of scalars, vectors or matrices on a device, structure-of-arrays layout, implicit arrays computed from their index (tack.arrays), exchange with NumPy Arrays and Types, Memory and Parallel Correctness Devices and backends devices as values, a default device, several GPUs, launches queued on GPUs and waited for when you read Backends Parallel algorithms tack.algorithms: reductions, scans, sorts, segmented reductions and statistics, the building blocks of data-parallel programs Reductions and Scans Communication tack.communication: work split into blocks over devices and MPI ranks, with exchanges, ghost plans, routing and distributed sorting Communicate Between Blocks Interoperability sharing memory without copies through DLPack and external pointers, with PyTorch, CuPy, Warp and VTK Sharing Arrays Tools the generated code (tack.inspect), bounds checks in debug mode, timing, the kernel cache Debugging and Timing, The Kernel Cache

The User's Guide teaches these in order: start with Getting Started and From Python to a Tack program, then the language chapters. Its worked examples are complete programs with independent checks: heat diffusion, dye advection, trail-following agents, marching squares, a particle-to-grid simulation and tiled N-body forces.

docs.title: Tack vis: datasets and visualization
docs.text:
Tack vis brings scientific visualization to Tack: the data model and filters of VTK, written data-parallel as Viskores writes them, with fields in function spaces as finite-element codes such as MFEM define them. Its algorithms -- contour, slice, clip, threshold, gradients, probes, streamlines, point-cloud cleaning, halo finding and many more -- are Tack kernels, so they run on every backend, on one dataset or on one cut into pieces over devices and MPI ranks. Tack draws nothing itself: results go to VTK and ParaView, sharing memory where they can.

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

data = td.uniform_grid((17, 17, 17), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.125, 0.125, 0.125))
positions = data.positions()
values = tack.array((positions * positions).sum(axis=1), dtype=tack.f32)
data.fields["radius_squared"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), values)

surface = td.contour(data, "radius_squared", 0.5)     # a sphere of triangles

Using its filters needs no kernel programming. Writing your own needs the core's kernels and templates, because a filter of your own sees a mesh through the same views the built-ins use. The Visualization Guide goes in this order:

  1. Visualization and Tack: what visualization does with data, and where Tack vis comes from.
  2. The data model: function spaces, datasets, fields, cell types and bases, physical units.
  3. Working with data: building meshes, point clouds, AMR and octrees, the filters, writing mesh algorithms and filters of your own, sampling and connecting simulations, streaming time steps.
  4. Data in pieces: partitioned datasets with ghost cells, and algorithms across pieces, devices and ranks.
  5. Examples and the Gallery, then the reference.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Tack is not on PyPI yet; install it from a clone of the repository:

git clone https://github.com/berkgeveci/tack.git && cd tack
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[cpu]'      # Tack core: CPU only
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[metal]'    # ...or Apple silicon
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[cuda]'     # ...or NVIDIA
pip install -e packages/tack-vis              # Tack vis, on top of the core

See Backends for what each extra pulls in and which scalar types each backend supports.

docs.title: The documentation
docs.text:
• User's Guide

    Tack core: writing kernels, arrays and types, control flow, device functions, templates, atomics and shared memory, reductions and scans, backends, communication and interoperability.

  • Visualization Guide

    Tack vis: the data model, meshes, point clouds and field spaces, scientific filters, custom cell and face kernels, probing and streamlines, data in pieces, and simulation pipelines.

  • Developer's Guide

    How a decorated function becomes machine code: the AST transform, the IR and its passes, the code generators, and the runtime that caches and dispatches them.

  • Design and Implementation

    Why Tack is built the way it is: the principles, the compilation pipeline, specialization and caching, numerical semantics, parallel execution, memory and aliasing, and interoperability.

  • Contracts

    What Tack promises and what callers must ensure: the kernel language contract, backend capabilities, the runtime API and its errors, and how conformance is tested and validated.

  • Backends

    The capability table: codegen, runtime compiler, dispatch, buffer type and supported dtypes for each backend.

  • API

    The public surface, generated from the source.

docs.title: What Tack is not
docs.text: It is not a drop-in NumPy replacement and not an autograd framework. Kernels are written in a restricted subset of Python that is read as source and compiled — the User's Guide covers what that subset includes. And it is not a renderer: Tack vis computes what is drawn, and VTK or ParaView draws it.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Tack's visualization filters against VTK and Viskores, on the CPU and the GPU, on synthetic meshes and on real simulation data. Every Tack output is checked against VTK's before its time counts: counts, sums of positions and values, areas and volumes.

Each entry below is how many times faster Tack is: the other system's time over Tack's, so above 1× Tack is faster. Tack's time is its fresh time, which includes deriving the connectivity it needs (faces, point links) from a mesh it has not seen, since VTK and Viskores rebuild theirs on every call. The running times, fresh and warm, are at the bottom.

docs.title: Streamlines on the GPU, against Viskores
docs.text:
Viskores' streamlines on CUDA against Tack's, on the ONERA M6 wing (46.9M tetrahedra and wedges, graded toward the wing in a far field a hundred chords wide) and the aneurysm (8.7M tetrahedra), by seed count. Viskores builds its cell locator, a two-level grid, on every call; the column shows how much of its time that is. Tack's topology keeps its locator, so a later call on the same mesh reuses it. Tack is shown both ways: building a new locator each call, as Viskores does, and with the locator kept.

mesh seeds Viskores (its locator) Tack, new locator Tack, locator kept Viskores / Tack, new locator M6 wing 1 3,526 (3,059) 107 15.2 33× 17 4,143 (3,019) 188 81.5 22× 1,024 4,767 (3,041) 238 146 20× 16,384 4,705 (3,043) 197 106 24× aneurysm 1 1,714 (1,545) 31.7 3.6 54× 25 2,113 (1,539) 55.2 22.6 38× 2,000 2,887 (1,569) 88.9 60.9 32× 20,000 6,812 (1,548) 561 578 12×
  • The paths agree. On the M6, every path is the same length in both, and they lie within 1.6e-6 of each other at 17 seeds and within 3.5e-6 at 16,384. On the aneurysm the agreement is within 2.1e-6 over the first quarter at 25 seeds. At 20,000 seeds, paths through its recirculation separate further: 19,730 of 20,000 are the same length (Viskores computes in double precision, Tack in the geometry's single precision).
  • Before Tack's two-level grid (#175) it scanned the M6's crowded bins near the wing: 28–105 s on this GPU.

Machine: jura (NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada). Viskores 1.2.0 (CUDA, double precision), run through a C++ driver of its Streamline filter. Tack main at 2bbaf7e with #184, the default two-level locator (2026-10-28). Times are warm, in ms; the first call compiles.

³ Measured 2026-10-27, after the two-level grid (#175). Tack's streamlines try the cell a particle was last found in, then search its two-level cell grid, so a location near the M6's wing no longer scans thousands of cells (it was 1.0 s with one level of bins). VTK's default interpolator finds cells through the nearest point, which ends 7 of the M6's 17 paths early, inside the mesh. With VTK's cell-locator interpolator, every path runs its full length, within 3.8e-6 of Tack's, in 22.9 s.

docs.title: How these were measured
docs.text:
• One process per comparison. Tack runs in the same process as VTK (the CPU) or Viskores (the GPU), on the same mesh, and its output is checked against the other's before any timing.
  • Viskores through VTK: its filters are VTK's Viskores filters (vtkmContour and the others). On the GPU it was handed Tack's device arrays and kept its output on the device, and a trace of every run confirmed no transfers beyond sizes and counts. It ran with cudaMalloc (NO_VISKORES_MANAGED_MEMORY=1): its default, cudaMallocManaged, was 4.7–25× slower from page faults on new buffers.
  • Warm and fresh. A warm Tack run reuses the connectivity its topology keeps from an earlier filter on the same mesh; a fresh one derives it.
  • Timing. Repeated runs for a fixed budget, the median taken; Tack's timing ends with tack.sync(), since GPU launches are queued. On the Linux machine, two passes: the VTK and Tack columns take the better of the two, the Viskores column their mean (the second pass in reverse order); on the Mac, one.
  • Harness: benchmarks/vtk_compare (VTK and Tack) and benchmarks/viskores_compare (Viskores and Tack), on the meshes of benchmarks/vtk_compare/meshes.py. Point gradients against VTK (vtkGradientFilter) are a pair of vtk_compare since 0.6.1's run (#195).

docs.title: Kernel throughput (historical)
docs.text:
Earlier microbenchmarks, from before October 2026

These measurements predate safe floating-point math on CUDA and Metal, the CPU threading policy's repairs, the CPU's disjoint-array variants, queued GPU launches and the CPU thread pool, all in October 2026. Their reproduce scripts time a call without tack.sync(), so their GPU columns would now time the launch rather than the kernel. They are kept as a record and have not been edited.

64 MB of f32 data (16,777,216 elements), median of 30 trials after warmup.

Reproduce: uv run python benchmarks/bench_64mb.py

  reduce  |     1.636 |      0.062 |     26.5x

Data size: 64 MB of f32 (16,777,216 elements), median of 5 trials after warmup.

docs.text:

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Metal GPU vs CUDA GPU are in the same ballpark (~19-29 G elem/s) despite very different architectures. Both are memory-bandwidth limited for simple kernels, compute-limited for transcendentals.

  • CPU/NumPy gap between Mac and Linux is mostly memory bandwidth: Apple Silicon unified memory delivers ~100-200 GB/s vs ~4 GB/s effective on this DDR3 Xeon box. The CPU itself (Sandy Bridge 2012 @ 2.0 GHz, AVX1 only) also contributes to the gap.

  • FILL hits 62 G elem/s on CUDA (write-only, no reads) — close to the 4060 Ti's theoretical 288 GB/s (62G × 4 bytes = 248 GB/s).

  • sin/exp show the largest CUDA-vs-CPU speedup (34-45x) because CUDA's Special Function Units (SFUs) compute transcendentals in hardware.

  • reduce favors Metal (39G vs 26G) — likely benefiting from unified memory avoiding a writeback path for partial sums.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
The guides show how to use Tack. The contracts state what Tack promises: what is guaranteed, what the caller must ensure, and what happens when either side gets it wrong. When a guide and a contract disagree, the contract governs. When a contract and the code disagree, the discrepancy is a defect to report, not a reading to choose between.

Status

The kernel language contract is a draft under review. It was baselined at 05174e1 and last updated for the fifth numerical-semantics increment on 2026-10-03. The other three pages describe release candidate 23d6e1d. Their statements are read from the source at that hash and cite where each one lives; Backend capabilities and Runtime API were since updated for the queued GPU launches, the disk cache, debug mode and the CPU pool merged through b94af23. The hardware validation status in Conformance was recorded at 745e01f, before those changes.

docs.title: How to read a contract
docs.text:
Every statement in a contract carries one of five labels. The language contract defines the first four in its Status and interpretation section:

Label Meaning Required "An intended correctness property. A current violation is a compiler defect, including when existing examples happen to work." Current behavior "Describes the implementation without making that behavior a permanent language guarantee." Proposed "A policy this draft recommends but that needs agreement before becoming a public guarantee." Open "No portable result is promised by this draft for that case. An open decision is not permission to change existing behavior silently." Required caller constraint An obligation on the program, not on Tack. Violating it leaves the result outside the contract. Tack does not promise a diagnostic, so a missing diagnostic is not a defect.

The fifth label covers obligations that the language contract states as "access only in-bounds elements and initialized values; write only to writable storage". It is the counterpart of Required. A failed Required property is a bug in Tack. A violated caller constraint is a bug in the program, even when Tack happens to produce the expected answer.

Two more conventions apply on every contract page:

  • Errors are part of the contract. When a page says that something is rejected, it names the exception type and where the exception is raised: at decoration, at first dispatch, on every dispatch, or at inspection. It also gives the shape of the message. A rejection raised before compilation or launch leaves array storage unchanged.
  • Current behavior is not a promise. It is recorded so that you can rely on it today and so that any change to it is deliberate. Don't build a portable program on a Current behavior item when a Required item or a caller constraint covers the same ground.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
Contract Scope Status Kernel language contract What a kernel means: supported constructs, execution and ordering, memory and aliasing, integer and floating-point semantics, reductions, workgroups, atomics and specialization identity. Regression IDs LC1–LC8 Draft under review, normative for the compiler hardening work Backend capabilities The Backend base class, the meaning of each capability attribute, the capability matrix for each backend, how launches are queued, and what each capability rejects and when Describes 23d6e1d, updated through b94af23 Runtime API Devices (tack.device, the default device, launch placement) and debug mode, arrays and their host operations, tack.sync, reductions, pointer and DLPack interop, tack.inspect, the decorators, kernel call rules, environment variables, tack.cache and exception types Describes 23d6e1d, updated through b94af23 and the device model of bba0846 Conformance and validation How each contract area is tested, which oracles the tests use, how a hardware validation is run and recorded, and the most recent status of each backend Describes 23d6e1d, with validation status recorded at 745e01f

The language contract is long because it defines semantics. The other three pages are shorter and more mechanical. They describe the surface around the language, and you can check most of their statements by reading one function.

docs.title: Contracts and the rest of the documentation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Design<br/>(why and how)"] --> C["Contracts<br/>(what is promised)"]
    C --> T["Tests<br/>(evidence)"]
    T --> V["Hardware validation<br/>(evidence per backend)"]
    G["Guides<br/>(how to use it)"] -. examples of .-> C
  • Design explains why Tack is built the way it is and how the implementation meets its contracts. For example, Specialization and Caching explains why the variant key includes baked shape constants, while the contract says only that reusing a variant must behave like a fresh compile.
  • Contracts say what is promised. They describe a mechanism only when it is observable, such as which pass raises an error.
  • Tests are the evidence. Conformance maps each contract area to its test modules. Expected values come from independent oracles, such as Python integers, NumPy, exact rationals and reference renders, and never from recording Tack's own output.
  • Hardware validation is the evidence that a backend meets the contract on a real device. A CPU run doesn't validate GPU execution, and a host-side syntax check of generated GPU source doesn't validate device behavior.
  • Guides (User's Guide and Developer's Guide) are examples. They aren't an exhaustive specification, and parts of them predate the contracts.

docs.title: Changing a contract
docs.text:
• A change to a Required item, or a decision on an Open item, changes the contract text and its tests together. The language contract says this explicitly for device assertions, and the rule applies everywhere.
  • Don't waive a failing numerical case by marking it as an expected failure. The regression baseline keeps LC1–LC8 as ordinary assertions.
  • Report a discrepancy between code and contract. Don't resolve it by editing whichever side is easier. The language contract is under human review, and changes to it go through that review.

docs.title: Backend capabilities
docs.text:
Tack compiles one kernel source for five targets, but the targets don't all offer the same things. Metal has no f64, the CPU has no workgroups, and atomics are narrower on some GPUs than ordinary arrays. This page is the contract for those differences. It covers what a backend declares, what each declaration means, what each one rejects and when, and the subset of the language that runs everywhere.

All statements describe release candidate 23d6e1d, updated for the queued launches, disk cache, debug mode and CPU pool merged through b94af23, and for the device model of bba0846. The declarations live in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/backend.py (class Backend) and in the five subclasses in runtime/cpu.py, runtime/metal.py, runtime/cuda_backend.py, runtime/hip_backend.py and runtime/level_zero_backend.py. For the kernel semantics that these capabilities gate, see the kernel language contract. For the implementation story, see Backend Implementations.

docs.title: The Backend contract
docs.text: Required: every backend subclasses Backend and declares its capabilities as attributes. Callers read those attributes and don't probe for methods with hasattr or compare backend class names. Anything that can be derived is derived, so two declarations can't disagree.

docs.title: Required methods
docs.text:
Method Contract allocate_array(dtype, shape, exportable=False) Allocates backend storage and returns a DeviceBuffer. exportable=True asks for memory that Array.export_memory() can share without a copy. Only CUDA acts on the flag, and the other backends ignore it wrap_ptr(ptr, dtype, shape) Wraps existing memory as a DeviceBuffer without copying or taking ownership. What counts as ptr is backend-specific. See Pointer interop execute(kernel, args, kwargs) Compiles or reuses a variant and runs it. All five backends delegate to resolve_variant() in runtime/kernel_utils.py, which is where every capability check below runs

The base class raises NotImplementedError for all three.

docs.title: Optional methods with defaults
docs.text: Method Default Overridden by synchronize() Does nothing, which is correct for a backend whose launches complete before execute() returns. Otherwise it waits for every launch, fill and copy queued so far, and a queued launch's error is raised here. tack.sync() calls it on every backend, Device.synchronize() on one Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, which queue launches (see Launches) fill_array(array, value) Returns False, and Array.fill fills the buffer in place CPU, which runs a fill of 256 KiB or more of its own buffers as a kernel through its dispatch, so the threads first-touch the pages cache_target() Returns None: compiled variants are not stored on disk, only lowered IR. Otherwise a string naming what compiled code depends on besides the kernel (the device, the compiler and driver versions, the compile options) all five variant_artifact(payload), load_variant(ir_func, artifact, effective_args) Raise NotImplementedError. Called only when cache_target() is not None: the picklable part of a compiled variant, and the payload rebuilt from it in another process. effective_args lets a GPU backend remake its scalar pack buffers all five memory_space(ptr) Returns "cpu", which is correct for backends whose allocations are host-addressable CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, which ask their driver. CPU overrides it with the same answer reduce_array(array, op) Raises NotImplementedError. Called only when supports_device_reductions is true Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero texture_in_hardware(shape_3d) Returns False: a Texture3D keeps a private f32 array and the generated code interpolates it in software Metal and CUDA (always True), HIP and Level Zero (per device and extent) create_texture_image(shape_3d) Raises NotImplementedError. Called only when texture_in_hardware() is true. Returns an image object with upload(array), owned by one Texture3D Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero _store_texture_shapes(ir_func, args) Records each Texture3D argument's extents on its parameter HIP and Level Zero, which clear the parameter's _is_texture flag when texture_in_hardware() is false

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Kind Meaning name declared Device type, as a device spec writes it (tack.device("cuda")) and Device.type reports it: cpu, metal, cuda, hip or level_zero ordinal declared Which of the type's devices the backend drives (Device.index). Always 0 for now display_name declared How messages spell the backend, if different from name label derived display_name or name. Use it in messages supported_dtypes declared A frozenset of the scalar types the device's arrays may have. Making an array of another type raises TypeError, and dispatch checks every array argument against this set supports_f64 derived f64 in supported_dtypes supports_device_reductions declared True when Array.sum(), min() and max() can run on the device. When false they run in NumPy on the host. It selects a path and never rejects anything supports_workgroups declared Native workgroup execution for shared, shared_like, barrier, thread_id and block_sum/block_min/block_max. It does not promise uniform participation, atomic support or safe partial workgroups supported_atomic_dtypes derived Array dtypes that support atomic_add, atomic_min and atomic_max. This is the backend's entry in ATOMIC_DTYPES (lang/atomic_support.py) intersected with supported_dtypes device_options declared Keyword options that tack.device() forwards to the constructor. tack.device() rejects any other option memory_domain derived What the backend's arrays are valid in, (name, ordinal). Level Zero adds its context handle. A backend runs kernels on another backend's arrays when the domains are equal (two CPU devices with different thread counts); arrays from two domains in one launch are refused device_memory_spaces declared memory_space() results that array_from_ptr() accepts. When the set is non-empty, every pointer must be an address (anything int() accepts) and is checked. An empty set means that the backend doesn't distinguish memory spaces and nothing is checked dlpack_refusal_note declared Text appended to the error when a DLPack import is refused, for backends whose reason the device type doesn't convey

Because supported_atomic_dtypes is an intersection, a device without f64 also loses f64 atomics. That matters on Level Zero, where supported_dtypes depends on the device.

docs.title: Level Zero and f64
docs.text:
Current behavior: LevelZeroBackend._query_device() runs during construction and calls zeDeviceGetModuleProperties. It then shadows the class attribute with an instance frozenset: all ten types when the reported fp64flags is nonzero, else the nine non-f64 types. supports_f64 and supported_atomic_dtypes follow automatically. To find out what the current device supports, ask:

import tack
from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend

tack.set_default_device("level_zero")
be = get_backend()
print(be.supports_f64, sorted(t.name for t in be.supported_atomic_dtypes))

docs.title: Textures
docs.text:
On every backend, a texture samples the data its array held when tack.texture3d() created it, or when tex.update() last copied it (see Memory and aliasing in the language contract). Writes to the array in between, whether by kernels, tack.copyto, or external and DLPack writers, don't reach the texture. The copy is storage the Texture3D owns (tex._storage): a hardware image from create_texture_image() where texture_in_hardware() is true, else a private f32 array. Dispatch binds that storage through bind_textures() (runtime/kernel_utils.py), never the source array. No compiled variant caches images, and an image is released with its texture. Two textures over one array are separate copies.

tack.texture3d() raises ValueError for an array that isn't f32, because every hardware path builds a single-channel 32-bit float image (R32Float on Metal, CU_AD_FORMAT_FLOAT on CUDA and HIP, ZE_IMAGE_FORMAT_TYPE_FLOAT on Level Zero). It also rejects an interp other than "linear", since sampling is trilinear on every backend, and a shape whose W*H*D differs from the array's size.

The variant key records which texture path a call uses, because the path changes the generated code. HIP and Level Zero answer texture_in_hardware() per device and extent, and their _store_texture_shapes() asks it again before the key is built, so a texture always holds the storage its compiled kernel binds:

  • HIP uses hardware sampling when hipDeviceAttributeImageSupport is nonzero and every extent is within the smallest reported maximum 3D texture extent. If any reported maximum is non-positive, the extents are treated as unbounded. CDNA parts such as MI300 report no image support, so they sample in software.
  • Level Zero uses hardware sampling when the device reports maxSamplers > 0 and every extent is at most maxImageDims3D. Xe-HPC (Ponte Vecchio) reports no samplers.

Metal and CUDA always answer true. CPU uses the base class's false.

docs.title: Launches
docs.text: Current behavior: the CPU's kernel call returns once the range has run. Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero queue the launch and return: Metal into an open command buffer, CUDA on one stream per context, HIP on one stream per device, Level Zero on one asynchronous immediate command list with a barrier after each command (a driver without zeCommandListHostSynchronize gets a synchronous list). On every backend, launches, fills and host writes take effect in the order they were made, host reads wait for the launches before them, an array dropped while a queued launch uses it outlives that launch, and a launch that binds memory handed outside Tack (a wrapped pointer, a DLPack export) completes before it returns. CUDA, HIP and Level Zero also complete a launch that samples a hardware texture. A queued launch's error is raised at the next wait. The user-facing rules are in Runtime API; the implementation is in Backend Implementations.

docs.title: What each capability gates
docs.text:
All dispatch-time checks run inside resolve_variant(). "Cold" means the first call with a new variant key, before optimization, code generation and compilation. "Every dispatch" also covers cached calls, and those checks run before launch.

Capability Checked by When Rejection device_options tack.device() in runtime/dispatch.py When a device is made with options, after the backend module imports and before construction ValueError: "The 'metal' device does not accept the option(s) num_threads. Accepted: none." The default device is unchanged supported_dtypes check_dispatch_types() in lang/type_inference.py Cold dispatch and inspection. A new dtype always produces a new key TypeError naming the kernel once: "Kernel 'k': parameter 'data' has dtype tack.f64, which is not supported on Metal. Supported dtypes: ..." supports_workgroups check_workgroup_support() in lang/workgroup_support.py Every dispatch, before the key lookup. The feature scan is memoized on the IR template. Also runs during inspection and direct LLVM generation NotImplementedError naming the kernel, backend and primitives, with the hint "use local_array or local_array_like". Dispatch wraps it in RuntimeError ("Kernel 'k' failed on CPUBackend: ..."). Inspection raises it directly Workgroup participation check_workgroup_participation() in lang/workgroup_participation.py Cold dispatch and inspection, on backends with supports_workgroups ValueError: "Kernel 'k': barrier at <IR path> requires uniform workgroup participation: ..." Full 256-lane groups check_workgroup_launch() Cold dispatch, every cached dispatch, and inspection, for kernels with barriers or block reductions ValueError: "...workgroup collectives require complete 256-lane groups; iteration count N would create a partial workgroup." Device group size CompiledMetalKernel and CompiledL0Kernel At compilation, for collective kernels, when the Metal pipeline or Level Zero device allows fewer than 256 lanes ValueError: "...workgroup collectives require 256 lanes; this pipeline/device selects n." supported_atomic_dtypes check_atomic_support() in lang/atomic_support.py Cold dispatch and inspection in every mode, including structurally unreachable atomics and empty grids TypeError: "Kernel 'k': metal atomic_add does not support target dtype tack.i64". The same check rejects targets that aren't global array parameters Atomic alignment check_atomic_alignment() Every dispatch and inspection ValueError: "Kernel 'k': atomic target parameter i requires n-byte alignment" Read-only arrays check_writable_arrays() in runtime/kernel_utils.py, over the indices the variant recorded in KernelVariant.written_arrays Every dispatch ValueError: "Kernel 'k': parameter 'out' may be written, but its array is read-only. ..." Launch size check_launch_size() in runtime/kernel_utils.py, against the limit in the capability matrix Every GPU dispatch, and every native f32 reduction on CUDA, HIP and Level Zero ValueError: "Kernel 'k': N iterations exceed the M that one CUDA launch can index; split the work across several launches." A reduction is named "Array sum()" and so on. Metal reduces arrays of 2^32 or more elements through NumPy instead device_memory_spaces array_from_ptr() in lang/array.py When wrapping, for any ptr, on backends with a non-empty set TypeError if ptr isn't an address. ValueError: "Pointer is in 'cpu' memory but the device is 'CUDA'. array_from_ptr() requires a device pointer. ..." DLPack device type dlpack_to_array() in lang/dlpack.py On import, when device= names a device that cannot wrap the tensor (without it, the tensor's own device is used) RuntimeError naming the device and DLPack device type, followed by dlpack_refusal_note if set. ValueError for an unknown device type and for kDLMetal supports_device_reductions Array._reduce() Never rejects Selects the device or NumPy path. See Reductions Texture hardware texture_in_hardware(), at texture3d() and in _store_texture_shapes() (HIP, Level Zero) At texture creation, and before the key is built Never rejects. Falls back to software sampling

A TypeError raised during dispatch reaches the caller prefixed with Kernel '<name>': unless its message already names the kernel, and with the original exception chained. ValueError passes through unchanged. See Exceptions.

For the full text of the workgroup and atomic rules, see Workgroups and synchronization and Atomic array updates.

What inspection does not check

tack.inspect() runs the dtype, workgroup, participation, workgroup-launch, atomic and alignment checks above, and it makes the texture decision through the backend's _store_texture_shapes(), so the source it shows is the source dispatch would compile. It doesn't check read-only arrays or the backend's launch-size limit, which belong to a launch rather than to the generated code.

docs.title: Device reductions
docs.text: supports_device_reductions does not mean that every reduction runs on the device. Current behavior: on every GPU backend, reduce_array() reduces only f32 arrays natively, and other dtypes use the shared NumPy fallback. Level Zero also falls back when the device's maximum group size is below 256. Empty arrays return without a device launch. CUDA, HIP and Level Zero pass the element count as a 64-bit kernel argument and reject an array larger than one launch can index. Metal's reduction kernel holds the count and thread position in 32 bits, so Metal reduces an array of 2^32 or more elements with NumPy over the shared buffer. The reduction contract defines results, precision and ordering for both paths.

docs.title: Backend notes
docs.text:
CPU. There is no workgroup model, and the CPU doesn't emulate one. tack.device("cpu", num_threads=n) makes a CPU device with that worker count; it shares memory with the other CPU devices. Kernels that use shared memory, barriers, thread_id or block reductions are rejected even when the primitive is unreachable. For private scratch storage, use local_array or local_array_like. Parallelism comes from a thread pool JIT'd from LLVM IR, or a ThreadPoolExecutor with TACK_CPU_POOL=python, on Windows, or where the pool cannot be made. See CPU Threading Policy. The CPU backend also compiles a separate noalias variant for calls whose written arrays provably don't overlap other arrays. See Memory and Aliasing.

Metal. There is no f64, because Apple GPUs don't implement double precision. Arrays are shared buffers in unified memory, so memory_space() answers "cpu" for them and array_from_ptr() wraps an MTLBuffer object, not an address. Collectives need a pipeline whose maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup is at least 256.

CUDA. If a CUDA context is already current on the device, for example one that a simulation framework created, the backend adopts it and never destroys it. Otherwise it creates one for the device. With a second device (or a context not current where it was made), every operation makes its context current for its duration. exportable=True allocates through the CUDA virtual memory management API, so export_memory() can hand out an OS handle without a copy.

HIP. The code generator is the CUDA generator with a different include and texture handle type. hipRTC compiles with -ffp-contract=on, so contraction stays inside one expression. Texture hardware is queried at initialization (see Textures).

Level Zero. f64 depends on the device (see Level Zero and f64). external_context takes a mapping with non-null driver, device and context handles, so that Tack allocates in a context that another library owns. A missing or null handle raises ValueError. For VTK, call tack.interop.vtk.init_level_zero() instead of tack.set_default_device("level_zero"). See Interoperability.

Warp (prototype). codegen/warp_gen.py writes each variant as a @wp.kernel from the typed IR, every operand converted to its annotated type, arrays passed by address and accessed through wp.func_native helpers at 64-bit indices, with helpers where Warp's semantics differ from Tack's (wrapping integers in an unsigned carrier, floor // and %, 64-bit trip counts, NaN-preferring min/max, signed zeros, no contraction across statements). Scalars are Warp kernel arguments, so nothing is packed and no dispatch lock is held. supports_inspect is false: tack.inspect raises NotImplementedError. A texture sample has no code generator and fails at compilation. See Backends.

docs.title: Portable subset
docs.text:
A program stays within every backend's capabilities if it keeps to the following rules. Everything else in the kernel language contract still applies.

Area Portable on all five backends Array and scalar dtypes i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32. Don't use f64, which Metal and some Level Zero devices lack. A Python float scalar becomes f64 only when an array argument is f64 Atomics atomic_add, atomic_min and atomic_max on i32, u32 or f32 global arrays, as statements Launch size At most 2^32 − 256 iterations per launch, HIP's cap, unless the CUDA or Level Zero device reports a lower limit. Split larger work across launches Workgroups None. If you don't need the CPU, collectives are portable across the four GPU backends in complete 256-lane groups with proven-uniform participation Scratch storage local_array and local_array_like Textures f32 sources, refreshed with tex.update() after the array changes Reductions Array.sum(), min(), max() and mean() on any dtype. Only f32 is reduced natively on the device Interop Backend-specific by nature. DLPack device types and pointer kinds differ per backend

To keep code portable, branch on declared capabilities rather than on backend names, as the test fixtures in conftest.py do:

from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend

be = get_backend()
dtype = tack.f64 if be.supports_f64 else tack.f32
use_block_sum = be.supports_workgroups
use_atomic_i64 = tack.i64 in be.supported_atomic_dtypes

test_backend_contract.py checks that the declarations match behavior. For example, it checks that f64 dispatch agrees with supports_f64, that reductions agree with supports_device_reductions, and that the memory spaces are self-consistent. See Conformance.

docs.title: Conformance and validation
docs.text:
A contract is only as good as the evidence that the implementation meets it. Tack has two kinds of evidence:

  • the test suite, which runs on every machine and exercises every backend that machine has
  • hardware validation, a recorded run of the full suite and the example sweeps on a named device at an exact commit

This page maps the contracts to their tests at release candidate 23d6e1d (with the modules added through b94af23), describes the oracles the tests trust, and gives the procedure for a hardware validation and the most recent status of each backend, recorded at 745e01f.

What counts as evidence

A CPU run does not validate GPU execution. A host-side syntax check of generated CUDA, HIP, MSL or OpenCL source shows that the source is well-formed, not that it runs correctly on a device. A skipped or deselected test is not a pass. Expected results come from independent oracles, never from recording what Tack currently outputs.

docs.title: How the suite is organized
docs.text:
pyproject.toml sets testpaths to the two packages' tests/ directories. The root conftest.py probes every backend once at import and provides capability fixtures, so which backends a test runs on depends on the machine, not on the test file:

Fixture Runs the test once per backend Available backend f64_backend Available backend with supports_f64 reduction_backend Available backend with supports_device_reductions workgroup_backend Available backend with supports_workgroups

Capability skips read the declared attributes described in Backend capabilities. They don't compare arch names. A backend that fails to initialize with ImportError, RuntimeError, OSError or AttributeError is left out of every fixture.

Three pytest markers are registered:

  • slow marks the example sweep in test_examples.py. It is deselected by default (addopts = "-m 'not slow'"). Run it with pytest -m slow.
  • timing marks tests in test_cpu_threading.py that assert what the CPU scheduler actually did. They skip themselves, and print the load, when the one-minute load average exceeds half the CPU backend's thread count. Let the load settle before a validation run so that they execute.
  • quick marks a module per area of the code, the inner-loop set (pytest -m quick -n 4). It selects; it does not deselect anything from a full run.

The root conftest.py sets TACK_CACHE=off unless the environment chooses a mode, so the suite compiles from scratch rather than reading the disk cache. pytest -n auto runs the suite across processes (pytest-xdist); each worker is a process with its own backends.

docs.title: Oracles
docs.text:
A test is only independent if its expected value doesn't come from the code under test. The suite uses these kinds of oracle:

Oracle Used for Example modules Plain arithmetic and NumPy Ordering, aliasing and control flow, where the answer is obvious by hand test_compiler_contract.py Serial Python execution of the same source Differential testing: the kernel body runs as ordinary Python over independent NumPy arrays, and every array is compared test_differential.py Python big integers Fixed-width wrapping, division, remainder, power and casts, computed exactly and then reduced modulo the width test_integer_semantics.py, test_integer_division.py, test_integer_expression_differential.py, test_division_and_power.py Exact rationals and correctly rounded sums Contraction and rounding (fractions.Fraction), and reduction error budgets (math.fsum) test_float_semantics.py, test_reduction_semantics.py Structural invariants Properties that must hold whatever the output, such as surface watertightness and analytic surfaces tack-vis/tests/test_dataset_filters.py, test_polyhedra.py Negative controls Show that an oracle can fail: a mutation reference with Tack's IR optimizations bypassed, a final-only wrapping oracle that a late-wrapping compiler would satisfy, and generator shapes that a device previously rejected test_compiler_contract.py, test_integer_expression_differential.py, test_opencl_compilation.py

Generated cases use fixed grammars and reproducible seeds. A failure report names the seed, backend and input, so it can be reproduced without rerunning the whole generator.

docs.title: Host compiler checks
docs.text:
Several modules compile generated GPU source on the host with Clang, as OpenCL C or C++ syntax checks, and some run host helpers under UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. The shared helper require_clang() in tests/compiler_tools.py picks the compiler:

  • TACK_CLANG selects the C/OpenCL driver. TACK_CLANGXX selects the C++ driver. Without TACK_CLANGXX, the C++ driver is the clang++ sibling of TACK_CLANG. If neither is set, the helper searches PATH for clang and then clang-23 through clang-14.
  • Each mode (opencl, cxx, ubsan) is preflighted with a real probe compile, and for ubsan a probe run. The probe result is cached per compiler and environment.
  • On an unconfigured machine, missing or unusable tooling skips the check. An explicit TACK_CLANG or TACK_CLANGXX, or TACK_REQUIRE_CLANG set to anything other than empty or 0, turns the same condition into a failure. An explicit choice that fails never falls back to another compiler on PATH.

Hardware validation runs with TACK_REQUIRE_CLANG=1, so these checks can't silently disappear.

docs.title: Examples and the validation harness
docs.text:
Example sweep. test_examples.py runs every numbered example in packages/*/examples/ as a subprocess with --arch $TACK_EXAMPLES_ARCH, which defaults to cpu. An example skips, with the reason, when it needs an optional third-party package or doesn't offer the selected backend. A missing tack module is a failure. The test is marked slow:

TACK_EXAMPLES_ARCH=cuda uv run --no-sync pytest -m slow -q -ra packages/tack-core/tests/test_examples.py

Harness. packages/tack-core/examples/validate_all.py runs seven workloads (vector add, SAXPY, reduction, Mandelbrot, N-body, Jacobi and matrix multiply). Each runs four times on fresh arrays, every call is verified, and the first and fastest warm times are printed. With --arch, the harness initializes exactly that backend, confirms that get_backend().name matches, and prints Backends: <arch>. Without --arch, it validates every backend it can initialize. test_validation_harness.py checks that the harness never discards a wrong result and never reports a backend it didn't run.

docs.title: Running a hardware validation
docs.text:
A hardware validation establishes that one exact commit meets the contracts on one named device. Run every step at the same hash, one job at a time.

  1. Pin the source. git rev-parse HEAD must print the full hash under test, and git status --short must be empty before and after.
  2. Prepare the environment. Unset TACK_NO_REINIT, because it suppresses backend switching and invalidates a multi-backend run. Set TACK_REQUIRE_CLANG=1 and TACK_CLANG to a working Clang. Use uv run --no-sync so that the installed backend extras are kept.

  3. Run the full suite with the backend required. Initialize the backend explicitly, assert that it is the one requested, and print it before pytest starts. A backend that silently fails to initialize would otherwise turn every device case into a skip:

    uv run --no-sync python - cuda <<'PYTEST'
import sys, pytest, tack
arch = sys.argv[1]
device = tack.set_default_device(arch)
assert device.type == arch
print('Required hardware backend:', device, flush=True)
raise SystemExit(pytest.main(['-q', '-ra']))
PYTEST

  4. Run both example sweeps, with TACK_EXAMPLES_ARCH=<backend> and with TACK_EXAMPLES_ARCH=cpu.

  5. Run the harness on both selections: validate_all.py --arch <backend> and validate_all.py --arch cpu. Each must print only the requested backend and report 7 of 7 workloads OK.
  6. Explain every skip. -ra lists them. Each must be a capability, an absent optional dependency, or an absent device, and the record says which. Confirm that the timing tests ran and didn't skip because of load.

For a focused run, prefer whole files to -k <backend>. -k is a substring match. For example, -k hip also selects test IDs that contain relationships, and a [hip-...] label doesn't guarantee that the case executed on the device. Pre-build rejections and source checks never launch.

Record the hash and clean status, the printed backend line, the device, driver, runtime and binding versions, the Python, NumPy and llvmlite versions, the load before the suite, the pass, skip and deselect counts, every skip reason, whether the timing tests ran, and the first failure if there was one. Don't waive a numerical failure with an expected-failure marker. Preserve its log and report it.

There is one exception: a defect in a vendor toolchain, shown with a reproducer that doesn't use Tack, after the generated source has been shown to be correct. Such a marker is strict, applies only to the toolchain releases that were shown to fail (ROCm 7.0 and 7.1, by the HIP runtime's major and minor version, for the case below), names the defect, and is listed in the backend's documentation. The only one so far is the ROCm 7.0.2 and 7.1.1 miscompile of generated integer seed 31 (see Backend Implementations).
