docs.title: Runtime API
docs.text:
This page is the contract for Tack's host-side surface: choosing devices, creating and moving arrays, reductions, sharing memory with other libraries, inspecting generated code, the decorators, and the rules for calling a kernel. Each entry gives the signature, what is guaranteed, what the caller must ensure, and which exception a violation raises. What a kernel computes is defined by the kernel language contract. What each backend supports is defined in Backend capabilities.

All statements describe release candidate 23d6e1d, updated for the queued launches, disk cache, debug mode and CPU pool merged through b94af23, and for the device model of bba0846. They use the labels defined in Contracts.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text: Defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/dispatch.py and re-exported as tack.device, tack.Device, tack.device_count, tack.set_default_device, tack.get_default_device, tack.set_debug, tack.sync and tack.sync_async.

docs.title: tack.device(spec="cpu", **options)
docs.text:
Returns the tack.Device that spec names. A Device passed as spec is returned as it is.

spec "cpu", "metal", "cuda", "hip" or "level_zero". The numbered types (cuda, hip, level_zero) also take "type:N", such as "cuda:1": device N as its runtime numbers it (the CUDA device ordinal, the HIP device id, the index among the first Level Zero driver's devices). A bare "cuda" or "hip" is the device the calling thread already uses: the device of a CUDA context another library made current on the thread, or HIP's current device (hipGetDevice()), else 0. "level_zero" means "level_zero:0". cpu and metal are written bare **options Forwarded to the backend constructor. Each option must be in that backend's device_options. CPU declares num_threads, which takes precedence over TACK_CPU_THREADS, and Level Zero declares external_context (the driver, device and context handles of a context owned by another library). The other backends declare none

Current behavior:

  • Without options, each (type, index) is made on first use and is the same Device on every later call. Its compiled kernels and its arrays are shared by everything that asks for it.
  • With options, every call makes a new device, which is not equal to the one without options or to another made with the same options.
  • Every device of cuda, hip and level_zero is reachable; tack.device_count(type) says how many there are. A bare spec is resolved at each call, so after another library changes the thread's device, "cuda" or "hip" names the other device.
  • Each CUDA device has its own context, and each Level Zero device its own context unless external_context names one. A CUDA context already current on the calling thread, such as one an embedding framework created, is adopted for its device and never destroyed. It must be current before the first call that names that device: the device is made once, so a context made current later is not adopted.
  • Otherwise Tack works in the device's primary context, the one the CUDA runtime and libraries on it use (PyTorch, CuPy, Warp), retained when the device is made and released, never destroyed, when the last backend on it goes. Made while no context is current, it stays current on that thread; made while another is current, it is not, and the thread keeps its own. As long as Tack holds one context and it is current where it was made, nothing is switched. Once it holds two, or a context is not current on the thread that made its device, every CUDA operation makes its own context current for its duration and restores the thread's afterwards. HIP does the same with its current device once a device other than 0, or two devices, are in use. See Calling a kernel.

Errors:

Condition Exception spec neither a string nor a Device TypeError: "a device is a Device or a string such as 'cpu' or 'cuda:0', not ..." Options with a Device TypeError: "options make a new device: pass a device spec, not a Device" Unknown type ValueError: "Unknown device type: 'vulkan'. Available: cpu, cuda, hip, level_zero, metal" A number on cpu or metal, or a non-numeric suffix ValueError: "'cpu:0' is not a device: write 'cpu'" (with "or 'cuda:N'" for numbered types) A device past the last ValueError: "cuda:2: this machine has 2 CUDA devices" (Level Zero: "the first Level Zero driver has ..."). Raised by the constructor, so it propagates unwrapped external_context with a number other than its device's ValueError: "level_zero:1: the external_context's device is level_zero:0; ..." Missing Python dependency (an ImportError from the backend module or constructor) RuntimeError: "Cannot start the 'hip' device: missing dependency." followed by the original error and install instructions. The original exception is chained Option not in device_options ValueError: "The 'metal' device does not accept the option(s) num_threads. Accepted: none." Raised after the backend module is imported, so a missing dependency is reported first Device or runtime failure (a RuntimeError from the constructor) RuntimeError: "Cannot start the 'cuda' device on Linux." followed by the original message and install instructions. Chained Any other constructor failure, such as ValueError for an incomplete external_context or a non-integer TACK_CPU_THREADS Propagates unwrapped

docs.title: tack.Device
docs.text: Member Meaning d.type "cpu", "metal", "cuda", "hip" or "level_zero" (the backend's name) d.index Which of the type's devices (the backend's ordinal): N in "cuda:N". A bare spec gives the device it resolved to, so str(tack.device("cuda")) may be "cuda:1". 0 for cpu and metal d.synchronize() Waits for every kernel launched on this device so far, and raises a queued launch's error str(d) The spec: "cuda:0" for numbered types, "cpu" and "metal" bare. repr(d) is Device('cuda:0') d == e True when both are the same backend; hashable on the same terms with d: Makes d the default device inside the block, on this thread only. Blocks nest; leaving one restores the previous default

docs.title: tack.device_count(type)
docs.text: Returns how many devices of type the machine has, without making any: tack.device(f"{type}:{n}") is valid for n below the count. The CPU counts 1, and Metal 1 where there is a Metal GPU. A type whose backend cannot load or start (a missing dependency, no driver) counts 0. An unknown type raises ValueError as tack.device does.

docs.title: tack.set_default_device(spec="cpu", **options)
docs.text:
Makes tack.device(spec, **options) the default device and returns it. The default device is where arrays are allocated when no device= is given, and where kernels with no arrays run. It is process-wide; a with block overrides it on its own thread.

Current behavior:

  • With nothing set, the default is the CPU, chosen at the first allocation, launch or get_default_device() call.
  • Without options, set_default_device builds nothing new: the device is the one tack.device(spec) always returns. Arrays made before a switch keep their device and keep working, and kernels given them run there (below). Compiled kernels survive a switch and back.
  • TACK_NO_REINIT: if a default is already set (including the CPU default picked by an earlier allocation or launch) and this variable is switched on, set_default_device returns the current default. It ignores spec and options, and it doesn't validate either. The variable is read by dispatch.env_flag: unset, empty, 0, false, no and off (in any case, ignoring surrounding spaces) mean off, and any other value means on. This exists for embedding, for example inside an ANARI device that shares the process.

Errors are those of tack.device. If the device cannot be made, the previous default stays.

docs.title: tack.get_default_device()
docs.text: Returns the default device: the innermost with block's on this thread, else the one set_default_device chose, else the CPU. tack.runtime.dispatch.get_backend() returns the same device's Backend.

docs.title: tack.set_default_float(dtype) and tack.get_default_float()
docs.text:
Defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/types.py. set_default_float makes dtype (tack.f32 or tack.f64, or a NumPy float type) the default float type and returns it; get_default_float returns it. It is f32 until set, and process-wide.

Current behavior:

  • It is the type of: empty, zeros and ones without a dtype; Python floats in array, full and arange; the components of vec, mat and vec2 ... mat4 without a component type; floats in tack.arrays' implicit arrays (ConstantArray, CountingArray, UniformCoordinates, CartesianProduct, Function, host values an array holds); and tack.dataset's constructors, sources and readers without a dtype (DataSet, uniform_grid, rectilinear_grid, point_cloud, wavelet, tangle, amr_gaussian_pulse, vtk_to_dataset, mfem_to_dataset, mfem_field). It is read when each is called.
  • A NumPy array keeps its type, a *_like its prototype's, and arrays already made keep theirs. vtk_to_dataset(dtype=None) keeps VTK's types.
  • Kernels are unchanged: scalar arguments, literals and casts are typed by the rules of the language contract, which follow the arrays a call passes. Library code chooses its types explicitly and doesn't depend on the setting.
  • Any other type raises TypeError. On a device without f64 (Metal), an array that the setting makes f64 is refused where it is made, and the message names the setting.

docs.title: Where arrays live and kernels run
docs.text:
• Every array records its device: a.device is a tack.Device. Every constructor takes device= (a Device or a spec): empty, zeros, ones, full, arange, array, asarray, array_from_ptr and memory_space, which default to the default device; empty_like, zeros_like, ones_like and full_like, which default to a Tack prototype's device; and from_dlpack, which defaults to the default device when that can wrap the tensor, else the tensor's own device.
  • a.to_device(device) returns a itself when its memory is usable on device, else a copy made through the host. tack.array(a, device=...) and tack.asarray(a, device=...) move a Tack array the same way.
  • Copies, astype, reshape, reductions, fill, concat (the first array's device) and textures stay on their array's device.
  • Launch placement: a kernel runs on the default device when that device can address all its arrays, or when it has none; otherwise on the arrays' own device. A device can address an array when both are in one memory domain (Backend.memory_domain): two CPU devices with different thread counts share one, so a default tack.device("cpu", num_threads=1) runs kernels on CPU arrays made before it. A @tack.device_class object's arrays choose the device when no plain array does, and must agree with it. tack.inspect makes the same choice.
  • Arrays in two memory domains raise ValueError: "Kernel 'k' was given arrays on two devices (cpu and cuda:0); a launch runs on one. Copy them to one device first (a.to_device(...))." The check runs on the dispatch fast path too.
  • tack.algorithms functions allocate their temporaries and launch on their first array argument's device. They, tack.copyto from a Tack array and tack.concat refuse arrays in two memory domains under their own name: "exclusive_scan() was given arrays on two devices (cpu and cuda:0); ...", not the name of an internal kernel.
  • An array holds its device, so a device's backend (and a CUDA context it created) lives at least as long as any of its arrays.

docs.title: tack.set_debug(enabled=True)
docs.text:
Turns debug mode on or off for every kernel launched from then on. TACK_DEBUG (a boolean flag, read like TACK_NO_REINIT) turns it on when Tack is imported. tack.runtime.dispatch.debug_enabled() reports the current setting.

Debug mode checks every index of every array access, one dimension at a time: an array's leading dimension against its length, the others against theirs, a flat index against the element count (a component count for a scalar atomic on a vector array), and a local or shared array index against its size. Constant tables and textures clamp and are not checked.

  • An access with an index outside its extent is not performed: a load gives 0 of its type, an atomic's value is 0, and a store or atomic does nothing. The rest of the launch runs.
  • After the launch, Kernel.__call__ raises IndexError for the first violation it recorded: the kernel (and the device function an access was inlined from), the file, line and column, the access as written, the index, its dimension when there are several, the extent, and how many more accesses were skipped. Which violation is first is unspecified when several threads go out of bounds.
  • Kernels lower and compile separately in debug mode, and the extents are run-time arguments: debug mode compiles no variant per array length. Each launch is checked when it returns, which on the GPU backends means waiting for it, since their launches are otherwise queued. Launches from different threads report their own violations.
  • tack.inspect shows the code a debug launch runs.

Implemented in lang/ir_bounds.py (the checks and guards), runtime/debug_bounds.py (the hidden arguments and the error) and the code generators (codegen/bounds.py, llvm_gen.py).

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text: tack.Array is defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/array.py. Its dtype describes one scalar, vector or matrix element; shape is the array's dimensions, excluding component dimensions. size counts elements. scalar_dtype, scalar_size and storage_shape describe the scalar storage. The buffer belongs to the array's device (a.device; see Where arrays live and kernels run). tack.dataset.Field is a separate class coupling a space with coefficient values.

docs.title: Creation
docs.text:
Function Contract tack.empty(shape, dtype=f32, *, device=None, exportable=False) Allocates on device, by default the default device. An int shape becomes a 1-tuple. exportable=True requests memory that can be exported without a copy (CUDA only) tack.zeros(shape, dtype=f32, *, device=None), tack.ones(...), tack.full(shape, fill_value, dtype=None, *, device=None) empty() followed by fill(). zeros skips the fill where the buffer starts zeroed (starts_zeroed: a new Metal buffer, which Metal clears; not one reused from its pool). full without a dtype makes f32 from a Python float and i32 from an int (i64 if the value needs it); a sequence fill_value needs an element dtype tack.arange([start,] stop[, step], dtype=None, *, device=None) Built in NumPy and copied in. Without a dtype, integer arguments give i32 (i64 if a value needs it) and a float argument gives f32 tack.array(obj, dtype=None, *, device=None) Copies values into independent storage. Without dtype, uses all input dimensions; a NumPy array keeps its dtype, Python floats give f32 and Python ints i32 (i64 if a value needs it). An element dtype consumes matching trailing component dimensions; a mismatch raises ValueError. Existing Tack arrays copy on their device, or through the host to another device tack.asarray(obj, dtype=None, *, device=None) obj itself when it is a Tack array, dtype is None or equals its dtype, and device is None or can address it; otherwise a converted or moved array tack.empty_like(prototype, dtype=None, *, device=None) Allocates independent, writable storage on device, by default a Tack prototype's device (else the default device), without reading or copying values. Accepts a NumPy array or Tack array; takes its dtype unless overridden. A scalar override of a vector/matrix prototype keeps the element dimensions. NumPy arrays produce scalar arrays with the array's shape. Contents are unspecified tack.zeros_like, tack.ones_like, tack.full_like(prototype, fill_value, dtype=None) empty_like() followed by fill(), as for zeros, ones and full tack.concat(arrays) A new 1-D array holding all elements in order, copied on the first array's device tack.texture3d(array, shape=None, interp="linear") A Texture3D holding a copy of the array taken at creation, for sample(u, v, w) in kernels. tex.update() copies the array again. See Textures

Current behavior:

  • A new array's contents are unspecified until a kernel, tack.copyto or fill writes them (the language contract); use tack.zeros for zeros. The CPU leaves a new array untouched, so that the kernel that writes it touches its pages first; the GPU backends currently zero new buffers, which is not a promise.
  • On the CPU, a fill of 256 KiB or more runs as a kernel through the dispatch, in parallel when the threading policy fans it out, and stores and refuses exactly what ndarray.fill would.
  • An array is made only of a dtype in its device's supported_dtypes: empty (and every constructor, copy and to_device built on it), array_from_ptr and DLPack imports raise TypeError otherwise, so an f64 array cannot be made on Metal. The dispatch check still rejects an array a kernel's backend cannot take.
  • There is no tack.fields() function.
  • Vector/matrix arrays expose their array shape and element dtype on both host and device. numpy() appends component dimensions.

Required caller constraints:

  • dtype is a Tack scalar or element type, or anything np.dtype() accepts that maps to a Tack scalar type (np.float32, "int64"; float means f64, as in NumPy). Other values raise TypeError.
  • Shapes contain integer, nonnegative extents. Noninteger extents raise TypeError; negative extents raise ValueError.

Errors:

Condition Exception A dtype, given or inferred, that has no Tack type, such as float16 TypeError: "Unsupported numpy dtype: float16" Boolean host values without a dtype TypeError: "Tack has no boolean arrays; ..." empty_like (or another *_like) with a prototype other than a NumPy array or Tack array TypeError: "expected a Tack array or NumPy array as the prototype" concat([]) ValueError concat with mixed dtypes TypeError texture3d on an array that isn't f32 ValueError: "texture3d requires an f32 array, got f64; convert it first with array.astype(tack.f32)" texture3d without a 3-D shape ValueError: "texture3d requires a 3D shape" texture3d with a shape whose W*H*D differs from the array's size ValueError naming both element counts texture3d with interp other than "linear" ValueError: "texture3d supports interp='linear' only, ..."

docs.title: Host operations
docs.text:
Operation Guarantee Errors tack.copyto(a, src) With host src (a NumPy array, sequence or scalar): converts it to a's scalar dtype with np.asarray, an unchecked cast, and copies it in. Its shape must be a.numpy()'s shape or broadcast to it, as in np.copyto; a flat array is not accepted for a vector or matrix array. Works on reshaped views. With a Tack array src of the same shape and scalar count on a's device: a device copy (src.to_device(a.device) brings one from another device) RuntimeError if a is read-only. ValueError "copyto() into an array whose values have shape (8,): cannot broadcast shape (4,)", for a Tack src of another shape, or "copyto() was given arrays on two devices ..." for one on another device. TypeError if a is not a Tack array a.numpy(), np.asarray(a) Returns a new NumPy array with the scalar component dtype and component axes appended to a.shape. Never a view, including on Metal; np.asarray(a, copy=False) raises ValueError — a.fill(value) Sets every element to a scalar, or, for a vector or matrix array, to one element's components RuntimeError if read-only. TypeError for a sequence on a scalar array; ValueError for a sequence of the wrong element shape a[i], a[i, j], a[()] Reads one element: a Python number, or a NumPy array for a vector or matrix element. a[()] reads a 0-d array, as in NumPy. There is no host assignment: a[i] = x and iteration raise TypeError TypeError for anything but one integer per dimension, including a[None], whose message names a[()]; IndexError out of range a.reshape(*shape) A metadata-only view that shares the buffer, the element type, the writability and any DLPack hold. Takes a tuple or separate integers; one extent may be -1 ValueError if the element count differs or more than one extent is -1 a.copy() / a.astype(dtype) A new array on a's device, filled by a device copy kernel. astype converts with the kernel language's conversion rules; a scalar dtype keeps a vector or matrix element's dimensions Kernel errors, if any. TypeError if astype would change element dimensions a.shape, a.ndim, a.size, len(a), a.nbytes shape, ndim and size count elements, not components. len is shape[0]. nbytes is the storage in bytes TypeError from len of a 0-d array a.export_memory() Returns an ExportedMemory handle for cross-API sharing. On CUDA, an array allocated without exportable=True is copied once into exportable memory, so the export is a snapshot RuntimeError on CPU, HIP and Level Zero

Current behavior: on Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero a kernel call returns once the launch is queued, not once it has run. Host operations keep this invisible: numpy, a[i] and reductions wait for the launches before them; copyto and fill take effect after them (on CUDA, HIP and Level Zero they are queued in order; on Metal they wait first). A queued launch's error, such as a device fault, is raised at the next wait rather than by its own call. An array dropped while a queued launch uses it is freed after that launch.

Required caller constraint: an array is synchronized at kernel-call and host-operation boundaries only. Host reads and writes between calls are safe. Host access during a call from another thread is not. Memory that another library reads or writes without a Tack call in between must be ordered with tack.sync(), except where Tack does it: a DLPack export and a wrapped pointer make every launch that uses them complete before it returns (see DLPack).

docs.title: tack.sync()
docs.text:
Defined in runtime/dispatch.py (sync). Waits until every kernel launched so far, on every device, has finished, by calling each backend's Backend.synchronize(); a no-op on the CPU, whose launches complete before returning. d.synchronize() waits for one device. Most code never needs it, since reading an array waits already. It is for timing kernels, and for memory shared with another library that reads it without Tack. It raises the error of a queued launch that failed.

tack.sync_async() (runtime/aio.py) is the asyncio form, for every device as tack.sync is: awaited, it waits in one of Tack's worker threads for the launches made before the call, not for later ones, and raises a queued launch's error at the await, after waiting for the other devices; await a.numpy_async() does the same for a read. A backend waits off the loop through Backend.async_marker(); without one (the CPU), the wait is inline.

docs.title: Reductions
docs.text:
f.sum(), f.min(), f.max() and f.mean() reduce every element and return a Python float. Integer arrays included.

sum min / max mean Empty array 0.0 ValueError: "min reduction requires a nonempty array" nan Path On the device when the array's device has supports_device_reductions and the array is f32. Otherwise NumPy on the host same sum() / size in host binary64

Accumulation precision, NaN and signed-zero rules, permitted reordering and the error budget are Required items of the reduction contract. A reduction runs on the array's device, whatever the default.

docs.title: tack.array_from_ptr(ptr, shape, dtype, *, device=None, writable=False)
docs.text:
Wraps existing memory as an array without copying. shape counts elements; dtype may be an element type such as tack.vec3(). Tack never frees it.

Backend What ptr must be CPU An integer address or a NumPy array Metal An MTLBuffer object. Any other value raises TypeError ("the Metal backend wraps an MTLBuffer object, not int ...") CUDA, HIP A device address: an int, or anything int() accepts, such as a NumPy integer or a CUdeviceptr Level Zero A USM device or shared address in the same forms, allocated in Tack's context

Guarantee: on a backend that declares device_memory_spaces (CUDA, HIP and Level Zero), every pointer is converted with as_address (runtime/kernel_utils.py) and classified with memory_space(). A value that isn't an address raises TypeError ("array_from_ptr() on the CUDA backend takes a device address ..."), and a pointer outside those spaces raises ValueError ("Pointer is in 'cpu' memory but the device is 'CUDA'. ..."). On Level Zero the driver answers for pointers from any context on the device, so the check can't detect a pointer from a different context.

Guarantee: an array created with writable=False, the default, is read-only on the host and in kernels. fill() and tack.copyto() raise RuntimeError. A dispatch that binds it to a parameter the kernel may store to, or use as an atomic target, raises ValueError before the launch: "Kernel 'k': parameter 'out' may be written, but its array is read-only. ...". A parameter whose stores can't be traced counts as written.

Required caller constraints:

  • Keep the memory alive and unmoved for the array's lifetime.
  • Provide at least prod(shape) * itemsize contiguous bytes.

docs.title: tack.memory_space(ptr, *, device=None)
docs.text: Delegates to device's memory_space() (by default the default device's). CPU and Metal always answer "cpu". CUDA answers "cuda", "cuda_pinned", "cuda_managed" or "cpu". HIP answers "hip", "hip_pinned", "hip_managed" or "cpu". Level Zero answers "level_zero" or "cpu". A value that can't be a 64-bit address answers "cpu" without querying the driver. On Level Zero, a failed driver query raises RuntimeError instead of being reported as host memory.

docs.title: DLPack
docs.text:
Defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/dlpack.py.

Export: Array.__dlpack__(*, stream=None, max_version=None, dl_device=None, copy=None) and Array.__dlpack_device__().

  • Zero-copy. The capsule keeps the array alive until the consumer calls the deleter.
  • A consumer passing max_version >= (1, 0) receives a versioned capsule that carries the read-only flag for non-writable arrays. The legacy capsule can't express read-only.
  • The device type is kDLCPU on CPU and Metal, kDLCUDA on CUDA, kDLROCM on HIP, and kDLOneAPI on Level Zero. The device id is always 0.
  • Strides are C-contiguous. All ten Tack dtypes are exported.
  • copy=True raises BufferError. stream and dl_device are ignored.
  • On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero the export waits for the launches queued so far, and from then on every launch that uses the array completes before it returns (DeviceBuffer.share()), so the consumer may read the memory at once and after later launches.

Import: tack.from_dlpack(source, *, device=None, copy=False). The array belongs to device. By default that is the default device when it can wrap the tensor, else the tensor's own device, as the array API's from_dlpack keeps an array on its device: CUDA memory imported with the CPU as default is a CUDA array, and host memory imported with Metal as default (which cannot wrap a host pointer) is a CPU array. Neither is copied.

  • source is a capsule or an object with __dlpack__. A versioned capsule is requested first.
  • With copy=False, the array shares the tensor's memory and holds the capsule until the array and every view of it are collected. Then the producer's deleter runs exactly once.
  • A read-only versioned tensor produces a non-writable array, which host writes and kernel stores refuse as for array_from_ptr.
  • As for array_from_ptr, a launch that uses the imported array completes before it returns.
  • With copy=True, the source is read through np.from_dlpack and copied into a new array with tack.array. That works only for sources that NumPy can read on the host.
Condition Exception Capsule already consumed ValueError Null data pointer ValueError Non-C-contiguous strides ValueError: "only C-contiguous tensors can be wrapped without copying; ..." DLPack dtype without a Tack type, or lanes != 1 TypeError Unknown device type ValueError kDLMetal tensor ValueError: "Metal DLPack tensors (kDLMetal) cannot be imported: ..." Device type that device can't wrap RuntimeError naming the backend and the device type, followed by dlpack_refusal_note Wrapped pointer outside device_memory_spaces ValueError from array_from_ptr

Current behavior: Metal has no zero-copy import. Host tensors (kDLCPU) are refused with an explanation, because wrapping a host pointer as an MTLBuffer without a copy needs page alignment. kDLMetal tensors are refused up front on every backend, because their data is an opaque MTLBuffer handle plus a byte offset, which nothing in Tack can wrap yet. On Metal, use copy=True with a host tensor.

docs.title: VTK
docs.text:
tack.interop.vtk (package tack-vis) provides vtk_to_array(vtk_array, flatten=False), array_to_vtk(array, n_components=None, name=None) and init_level_zero(). Both directions are zero-copy through DLPack and need VTK with vtkmodules.util.dlpack_support. Without it they raise RuntimeError. array_to_vtk validates the layout before importing VTK and raises ValueError for a contradictory n_components or for arrays with more than two dimensions.

Required for Level Zero: start Tack with tack.interop.vtk.init_level_zero() instead of tack.set_default_device("level_zero"). It makes a Level Zero device in the context that VTK's device uses the default, and returns it, so that Tack allocates there. Exporting an array of a Level Zero device in another context, or importing while the default Level Zero device is in one, raises RuntimeError. The check is necessary because the driver accepts pointers from any context. See Interoperability.

docs.title: Communication between blocks
docs.text:
Defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/. A guide: Communicate Between Blocks.

Blocks and worlds. Blocks(devices, world=None) holds this rank's blocks, one per entry of devices. Global ids run over every rank's blocks, contiguous by rank (rank 0's first), and Blocks.local is the range of this rank's. World() is one process; World(comm, gpu_aware=False) takes an mpi4py communicator, or any object with Dup, Get_rank, Get_size, allgather, alltoall, Isend and Irecv, and communicates on comm.Dup(), so its messages never meet the caller's. Tack imports no MPI module.

  • Collective. Every call -- the Blocks, Plan and Routing constructors, exchange, all_gather, all_reduce, exclusive_scan, link_by_bounds, Plan.run, Routing.send, Routing.reply, sort_by_key -- is made by every rank of the world, in the same order. Arguments keyed by global id name only this rank's blocks; the collectives and Routing need an entry for every one of them.
  • Independent of the assignment. all_reduce, all_gather and exclusive_scan combine in order of global id, so their results, a floating-point sum's bits included, do not depend on which rank holds which block. exchange returns each block's messages in order of source; sort_by_key and Routing decide by global id too.
  • Exchange. exchange({source: {destination: {name: Array}}}) returns {destination: {source: {name: Array}}} for every block on this rank, an empty dict where nothing came. A sent array is on its source block's device; a received one on its destination block's, the sent array itself where that device addresses its memory, so a sender must not write to what it sent. Element types and shapes arrive as sent. Every MPI request is complete when exchange returns.
  • Transport. Between ranks, a world stages each rank pair's arrays through one host buffer. With gpu_aware=True it hands MPI the arrays themselves through DLPack, or a device copy in Backend.allocate_mpi_array's memory where Backend.mpi_direct says the MPI may not take them (CUDA's and HIP's stream-ordered pools), and receives into such memory. A GPU-aware MPI uses the device current when MPI starts: make the rank's device before importing mpi4py.MPI.
  • Plans. Plan(blocks, sends, receives) checks, across ranks, that every send has a receive of its length and the other way round. Plan.run(values) writes received elements in place and leaves the others; a block sending to itself reads before anything is written.
  • Routing. A point is asked of every block whose box holds it, with a relative slack of 1e-6, and goes to the block whose holds gives the highest rank, the lowest block on a tie, or nowhere (-1) where every rank is 0. Coordinates travel as f64 bits. send delivers in order of origin block and then of the points there; reply answers in that order, zero for a point that went nowhere.
  • Sorting. sort_by_key takes one-dimensional i32, u32, i64 or u64 keys of one type on every block. Block 0 ends with the smallest keys, each block ascending; every copy of a key ends on one block; the sort is stable, by block and then index.
Condition Exception A global id out of range, or naming another rank's block where this rank's is needed ValueError A collective or Routing missing an entry for one of this rank's blocks ValueError A message or value that is not a dict of names to Tack arrays, or a structure of arrays TypeError An array not on its block's device ValueError A Plan whose sends and receives disagree in length across blocks ValueError Plan.run with element types that differ between blocks TypeError sort_by_key keys of another type, or of different types on different blocks TypeError all_reduce with an operation other than "sum", "min" or "max" ValueError World(gpu_aware=True) without a communicator ValueError

docs.title: tack.inspect(kernel, *args, mode="source")
docs.text:
Defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/inspect_kernel.py. Runs the compilation pipeline for these arguments on the device a call would run on (see launch placement) and returns a string. It doesn't execute the kernel, doesn't compile a GPU variant, and doesn't populate the backend's variant cache.

mode Returns "ir" Tack IR after resolution, inference, scalar localization, optimization and type annotation (ir.dump), before GPU scalar packing "source" The backend's source. On CPU, LLVM IR for the variant these arguments would select, including the disjoint-array specialization. On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, MSL, CUDA C, HIP C or OpenCL C after scalar packing "optimized" CPU only: the LLVM module after the backend's O3 pipeline. On any other backend it raises ValueError ("inspect mode 'optimized' is CPU only: ..."), after the kernel's own checks have run, because the GPU backends' optimizers run inside vendor compilers whose output is never shown

Guarantees: inspection enforces the same dtype, workgroup-support, atomic, alignment, participation and workgroup launch-count checks as dispatch, and it raises the frontend's errors. It records texture extents through the backend's _store_texture_shapes(), so on HIP and Level Zero devices without texture hardware the source it shows uses software sampling, as dispatch would. See the note on inspection for the dispatch checks it skips.

Errors: TypeError "Expected a @tack.kernel, got function" when the first argument isn't a Kernel. ValueError "Unknown inspect mode: 'ptx'. Use 'ir', 'source', or 'optimized'." Unlike dispatch, inspection doesn't wrap errors. For example, a workgroup primitive on CPU raises NotImplementedError directly, and an unsupported array dtype raises the dtype check's TypeError.

docs.title: @tack.kernel
docs.text:
Returns a Kernel (lang/kernel.py). Decoration reads the function's source with read_source (lang/func.py, a wrapper around inspect.getsource) and parses it. Current behavior: nothing is validated or compiled at decoration. Source validation, name resolution and lowering happen at the first dispatch or inspection, and their errors are raised there.

Condition Exception, and when Source isn't readable (exec(), a bare REPL, python -c before Python 3.13) RuntimeError at decoration, which explains where kernels must be defined Unsupported construct, including calls to functions that aren't statically bound @tack.funcs or intrinsics UnsupportedSyntaxError at first dispatch or inspection: "Kernel 'k': unsupported Assert at line 4, column 9". Lines refer to the dedented captured source Free name that is neither a parameter nor assigned NameError at first dispatch or inspection, naming the kernel or inlined device function and its position

docs.title: @tack.func
docs.text:
Returns a Func (lang/func.py) that is inlined at each call site in a kernel. Device-function binding, return restructuring and recursion rejection are Required items of the language contract. See Source and supported constructs.

Condition Exception Decorating something that isn't a def, such as a lambda TypeError at decoration Source isn't readable RuntimeError at decoration, the same explanation as for kernels, naming the device function. The OSError is chained Calling the function from Python RuntimeError: "@tack.func 'f' cannot be called from Python. ..."

docs.title: @tack.device_class
docs.text:
@tack.device_class (lang/device_class.py) marks a class so that its instances can be passed as kernel arguments, and it collects the class's @tack.func methods. When an instance is passed:

Attribute Becomes Recompiles when changed? Class-level int or float defined on the class itself A compile-time constant Yes. The value, with its type and float bit pattern, is part of the key Instance attribute that shadows such a class attribute A compile-time constant with the instance's value Yes Instance int or float A runtime scalar parameter Only when its inferred type changes. The attribute names are in the key, and the values are not Instance Array An extra array parameter Only when dtype, shape or vector width changes Names starting with _, and attributes of other types Ignored —

Calling a method that isn't a @tack.func, or referencing a self. attribute that is none of the above, raises ValueError at first dispatch. Specializations are keyed on the class object itself, so two classes with the same name don't share variants. When a class is garbage collected, its variants are dropped.

Instances are recognized by argument type (the class's _device_class flag), so a parameter that takes one needs no annotation.

docs.title: Calling a kernel
docs.text:
Kernel.__call__(*args) dispatches on the device its arrays choose (see launch placement) and returns None, or, for a kernel that ends in an annotated return, that value, read from a hidden one-element array (which waits for the launch). On the CPU the call returns after the kernel completes; on the GPU backends once it is queued (see Host operations).

Arguments, matched positionally against the parameters:

Argument Treated as Array An array parameter. Its dtype must be in supported_dtypes Texture3D A sampled texture parameter. The kernel samples the texture's own copy, not its array int, bool or NumPy integer A scalar: i32 if it fits, else i64, else u64. Outside the u64 range raises TypeError float or NumPy floating A scalar: f64 if any array argument is f64, otherwise f32. Textures are always f32. A NumPy float64 with only f32 arrays becomes f32 @tack.device_class instance Expanded as described above Anything else TypeError: "Unsupported argument type for parameter 'a': "

Current behavior:

  • Changing a scalar's value never recompiles. Changing its inferred type, an array's dtype or vector width, a baked shape dimension, or a texture extent compiles a new variant. See Specialization and compilation identity.
  • One kernel may be dispatched from several threads concurrently. Each thread's dispatch uses its own arguments. On CUDA and HIP, dispatches of the same compiled variant are serialized by a per-variant lock, KernelVariant.dispatch_lock, held from packing the scalars until the launch is queued, so different variants still dispatch concurrently. Metal launches own their argument buffer and scalars and are encoded one at a time under the backend's batch lock. Level Zero serializes all launches, reductions and copies on one backend lock (_launch_lock). CPU binds arguments per call and takes no lock, but fan-outs through its JIT'd pool run one at a time. test_concurrent_dispatch.py covers this.
  • Required caller constraint: on CUDA with one device in use, Tack's context is current only on the thread that made the device (the first tack.device("cuda"), set_default_device("cuda") or allocation on it). Another thread must make it current, for example with cuCtxSetCurrent(backend._context), before dispatching. Otherwise the launch fails with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CONTEXT. Once Tack switches contexts (two devices; see Devices), every operation makes its own context current, from any thread.

Rejected:

  • Keyword arguments. resolve_variant raises NotImplementedError("Keyword arguments not supported in kernels"), which reaches the caller as RuntimeError: "Kernel 'k' failed on CPUBackend: Keyword arguments not supported in kernels".
  • A wrong argument count. TypeError: "Kernel 'k' expects 2 arguments, got 1". Arguments are counted after template expansion.
  • A read-only array where the kernel may store. ValueError before the launch. See Pointer interop.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Read by Effect TACK_CPU_THREADS CPUBackend.__init__ CPU worker count. Read each time a CPU backend is constructed, unless tack.device("cpu", num_threads=...) gives one. Values below 1 become 1. 1 runs everything on the calling thread. A non-integer raises ValueError from tack.device TACK_CPU_POLICY CPUBackend.__init__ Accepted for old scripts only: unset, empty or v2, the one threading policy since v1 was removed. Any other value, v1 included, raises ValueError from tack.device TACK_CPU_MARGIN CPUBackend.__init__ Float override of the threading decision's safety margin TACK_CPU_POOL CPUBackend.__init__ python (or 0, off, no, false) fans out through a ThreadPoolExecutor instead of the JIT'd pool, which is the default wherever it can be made (not on Windows) TACK_CPU_POOL_SPIN The JIT'd pool, when it is made How many pause iterations a pool worker spins before sleeping (default 20000). For experiments TACK_CPU_MALLOC CPUBackend.__init__ Linux. A boolean flag read like TACK_NO_REINIT. When on, the first CPU backend sets glibc's malloc thresholds so freed blocks keep their pages (cpu._tune_malloc), process-wide. Off by default TACK_DEBUG import tack (runtime/dispatch.py) A boolean flag read like TACK_NO_REINIT: turns on debug mode's bounds checks. tack.set_debug overrides it (above) TACK_NO_REINIT tack.set_default_device A boolean flag (dispatch.env_flag): when on, set_default_device leaves an existing default alone. 0, false, no, off and empty mean off. See above TACK_CACHE The disk cache, at the first kernel compiled write (default), read, bundle (default under MPI) or off; also 0, false, no, none for off. Any other value raises ValueError. See The Kernel Cache TACK_CACHE_SIZE The disk cache, at the first kernel compiled The most the entries of every Tack version may take: bytes, a size such as 500M or 2G (binary units), or unlimited; default 1G. Past it, a process that stores entries deletes the least recently used, at most once an hour. Any other value raises ValueError TACK_CACHE_DIR The disk cache, at the first kernel compiled The cache directory. Default: the platform's per-user cache directory. It must belong to the user and be writable by nobody else, or it is not used (with a RuntimeWarning) TACK_DUMP_MSL Metal kernel compilation Metal only. A boolean flag read like TACK_NO_REINIT. When on, writes each compiled kernel's MSL to /tmp/tack_<entry>.msl and prints the path. A variant loaded from the disk cache is not generated, so not dumped. Other backends ignore it. Use tack.inspect instead TACK_REQUIRE_CLANG Test suite (tests/compiler_tools.py) Any value other than empty or 0 turns missing or unusable Clang tooling into a test failure instead of a skip TACK_CLANG, TACK_CLANGXX Test suite An explicit Clang driver for OpenCL/C and C++ host checks. An explicit choice that fails its preflight is a failure, and there is no fallback to PATH TACK_EXAMPLES_ARCH Test suite (tests/test_examples.py) Backend for the slow example sweep. The default is cpu

The CPU threading variables are tuning controls, not part of the language contract. They change scheduling and never change results of race-free programs. See CPU Threading Policy.

docs.title: tack.cache
docs.text:
Function Effect configure(directory=None, mode=None, max_size=None) Sets the directory, mode and size limit for this process over TACK_CACHE_DIR, TACK_CACHE and TACK_CACHE_SIZE; None leaves one to the environment. Takes effect at the next kernel compiled settings() (directory, mode, MPI rank or None) as they apply now size_limit() The size limit in bytes as it applies now, or None for no limit load_bundle(path=None, comm=None) Reads a bundle (by default the directory's, for this Tack version) into the process. With an mpi4py communicator it is collective: rank 0 reads and broadcasts. Returns the number of entries pack(directory=None) Writes this Tack version's entries into one bundle file; returns (path, count) prune(directory=None, max_size=None) Deletes the least recently used entries of every Tack version until they take at most 90% of max_size (default: the size limit), and abandoned temporary files; keeps bundles. Returns (files removed, bytes left) clear(directory=None, all_versions=False) Deletes this Tack version's entries and bundle, or every version's (only the names the cache makes); returns the number of files removed describe(directory=None) The settings, entry count, size and bundle, as a dict stats(), reset_stats() Hit, miss and write counters for this process

python -m tack.cache info | pack | prune [--max-size SIZE] | clear [--all] runs the same from a shell.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
Tack defines one exception class of its own, UnsupportedSyntaxError (lang/source_validation.py). It subclasses NotImplementedError, which in Python subclasses RuntimeError.

Kernel.__call__ translates exceptions as follows:

  • It re-raises UnsupportedSyntaxError unchanged.
  • It re-raises a TypeError as a TypeError prefixed with Kernel '<name>':, unless the message already starts with that name, so the kernel is named once.
  • It re-raises any other RuntimeError, including NotImplementedError, as RuntimeError("Kernel '<name>' failed on <BackendClass>: ..."), dropping an inner Kernel '<name>': prefix. For compiler failures, it uses a short "failed to compile" form that lists the error lines.
  • It passes everything else through unchanged, notably ValueError and NameError.

Translated exceptions keep the original as __cause__.

Exception Raised for Where UnsupportedSyntaxError Syntax outside the kernel language, in a kernel or a device function, including unreachable statements; a kernel without exactly one parallel loop directly in its body; a store, atomic, barrier, block reduction or print outside the parallel loop, including through an inlined device function or template method First dispatch or inspection (frontend) NameError A name that is neither a parameter nor assigned. Kernels don't capture Python globals First dispatch or inspection (frontend) TypeError A device spec that is neither a string nor a Device, options with a Device, argument count or type, an integer outside 64 bits, an array dtype unsupported by the backend (when made, and at dispatch), an unsupported atomic dtype or target, the MSL generator receiving f64, inspect of a non-kernel, @tack.func on a non-function, a dtype argument that is neither a Tack type nor a NumPy dtype with a Tack type, array, empty_like or DLPack dtypes, an invalid *_like prototype, concat dtypes, copyto into a non-array, host element assignment or iteration, a non-MTLBuffer on Metal, an array_from_ptr pointer that isn't an address on CUDA, HIP or Level Zero Dispatch (cold), inspection, host calls ValueError Unknown device type, device number or option, arrays on two devices in one launch, an unknown TACK_CPU_POLICY, incomplete external_context, workgroup participation, launch counts or device group size, a launch or reduction larger than one grid can index, atomic alignment, a read-only array the kernel may store to, array_from_ptr memory space, shape mismatches (including copyto shapes that do not broadcast), reshape, texture3d arguments, empty min/max, empty concat, unknown inspect mode or "optimized" off CPU, template method or attribute errors, malformed or kDLMetal DLPack tensors Device creation, dispatch (cold or every call), inspection, host calls NotImplementedError Workgroup primitives on CPU, keyword arguments, and the few lowering checks that source validation doesn't already report as UnsupportedSyntaxError Raised directly by inspection. Current behavior: every dispatch rejection listed on this page and in Backend capabilities is raised before the kernel launches, so a rejected call leaves array storage unchanged. test_workgroup_contract.py tests this property for workgroup rejections, test_atomic_contract.py for alignment, test_launch_limits.py for oversized launches, and test_outside_parallel_loop.py for effects outside the parallel loop.

docs.title: Design and Implementation
docs.text:
This section explains how Tack works and why it is built the way it is. It is written for contributors, and for advanced users who want to understand what happens between a @tack.kernel call and the machine code that runs.

Each page covers one part of the system at three levels:

  • Design: the problem, the approach taken, the alternatives that were rejected, and the tradeoffs accepted.
  • Implementation: the modules, classes, functions, data structures and algorithms involved, and the order in which they run. Source locations are given as file paths plus function or class names.
  • Contract: what the part guarantees, what it requires of callers, and what happens when a requirement is violated (which exception, raised where).

docs.title: How this section relates to the others
docs.text:
Section Answers Use it when Contracts What is guaranteed: the kernel language contract, backend capabilities, the runtime API, and how conformance is tested you need to know whether a behavior can be relied on Design and Implementation (this section) Why it is designed this way and how it is implemented you need to understand, review or change a part of the system Developer's Guide How to carry out a task: module layout, each compiler stage, adding a feature you are about to make a change and want a walkthrough

Where a design page and the normative kernel language contract disagree, the contract states the intended behavior and the code shows the current behavior. The design pages describe the code and point out such gaps.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
Start with Principles; most later decisions follow from it. Then read Compilation Pipeline and Specialization and Caching together: between them they describe the life of every kernel call. The remaining pages can be read in any order, as the topic requires.

flowchart LR
    P[Principles] --> CP[Compilation Pipeline]
    CP --> SC[Specialization and Caching]
    SC --> NS[Numerical Semantics]
    SC --> PE[Parallel Execution]
    SC --> MA[Memory and Aliasing]
    PE --> CT[CPU Threading Policy]
    MA --> BI[Backend Implementations]
    BI --> VW[Vendor Workarounds]
    BI --> IO[Interoperability]
    IO --> DA[Dataset API]
    DA --> PH[Polyhedra]

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
Array API. Typed backend storage, element dtypes, logical array shape, NumPy transfer semantics, and the distinction from dataset fields.

Principles. The ideas the rest of the system follows: Python syntax with Tack's own semantics; translate or reject, never silently drop; one kernel source with backend capabilities declared rather than probed; specialization with a cache key that names everything specialized on; correctness by default, with faster paths only where a per-call check justifies them; runtime policies measured rather than hard-coded; and independent oracles as the definition of correctness. Each principle comes with its costs.

Compilation Pipeline. The end-to-end path from Kernel.__call__ through resolve_variant, template rewrite, source validation, the AST transform and device-function inlining, the immutable IR template, the per-variant passes, verification at every pass boundary, code generation and native compilation, to dispatch. For each stage: its input and output, the invariants it establishes, what it rejects and with which exception, and whether it runs on a cache hit.

Specialization and Caching. What a compiled variant is and exactly what goes into its key: argument types and categories, vector widths, texture extents, template structure and constants, the shape signature of dimensions baked into code, and the CPU disjoint-arrays bit, and how debug mode's checked kernels are kept apart. It covers cache structure, lifetime and thread safety, the dispatch fast path that skips key derivation for a repeated call, the correctness argument behind the key, worked examples of which calls reuse a variant and which recompile, how to avoid unnecessary variants, and the disk cache that keeps lowered and compiled kernels across processes.

Numerical Semantics. How Tack implements its numerical rules: fixed-width integer types and promotion, division and power, floating-point precision and exceptional values, the compiler settings that keep fast math off, and reductions.

Parallel Execution. The execution model: one top-level parallel iteration space, sequential inner loops, ordering within an iteration, workgroups, barriers, block reductions and atomics, and how each backend maps them onto threads or grids.

Memory and Aliasing. Arrays, views and imported storage that may share memory; why generated code makes no unconditional no-alias promise; and how the CPU's disjoint-arrays specialization recovers performance safely.

CPU Threading Policy. How the CPU backend decides, per dispatch, whether to run a loop range serially or spread it across its thread pool, a pool JIT'd from LLVM IR, using measured per-kernel cost and measured fan-out cost rather than a fixed threshold.

Backend Implementations. How each of the five backends (CPU through LLVM, Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero) turns the shared IR into native code, allocates and moves memory, and launches work (queued in order on the GPU backends), along with the device-specific fallbacks each one needs.

Vendor Workarounds. Each place generated code or a runtime call is shaped around a defect in a vendor compiler, driver or binding rather than by the language contract: the symptom, the workaround, the test that guards it, and when it can go.

Interoperability. Sharing memory with other libraries and frameworks without copying: wrapping external pointers, DLPack, exported device memory, and VTK interop.

The two design records of tack.dataset are kept with the Visualization Guide:

Dataset API. The design record of tack.dataset: how its data model (topologies, spaces, fields, sets), its algorithms and its partitioned data and ghost marks were reasoned out. The API as it stands is the Dataset API reference.

Polyhedra. The design record of the polyhedral path in tack.dataset: faces shared between cells, their orientation, and the algorithms that run on arbitrary polyhedra.

docs.title: Arrays, element types and dataset fields
docs.text: Tack separates storage from the meaning of values on a mesh. tack.Array holds typed backend storage; tack.dataset.Field couples coefficient values with a function space on a topology. Lowercase tack.array and tack.empty are factory functions that return Array instances.

docs.title: Shape and element type
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
temperature = tack.empty((100,))
velocity = tack.empty((100,), tack.vec3(tack.f32))
stress = tack.empty((100,), tack.mat3(tack.f32))
velocity.fill([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
assert velocity.shape == (100,)
assert velocity.size == 100
assert velocity.dtype is tack.vec3(tack.f32)
assert velocity.numpy().shape == (100, 3)

All three arrays contain 100 elements. Their dtypes describe a scalar, a vector, and a matrix respectively. A scalar array of shape (100, 3) and a vector array of shape (100,) occupy the same number of bytes, but kernel indexing reads a scalar in the first case and a vector in the second. A matrix and a vector with the same number of components remain distinct.

vec(n, scalar_dtype) constructs a vector element type; vec2, vec3 and vec4 are conveniences. mat(rows, columns, scalar_dtype) constructs a matrix type up to 4x4, with square conveniences mat2, mat3 and mat4. Component types default to f32. Type descriptors are immutable and reusable. They allocate no backend storage and do not define a finite-element space.

docs.title: Construction and transfer
docs.text:
Operation Values Allocation and ownership empty(shape, dtype=f32, *, device=None) Uninitialized Independent storage on device, by default the default device array(values, dtype=None) Copies input values Independent storage; scalar dtype inferred if omitted empty_like(prototype, dtype=None) Does not read or initialize values Independent storage matching metadata zeros, ones, full, and their _like forms Initialized Same element types as empty array_from_ptr(ptr, shape, dtype) Shares existing values Borrowed external storage, read-only by default from_dlpack(source) Shares existing values Holds the source alive; preserves supported access constraints

Without an explicit dtype, array(np.zeros((n, 3), np.float32)) is a scalar array of shape (n, 3). It never infers vector elements from dimensions. Specifying dtype=vec3() consumes a trailing dimension of size three and gives array shape (n,). Matrix dtypes similarly consume two matching trailing dimensions. Wrong component dimensions raise ValueError.

array(existing_tack_array) copies on that array's device, or through the host when device= names another. empty_like reads only metadata and allocates on the prototype's device unless device= says otherwise. Every array records its device (a.device); a.to_device(d) returns the array itself when its memory is usable on d, else a copy. A scalar dtype override preserves vector/matrix dimensions and changes component precision; an element dtype override selects another element type at the same array shape.

docs.title: Views and operations
docs.text:
copy and astype allocate independent storage. Passing a scalar type to astype changes component precision while retaining element dimensions. An explicit element dtype must have the same component dimensions. reshape shares storage and changes the number of array dimensions while preserving the element type and count. A view preserves imported-storage lifetime and access restrictions.

numpy() and its async equivalent return a host snapshot with component axes appended to array shape: (n, 3) for vectors, (n, 3, 3) for matrices. DLPack exports the same scalar tensor dimensions; importing that tensor produces a scalar array with those axes because DLPack does not carry Tack's element-type distinction. It shares values without guessing vector types. Metal exports its host-addressable storage as a CPU tensor; importing a host tensor into Metal requires copy=True, because arbitrary host pointers cannot be wrapped as MTLBuffers without a copy.

scalar_dtype, scalar_size, and storage_shape expose storage metadata for implementation and interop. Storage is contiguous and unpadded, and interleaved unless the array is structure-of-arrays (below); matrices store rows together. The compiler continues to lower vector and matrix accesses to scalar component operations. Runtime type inference and backend capability checks use the component type; vector/matrix shape remains part of specialization keys.

Array reductions and tack.algorithms statistics reduce scalar components in storage order; a statistic's explicit n counts scalar components.

docs.title: Implicit arrays and the indexing protocol
docs.text:
tack.arrays holds arrays that compute each value from its index rather than store it (CountingArray, ConstantArray, CartesianProduct, UniformCoordinates, Function, Transform, Cast, random arrays) and arrays that rearrange others (Permutation, Concatenate, View, Strided, ExtractComponent, Components). They play the part of Viskores' fancy array handles: a kernel reads a[i] and the indexing expression is inlined into it.

They are ordinary @tack.device_class objects, and kernels index them through Python's own protocol, not a Tack-specific one: a device class whose __getitem__, __setitem__ and __len__ are @tack.func methods is indexed in a kernel as an array is.

@tack.device_class
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, n, start, step):
        self.n, self.start, self.step = n, start, step

    @tack.func
    def __getitem__(self, k):
        return self.start + self.step * k

    @tack.func
    def __len__(self):
        return self.n

Template rewriting (template_rewrite._Indexing) turns obj[i] into obj.__getitem__(i), obj[i] = v into obj.__setitem__(i, v), obj[i] += v into a get and a set sharing one evaluation of the index, and len(obj) into obj.__len__(); the calls then inline like any method. Several indices arrive as one vector. So the library's arrays have no privileged path: a user's class joins them by defining the same methods, and a kernel written for stored arrays takes any of them unchanged.

The choices this rests on:

  • Specialization, not dispatch. Each class, and each composition of them (a Permutation of a Transform of a CountingArray), compiles its own variant of the kernel, and a composed array inlines to the expression one would write by hand. There are no type lists to declare, as in Viskores, and no per-element virtual call, as in VTK's generic arrays. The cost is a variant per composition a program uses; the template part of the cache key keeps them apart and the disk cache keeps them across processes.
  • Values that change stay runtime parameters. Instance numbers (a length, a start, a step) and instance tuples of numbers (self.shape = (nx, ny), one scalar per entry) are kernel arguments, so a new length does not recompile. Class attributes, tuples included, are compiled in.
  • Writability composes. An array that wraps stored ones writes through: a View or Strided store lands in the wrapped array, a Permutation store is a scatter, Concatenate writes the part holding the index, Components writes each component to its own array. Each is writable exactly when what it writes into is. A computed array defines no __setitem__, and storing into it is a TypeError when the kernel compiles. Since every method of a held object is resolved, a missing method inside one is refused only when a kernel actually uses it (__tack_refuse__).
  • No address, no atomics. An atomic needs a storage location, so an atomic on an indexable object is refused.
  • Host operations materialize. sum, min, max and mean compute the values into a temporary array on the device of the arrays the implicit array holds (a.device), then reduce it as a stored array. tack.algorithms reads implicit inputs in its kernels without storing them.

docs.title: Structure-of-arrays storage
docs.text:
A vector or matrix array can keep each component in an array of its own:

pos = tack.soa(x, y, z)                                  # existing arrays, no copy
vel = tack.zeros((n,), tack.vec3(), layout="soa")        # new ones

The motivation is data that arrives that way: a simulation's coordinate arrays, or another library's tensors imported with from_dlpack or array_from_ptr, on the CPU or a GPU. Copying them into an interleaved buffer would double the memory and add a pass per exchange.

SOA is a layout of tack.Array, not a separate kind of object. A SoaArray has the dtype, shape, device and host API of any vector array; a.layout is "soa" ("aos" for interleaved and scalar arrays) and a.components gives the component arrays. Kernels index it exactly as an interleaved array, including component stores, augmented stores and vector atomics, so one kernel serves both layouts. tack.arrays.Components expresses the same layout through the indexing protocol; it differs in taking any arrays, computed ones included, and in being an implicit array rather than storage: it reads back with numpy() and reduces, but takes no copyto, fill or atomics, and is not an Array.

Lowering. A SoaArray has no buffer of its own, and backends never see one. Dispatch replaces it, in its place among the arguments, by its component arrays (_flatten_soa, after template expansion, so an SOA array a device class holds is flattened too), and lowering replaces its parameter, in the same place, by one parameter per component. Lowering learns the layout from the vector-array metadata (("soa", width)), and every access computes each component's location: (array, i * n + c) for an interleaved array, (component c, i) for an SOA one. Shape queries, the strides of multi-dimensional indexing and debug-mode extents read the first component, which has the array's shape. The consequences:

  • No backend changed. Each component is an ordinary scalar array argument, so what holds for those holds per component: the CPU's disjointness check (tack.soa(x, x) is simply not disjoint), Metal's argument buffer, read-only checks (reported as "component 1 of parameter 'a'"), atomic alignment and debug-mode bounds checks.
  • The layout is part of the call signature, the template keys and the vector-array metadata in the IR key, so a kernel holds one variant per layout and never runs one layout's code on the other.
  • The SOA array's own name is never a value in the IR. A kernel may index it, ask its shape or length, or pass it to a device function, which then uses the caller's component parameters; binding it to another name is refused.

What is refused, and why. A scalar atomic at a flat component index (atomic_add(a, 3 * i + 1, x)) names a position in one interleaved buffer, which an SOA array does not have; an atomic with a vector value works. For the same reason an SOA array is not exported whole through DLPack, export_memory or to VTK. Its components are, and tack.array(a, layout="aos") copies it into one buffer.

Host operations work per component: numpy() stacks the components as trailing dimensions, copyto and fill split values among them, and reductions combine the components' results. copyto between layouts, and array/asarray with another layout, copy element by element in a kernel. Statistics that pair the components of two arrays (dot) copy an SOA input to an interleaved buffer first, so pairs match whatever the layouts.

docs.title: Dataset fields
docs.text:
import tack.dataset as td

data = td.uniform_grid((2, 2, 2))
space = td.H1(data)
values = tack.empty((space.size,), tack.vec3())
values.fill([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
data.fields["velocity"] = td.Field(space, values)

The array's element type controls components; the field's space controls DOF association and interpolation on the mesh. A three-component array does not itself mean geometry, H1 velocity, or an H(div) finite-element field.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
The earlier names (field, field_from_numpy, field_from_ptr, Vector.field, Matrix.field, to_numpy/from_numpy) were later removed without compatibility wrappers, along with the flat host layout of vector and matrix arrays; host values move with numpy() and tack.copyto. Internal Field imports name Array.

Kernel value construction (Vector([...]), Matrix(...), and Matrix.identity(...)) was retained by this change, and later replaced without compatibility wrappers: in a kernel the element-type names build values (tack.vec3(x, y, z), tack.mat2([a, b], [c, d])), and tack.identity(n) is the identity matrix. On the host those names remain dtype descriptions.

docs.title: Backend Implementations
docs.text:
Every backend turns the same typed, optimized Tack IR into native code and runs it. What differs is the toolchain, how a device and context are chosen, how arguments reach the kernel, and which hardware features exist. This page walks through each backend in the order a kernel meets it — initialization, compilation, launch — and closes with the workarounds each one carries and why.

The shared front half — resolve_variant() in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/kernel_utils.py, which turns a call into a cached compiled variant — is described in Compilation Pipeline and Specialization and Caching. Each backend's execute() calls it with a build callback, and that callback is where this page begins.

docs.title: The Backend contract
docs.text:
All five backends subclass Backend (runtime/backend.py); the four GPU backends do so through GPUBackend (runtime/gpu_backend.py), which turns a call into a queued launch the same way for all of them and leaves each the hooks where they differ: how a kernel is compiled and launched, which lock a launch holds, how its packed scalars are owned, and whether it must complete before returning. Their code generators likewise share CFamilyCodeGen (codegen/c_family.py). It declares three required methods — allocate_array(), wrap_ptr() and execute() — and a set of capability attributes that callers read instead of probing with hasattr. Optional methods have defaults that suit a backend whose launches complete before execute() returns: synchronize() waits for every launch queued so far and is a no-op by default (tack.sync() calls it; see Launches are queued); fill_array() returns false, leaving Array.fill to the buffer (the CPU fills large arrays through its own dispatch); and cache_target() returns None, which keeps a backend's compiled variants off the disk cache, while variant_artifact() and load_variant() store and rebuild them (see Specialization and Caching). DeviceBuffer likewise has synchronize(), a wait for the launches queued on the buffer's device, and share(), which hands the storage outside Tack: it waits now, and makes every later launch that uses the buffer complete before returning. Anything derivable is derived: supports_f64 is a property over supported_dtypes, and supported_atomic_dtypes is a property that intersects the per-target table ATOMIC_DTYPES (lang/atomic_support.py) with supported_dtypes, so neither can disagree with the array types.

Attribute CPU Metal CUDA HIP Level Zero name cpu metal cuda hip level_zero display_name CPU Metal CUDA HIP Level Zero supported_dtypes all ten all but f64 all ten all ten nine, plus f64 if the device reports it supports_f64 (derived) yes no yes yes per device supports_device_reductions no yes yes yes yes supports_workgroups no yes yes yes yes supported_atomic_dtypes (derived) all ten i32, u32, f32 i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, f64 as CUDA i32, u32, f32 device_memory_spaces — — cuda, cuda_pinned, cuda_managed hip, hip_pinned, hip_managed level_zero device_options num_threads — — — external_context dlpack_refusal_note — set — — —

"All ten" is i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, f64. supported_dtypes is a frozenset on every backend. device_options lists the keyword arguments tack.device() forwards to the backend's constructor; tack.device() (runtime/dispatch.py) raises ValueError for any other keyword before constructing anything, so a misspelled option cannot be silently dropped. The user-facing summary of these capabilities is in Backends; the normative statements are in Backend Capabilities.
