live = count_live(cells, count, n)        # a Python int

The expression is evaluated once, after the launch, by a one-thread epilogue kernel that stores it into a hidden array the call reads back. So it may use arrays, arguments, constants and locals bound before the loop, but not a local the loop assigns, which has a value per thread. This replaces writing a one-element array and reading it with numpy() or f[0]; the cost is one extra, tiny launch and one element's transfer.

docs.title: Return the length of an atomic append
docs.text:
An atomic's result and a kernel's result have different roles. Inside the loop, atomic_add returns the counter's old value, giving that iteration a unique output slot. After the loop, the kernel returns the completed counter to Python:

@tack.kernel
def compact_positive(values, out, count, n) -> int:
    for i in range(n):
        if values[i] > 0.0:
            slot = tack.atomic_add(count, 0, 1)
            out[slot] = values[i]
    return count[0]

Allocate enough capacity and reset the counter before each call:

    values = tack.array(np.array([-2, 1, -0.5, 3, 0, 2], dtype=np.float32))
    out = tack.empty(values.shape)  # capacity for every input
    count = tack.empty((1,), tack.i32)
    count.fill(0)
    length = compact_positive(values, out, count, values.size)
    result = out.numpy()[:length]
    # Arrival order is unspecified: compare the values after sorting.
    assert length == 3 and isinstance(length, int)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.sort(result), np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32))

The returned length is deterministic; the order of the appended values is not. Only the first length output elements are valid. A scalar return does not turn the loop's per-iteration locals into a global reduction. For ordered output, use count → scan → write.

Download the complete program, or run:

uv run python docs/examples/kernel_results.py --arch cpu --check
uv run python docs/examples/kernel_results.py --arch metal --check

docs.title: Kernel Caching
docs.text:
Kernels are compiled on first call. A compiled variant is reused by later calls that agree on everything the generated code depends on: argument dtypes, which arguments are arrays, scalars or textures, vector widths, texture extents, @tack.device_class class constants and layout, any array dimensions the kernel bakes in (for example x.shape[1] used as a row stride), and on CPU whether the arrays overlap. Anything else is a runtime parameter.

So changing scalar values (passing alpha=2.5, then alpha=3.0) does not recompile, and neither does changing the length of a 1-D array used only as the parallel loop bound. Changing a dtype, a vector width or a baked-in dimension does. If a kernel recompiles for every array size, pass the size as a scalar argument instead of reading it from shape inside the body. Specialization and Caching lists exactly what goes into the key, with worked examples.

Compiled variants are also kept on disk, so a later process that calls the same kernel the same way starts warm; editing the kernel, a device function it calls, a constant or a template class compiles it again. See The Kernel Cache.

docs.title: Inspecting Generated Code
docs.text:
tack.inspect() shows the generated code for a kernel without executing it. This is useful for debugging, learning, and understanding what the compiler produces:

@tack.kernel
def saxpy(x, y, out, a):
    for i in range(len(x)):
        out[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]

n = 1024
x = tack.empty((n,))
y = tack.empty((n,))
out = tack.empty((n,))

# Tack intermediate representation
print(tack.inspect(saxpy, x, y, out, 2.0, mode="ir"))

# Backend-specific source (MSL, CUDA C, LLVM IR, etc.)
print(tack.inspect(saxpy, x, y, out, 2.0, mode="source"))

# Post-optimization LLVM IR (CPU backend only — runs LLVM O3 passes)
print(tack.inspect(saxpy, x, y, out, 2.0, mode="optimized"))

The three modes are:

Mode Output "ir" Tack intermediate representation "source" Backend source code: LLVM IR (CPU), MSL (Metal), CUDA C, HIP C, OpenCL C "optimized" Post-optimization LLVM IR (loop vectorization, unrolling, etc.). CPU only; other backends raise ValueError

The code is for the device the call would run on: the default device if it can address the arguments' arrays, otherwise theirs, chosen when inspect is called, as each call chooses. To see another backend's code, pass arrays on that device (tack.empty((n,), device="metal")); a with tack.device(...) block alone does not move a call whose arrays its device cannot address.

You must pass the same arguments the kernel would receive at runtime, since type inference, dimension resolution, and template expansion all depend on them. Inspection applies the same checks as a call, so arguments a call would reject (an i64 atomic on Metal, for example) raise here too, and on GPUs without texture hardware the source shows the software sampling the call would use. Templates and scalar arguments work as expected:

@tack.device_class
class Sim:
    GRAVITY = -9.81

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.pos = tack.empty((n,))
        self.vel = tack.empty((n,))
        self.dt = 0.01

    @tack.func
    def step(self, i):
        self.vel[i] = self.vel[i] + self.GRAVITY * self.dt
        self.pos[i] = self.pos[i] + self.vel[i] * self.dt

@tack.kernel
def update(sim):
    for i in range(len(sim.pos)):
        sim.step(i)

sim = Sim(1024)
print(tack.inspect(update, sim))  # shows template expansion + inlined methods

For complete applications that combine these constructs, see Heat diffusion, Physarum and the tutorial gallery.

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
@tack.kernel
def clamp(data, lo, hi, n):
    for i in range(n):
        val = data[i]
        if val < lo:
            val = lo
        if val > hi:
            val = hi
        data[i] = val

if/elif/else works as expected, and so do conditional expressions (a if cond else b), which evaluate only the selected arm.

docs.title: While Loops
docs.text:
@tack.kernel
def newton_sqrt(x, out, n):
    for i in range(n):
        val = x[i]
        guess = 0.0
        if val > 0.0:
            guess = max(val, 1.0)
            k = 0
            while k < 20:
                guess = 0.5 * (guess + val / guess)
                k += 1
        out[i] = guess

The example requires nonnegative inputs; the zero case is handled before the iteration, avoiding division by zero. A fixed iteration cap makes runtime bounded. For a convergence loop, combine a tolerance with such a cap and write a status array if the host needs to know which elements converged. A kernel cannot raise a Python exception from an individual iteration.

docs.title: Break and Continue
docs.text:
@tack.kernel
def find_threshold(data, out, threshold, n):
    for i in range(n):
        count = 0
        for j in range(100):
            if data[i * 100 + j] > threshold:
                break
            count = count + 1
        out[i] = count

break leaves the nearest sequential loop; continue advances it to its next iteration. They do not exit a whole launch. Do not use lane-dependent exits around a GPU barrier: all workgroup lanes must still participate. A return inside a sequential loop of a device function remains unsupported; record a result, break, then return after the loop.

docs.title: Math Builtins
docs.text:
The following math builtins are recognized inside kernels and device functions:

Function Description sqrt(x) Square root sin(x), cos(x), tan(x) Trigonometric asin(x), acos(x), atan(x) Inverse trig atan2(y, x) Two-argument arctangent sinh(x), cosh(x), tanh(x) Hyperbolic exp(x), exp2(x) Exponential log(x), log2(x), log10(x) Logarithmic floor(x), ceil(x) Rounding abs(x) Absolute value min(a, b, ...), max(a, b, ...) Min/max of two or more values pow(base, exp) Power

These are imported automatically — no import math needed. They compile to native math operations (e.g., sinf on CUDA, metal::sin on MSL). With two integer operands, pow and ** compute exact fixed-width power and preserve the base type; the exponent must be nonnegative. With a floating operand they use floating-point power at the promoted precision. See Arrays and Types for wrapping and division rules.

from math import sqrt, sin, cos, exp, log, floor, ceil, pow  # optional

@tack.kernel
def wave(out, t, n):
    for i in range(n):
        x = float(i) / float(n)
        out[i] = sin(x * 6.2832) * exp(-t)

docs.title: Conditions can guard loads
docs.text:
Scalar and/or and conditional expressions short-circuit. This is useful at boundaries: the following load is evaluated only for an in-range index.

@tack.kernel
def read_previous(data, out, n):
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = data[i - 1] if i > 0 else 0.0

A vector comparison instead produces one mask value per component. Use any(mask) or all(mask) for an if, and tack.select(mask, a, b) to pick component values. Vector masks evaluate component expressions rather than providing a scalar short-circuit guard for invalid loads. See Vectors and matrices.

docs.title: Cast at the point where the meaning changes
docs.text:
float(i) converts to f32, and int(x) truncates a finite representable value toward zero. For a grid cell containing a coordinate, use int(floor(x)) when negative coordinates are possible. Those are different operations:

Input int(x) int(floor(x)) 1.7 1 1 -0.3 0 −1

tack.f64(x) explicitly requests double precision where the backend provides it. An f64 output array does not retroactively change all intermediate operations: integer true division produces f32, so cast its operands for a double-precision quotient. Plain integer literals also participate in promotion; use typed constants for intentional unsigned wrapping arithmetic.

Math operations have input domains. A sampler's indices must be valid; an inverse matrix needs a nonzero determinant; log needs positive input for a finite result. Choose how your algorithm handles values outside those domains before running large inputs. The numerical contract defines which floating special cases are portable.

docs.title: Shader-style helpers
docs.text:
from tack import math as tm gives reusable functions such as clamp, mix, fract, smoothstep, step, sign, length, distance and normalize. These are device functions, so call them inside kernels or other device functions:

from tack import math as tm

@tack.kernel
def map_values(data, colour, n):
    for i in range(n):
        t = tm.clamp(data[i], 0.0, 1.0)
        colour[i] = tm.mix([0.1, 0.2, 0.8], [1.0, 0.8, 0.1], t)

Here colour is a three-component vector array. mix interpolates its arms; clamp limits a value component by component. fract(x) is x - floor(x), which is useful for repeating patterns. The dye tutorial uses interpolation over actual arrays, and marching squares uses interpolated edge crossings to build geometry.

docs.title: @tack.func
docs.text:
Functions decorated with @tack.func are inlined into kernels at the AST level. They let you write reusable device-side code:

@tack.func
def lerp(a, b, t):
    return a + t * (b - a)

@tack.kernel
def interpolate(src, dst, alpha, n):
    for i in range(n):
        dst[i] = lerp(src[i], 1.0, alpha)

When the kernel is compiled, lerp is inlined — no function call overhead.

Calls use the defining kernel or device function's Python bindings. You can import a device function under an alias or call it through an imported module. Two modules may define the same function name without interfering. Nested calls use the callee's namespace, and closure-bound device functions are supported. Template methods keep their defining bindings too.

Bindings are resolved when the IR specialization is first built. Cached kernels keep the inlined body; recreate a kernel to capture a changed callable binding. Runtime function parameters, ordinary Python callables, and recursive device calls are unsupported. This does not enable capturing numerical Python variables: pass those values as kernel arguments.

docs.title: Multiple Return Values
docs.text:
@tack.func supports returning tuples:

@tack.func
def polar_to_cart(r, theta):
    x = r * cos(theta)
    y = r * sin(theta)
    return x, y

@tack.kernel
def convert(r_array, theta_array, x_out, y_out, n):
    for i in range(n):
        x, y = polar_to_cart(r_array[i], theta_array[i])
        x_out[i] = x
        y_out[i] = y

The values may be vectors and matrices as well as scalars, in any mix, and the targets may be array elements:

@tack.func
def closest_hit(origin, direction):
    ...
    return distance, normal, color              # a scalar and two vectors

@tack.func
def polar(F):
    ...
    return R, S                                 # two matrices

@tack.kernel
def shade(origins, directions, depth, normals, n):
    for i in range(n):
        depth[i], normals[i], color = closest_hit(origins[i], directions[i])

A result made of several values is unpacked into one target each. A device function may also return another call's result as it is (return closest_hit(o, d)), and a name may hold it until it is unpacked (hit = closest_hit(o, d), then depth, normal, color = hit); using such a name as one value is rejected.

docs.title: Nested Calls
docs.text:
@tack.func functions can call other @tack.func functions:

@tack.func
def square(x):
    return x * x

@tack.func
def length(x, y, z):
    return sqrt(square(x) + square(y) + square(z))

docs.title: Passing Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays can be passed to @tack.func — they work just like in kernels:

@tack.func
def safe_load(data, i, default_val):
    result = default_val
    if 0 <= i < data.shape[0]:
        result = data[i]
    return result

docs.title: Texture Sampling in Functions
docs.text:
tex.sample() works inside @tack.func. Tack automatically propagates texture metadata through the inlining:

@tack.func
def sample_bilinear(tex, u, v, w):
    return tex.sample(u, v, w)

@tack.kernel
def render(tex, output, n):
    for i in range(n):
        output[i] = sample_bilinear(tex, 0.5, 0.5, float(i) / float(n))

docs.title: Local Arrays in Functions
docs.text:
Local arrays (tack.local_array) can be passed to @tack.func. The function accesses the caller's array directly — no copy:

@tack.func
def fill_weights(w, ct, pc0, pc1, pc2):
    for v in range(ct.num_points):
        w[v] = ct.weight(v, pc0, pc1, pc2)

@tack.kernel
def interp(ct, data, out, n):
    for i in range(n):
        w = tack.local_array(tack.f32, ct.num_points)
        fill_weights(w, ct, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)  # fills w in place
        # ... use w[v] ...

This also works with @tack.device_class methods — see Advanced Features for the cell set pattern.

docs.title: Reuse a numerical operation across element types
docs.text:
A device function is specialized on the values or arrays it receives. The same linear interpolation expression works for scalars and vectors:

@tack.func
def mix_values(a, b, t):
    return a * (1.0 - t) + b * t

The dye tutorial builds a bilinear sampler from four array loads and applies it to RGB vectors. The MPM tutorial uses matrix-valued arithmetic, and N-body shares one interaction function between the plain and tiled kernels.

Keep all return paths compatible in shape and type. Early returns in a sequential loop of a device function remain unsupported; use a result local and break, then return after the loop. Recursion is unsupported. Local arrays passed to a function are scratch storage shared with that caller iteration, whereas vector and matrix arguments behave as values.

docs.title: @tack.device_class
docs.text:
The template system lets you write generic kernels that work with different data structures. Classes decorated with @tack.device_class can be passed as kernel arguments. They are recognized by type, so the parameter that takes one needs no annotation.

The short examples below are fragments showing the class protocol. The rasterizer is a complete program with initialized input and a checked output; Physarum uses the same ideas in a simulation.

@tack.device_class
class AOSArray:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data       # tack.array → becomes a buffer parameter

    @tack.func
    def get_value(self, i):
        return self.data[i]

@tack.device_class
class ConstantArray:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value     # instance scalar → runtime parameter

    @tack.func
    def get_value(self, i):
        return self.value

A single kernel works with both:

@tack.kernel
def add_arrays(a, b, out, n):
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = a.get_value(i) + b.get_value(i)

# Works with any combination:
add_arrays(AOSArray(array1), AOSArray(array2), out, n)
add_arrays(AOSArray(array1), ConstantArray(3.14), out, n)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When a @tack.device_class object is passed as a kernel argument:

  • Class-level scalars (defined on the class, not in __init__) → compile-time constants baked into generated code. Changing them triggers recompilation.
  • Instance scalars (set in __init__) → runtime kernel scalar parameters. Changing them does not trigger recompilation.
  • Instance arrays (tack.Array set in __init__) → kernel buffer parameters
  • @tack.func methods → inlined at the call site

Each unique combination of template types and class-level constants produces a separately compiled kernel. Instance scalar values can change without recompilation. Replacing an array with one whose dtype, vector width or baked-in dimensions differ can create another variant; array metadata still matters.

docs.title: Class Constants vs Instance Scalars
docs.text:
Use class variables for structural constants that the compiler needs (allocation sizes, topology parameters). Use instance variables for runtime values (dimensions, coefficients, thresholds):

@tack.device_class
class ImageFilter:
    block_size = 16          # class variable → compile-time constant
    num_channels = 3         # class variable → compile-time constant

    def __init__(self, width, height, data):
        self.width = width   # instance → runtime parameter (no recompile)
        self.height = height # instance → runtime parameter (no recompile)
        self.data = data     # instance → array parameter

    @tack.func
    def get_pixel(self, x, y):
        return self.data[y * self.width + x]

For an object attribute used as an allocation size (tack.local_array, tack.shared), use a class constant. Literals, tack.constant values and resolved array dimensions can also supply sizes; an instance scalar is a runtime parameter. Other changing parameters can be instance variables.

@tack.kernel
def process(filt, out):
    for i in range(filt.width):              # runtime — OK as instance var
        buf = tack.local_array(tack.f32, filt.block_size)  # must be class constant
        # ...

Calling the same kernel with different image sizes reuses the compiled kernel:

filt_small = ImageFilter(256, 256, small_data)
filt_large = ImageFilter(1024, 1024, large_data)
process(filt_small, out1)   # compiles once
process(filt_large, out2)   # reuses compiled kernel — no JIT

docs.title: Inheritance and Function Attributes
docs.text:
A device class can derive from another. The subclass has its bases' @tack.func methods and class constants and may override either; a method may call an inherited one through self:

@tack.device_class
class Fluid:
    rho_0 = 1000.0

    @tack.func
    def pressure(self, rho):
        return self.stiffness * (rho / self.rho_0 - 1.0)

@tack.device_class
class WeaklyCompressible(Fluid):
    gamma = 7.0

    @tack.func
    def pressure(self, rho):                       # overrides Fluid.pressure
        return self.stiffness * ((rho / self.rho_0) ** self.gamma - 1.0)

An object can also hold a device function as an attribute and call it, which is how one class works with several interchangeable functions:

@tack.func
def cubic(r, h): ...

@tack.func
def spiky(r, h): ...

@tack.device_class
class Model:
    def __init__(self, smoothing):
        self.smoothing = smoothing                 # cubic or spiky

    @tack.func
    def density(self, r):
        return self.mass * self.smoothing(r, self.h)

The function is resolved when the kernel is compiled, so which function an attribute holds is part of the kernel's specialization, like a class constant: a kernel given Model(cubic) and then Model(spiky) compiles once for each. Assigning another function to the attribute of an existing object takes effect at the next call.

docs.title: Objects Holding Objects
docs.text:
A device-class object may hold others as attributes, to any depth, and reach their methods and attributes through them:

@tack.device_class
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, start, step):
        self.start, self.step = start, step

    @tack.func
    def get(self, k):
        return self.start + self.step * k

@tack.device_class
class Permuted:
    def __init__(self, ids, base):
        self.ids = ids                             # an array of indices
        self.base = base                           # any object with get(k)

    @tack.func
    def get(self, k):
        return self.base.get(self.ids[k])

@tack.kernel
def read(arr, out):
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        out[i] = arr.get(i)

read(Permuted(ids, Counting(10, 5)), out)          # out[i] = 10 + 5 * ids[i]
read(Permuted(ids, Permuted(more, Counting(0, 1))), out)

The tree is one template: every object's arrays and scalars become kernel parameters, its constants are compiled in, and its methods are inlined, so Permuted(ids, Counting(10, 5)) compiles to 10 + 5 * ids[i], the code you would write by hand. A kernel can reach in too (arr.base.step). Which classes the tree holds, and where, is part of the specialization: new values reuse the compiled kernel, another nesting compiles anew. An object may not hold itself, directly or not.

Each level costs a few microseconds per call on the host, where the tree is walked once to gather its arguments: about 4 us per level on the CPU backend of an M1 Max, against 8 us for a whole call with a one-level template. The compiled code pays nothing.

docs.title: Passing Objects to Functions
docs.text:
A device-class object, or one it holds, can be passed to a @tack.func or to another object's method, which then uses it as it would self:

@tack.func
def mean_of_two(arr, k):
    return 0.5 * (arr.get(k) + arr.get(k + 1))

@tack.device_class
class Blend:
    def __init__(self, weights):
        self.weights = weights

    @tack.func
    def mix(self, a, b, k):                        # a and b are objects too
        return self.weights[k] * a.get(k) + (1.0 - self.weights[k]) * b.get(k)

@tack.kernel
def smooth(arr, blend, other, out):
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        out[i] = mean_of_two(arr, i) + blend.mix(arr, other, i)

Each such call gets its own copy of the callee, with the object bound in, so it costs nothing at run time; a method may pass on self (helper(self, k)) or a held object (helper(self.base, k)) the same way. The callee cannot keep the object in a local or return it.

docs.title: Kernels as Methods
docs.text:
A kernel can be a method of the class. Called on an object, it receives that object as self, a template like any other argument, so the object's arrays, scalars, constants and methods are reached through it and nothing has to be passed in. Save this complete example in a .py file. It draws one initialized triangle into a (height, width) RGB array:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Rasterizer:
    def __init__(self, n, width, height):
        self.n = n
        self.width, self.height = width, height
        self.vertices = tack.empty((n, 3), tack.vec2(tack.f32))
        self.pixels = tack.empty((height, width), tack.vec3(tack.f32))
        self.pixels.fill(0.0)              # draw writes only covered pixels

    @staticmethod
    @tack.func
    def edge(p, a, b):                     # needs nothing from the object
        return (p.x - a.x) * (b.y - a.y) - (p.y - a.y) * (b.x - a.x)

    @tack.func
    def inside(self, p, t):
        a, b, c = self.vertices[t, 0], self.vertices[t, 1], self.vertices[t, 2]
        return self.edge(p, a, b) >= 0.0 and self.edge(p, b, c) >= 0.0 \
            and self.edge(p, c, a) >= 0.0

    @tack.kernel
    def draw(self, shade):
        for row, column in tack.ndindex(self.height, self.width):
            for t in range(self.n):
                if self.inside([column + 0.5, row + 0.5], t):
                    self.pixels[row, column] = [shade, shade, shade]

raster = Rasterizer(1, 32, 32)
tack.copyto(raster.vertices, np.array([[[8, 8], [8, 24], [24, 8]]], dtype=np.float32))
raster.draw(0.8)
image = raster.pixels.numpy()
np.testing.assert_allclose(image[10, 10], [0.8, 0.8, 0.8])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(image[0, 0], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
assert np.count_nonzero(image[:, :, 0]) > 0

The kernel compiles once per class and is shared by its objects, as a kernel taking the object as an argument would be; Rasterizer.draw(raster, 0.8) is the same call. A device function that uses nothing of the object can be a @staticmethod (the decorator goes above @tack.func) and is still called through self. The class must be decorated with @tack.device_class.

docs.title: Iterating an Object
docs.text:
A class can say what a loop over it runs through, and a kernel then loops over the object itself. __tack_iterate__ names one to three of its scalar attributes, fastest first:

@tack.device_class
class Grid:
    __tack_iterate__ = ("nx", "ny")

    def __init__(self, nx, ny):
        self.nx = nx
        self.ny = ny

    @tack.func
    def flat(self, c):
        return c[0] + self.nx * c[1]


@tack.kernel
def label(cells, out):
    for c in cells:
        out[cells.flat(c)] = cells.flat(c) + 1

With one name, for c in cells is for c in range(cells.n) and c is an integer. With two or three, it is a tack.ndindex over them, slowest first, and c is the vector of indices with c[0] running fastest; as the kernel's parallel loop it launches in that shape, so recovering the indices costs no division. The object's methods receive c as it comes, so the same kernel runs over a class that iterates one-dimensionally and one that iterates over a grid. Instance attributes are runtime extents, as any instance scalar is: a new grid size does not recompile.

docs.title: Indexable Objects
docs.text:
A class becomes indexable in kernels by defining Python's own indexing methods as device functions: __getitem__, __setitem__ for stores, and __len__. A kernel then indexes the object as it would an array:

@tack.device_class
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, n, start, step):
        self.n, self.start, self.step = n, start, step

    @tack.func
    def __getitem__(self, k):
        return self.start + self.step * k

    @tack.func
    def __len__(self):
        return self.n


@tack.kernel
def double(a, out):
    for i in range(len(a)):
        out[i] = a[i] * 2.0


double(tack.arange(5, dtype=tack.f32), out)    # a stored array
double(Counting(5, 1.0, 0.5), out)             # an indexable object

The two calls compile to two variants of one kernel: a direct load for the array, the inlined __getitem__ for the object. Nothing marks a as either. obj[i] = v calls __setitem__(i, v), and obj[i] += v calls __getitem__ and then __setitem__, with the index evaluated once. Several indices, obj[i, j], arrive as one vector, so __getitem__(self, k) reads k[0] and k[1]. len(obj) may be the parallel loop's bound: it is evaluated when the kernel launches, like an array's length. An object held by another is indexed the same way, self.base[k].

An instance tuple of numbers is one runtime scalar per entry, read with a literal index: self.shape = (nx, ny) gives obj.shape[0] and obj.shape[1], and len(obj.shape) is 2. A new shape does not recompile. A tuple on the class, shape = (4, 4), is read the same way but compiled in, as a class's numbers are: a fixed tile size the compiler can unroll.

@tack.device_class
class Grid:
    def __init__(self, values, nx, ny):
        self.values = values
        self.shape = (nx, ny)

    @tack.func
    def __getitem__(self, k):
        return self.values[k[1] * self.shape[0] + k[0]]

    @tack.func
    def __setitem__(self, k, v):
        self.values[k[1] * self.shape[0] + k[0]] = v


@tack.kernel
def bump(g):
    for i, j in tack.ndindex(g.shape[0], g.shape[1]):
        g[i, j] += 1.0

A store into an object without __setitem__ is refused when the kernel is compiled, and so is an atomic on an indexable object, which has no memory of its own to update. The methods run only in kernels: on the host, Python calls __len__ to truth-test an object, so test an indexable with is None, not if obj:.

docs.title: Cell Set Example
docs.text:
Templates are ideal for topology abstractions where the same algorithm should work with different mesh representations:

@tack.device_class
class CellSetStructured3D:
    points_per_cell = 8  # class constant — used for local_array sizes

    def __init__(self, nx, ny, nz):
        self.nx = nx               # runtime parameter
        self.ny = ny
        self.nxy = nx * ny
        self.nx_plus1 = nx + 1
        self.nxy_plus1 = (nx + 1) * (ny + 1)

    @tack.func
    def get_point_id(self, cell_id, local_idx):
        # Compute connectivity from grid dimensions — zero storage
        ci = cell_id % self.nx
        cj = (cell_id // self.nx) % self.ny
        ck = cell_id // self.nxy
        base = ck * self.nxy_plus1 + cj * self.nx_plus1 + ci
        result = base
        if local_idx == 1:
            result = base + 1
        # ... (7 more vertices)
        return result

@tack.device_class
class CellSetExplicit:
    points_per_cell = 4  # class constant — used for local_array sizes

    def __init__(self, connectivity):
        self.connectivity = connectivity    # tack.array

    @tack.func
    def get_point_id(self, cell_id, local_idx):
        return self.connectivity[cell_id * self.points_per_cell + local_idx]

One kernel, two cell set types:

@tack.kernel
def cell_average(cs, point_data, cell_data, n_cells):
    for c in range(n_cells):
        total = 0.0
        for v in range(cs.points_per_cell):    # loop count is a constant
            total = total + point_data[cs.get_point_id(c, v)]
        cell_data[c] = total / float(cs.points_per_cell)

The loop range(cs.points_per_cell) compiles to range(8) for hexes and range(4) for tetrahedra. The get_point_id call inlines to computed connectivity (structured) or a buffer load (explicit). Same algorithm, different generated GPU code.

docs.title: Cell Type Abstraction
docs.text:
You can separate topology (cell set) from geometry (cell type):

@tack.device_class
class Hexahedron:
    num_points = 8  # class constant

    @tack.func
    def center(self, dim):
        return 0.5

    @tack.func
    def weight(self, vertex, r, s, t):
        # Trilinear shape function
        wr = r
        if vertex % 2 == 0:
            wr = 1.0 - r
        ws = s
        if (vertex // 2) % 2 == 0:
            ws = 1.0 - s
        wt = t
        if vertex // 4 == 0:
            wt = 1.0 - t
        return wr * ws * wt

A generic interpolation kernel takes both:

@tack.kernel
def interpolate_to_center(cs, ct,
                          point_data, cell_data, n_cells):
    for c in range(n_cells):
        pc0 = ct.center(0)
        pc1 = ct.center(1)
        pc2 = ct.center(2)
        val = 0.0
        for v in range(ct.num_points):
            w = ct.weight(v, pc0, pc1, pc2)
            val = val + w * point_data[cs.get_point_id(c, v)]
        cell_data[c] = val

This single kernel works with any cell set + cell type combination.

docs.title: Organize an application around state
docs.text:
Use a device class when several kernels share the same arrays and model parameters. The Physarum tutorial gathers positions and headings into Agents, uses an initialization kernel as a method, and passes the object to three simulation stages. Class constants describe the sensing model; instance dimensions and arrays describe this particular simulation.

The cell-set sketches above show a more generic use: pass different topology implementations to one kernel. They illustrate a protocol; tack.dataset is the built-in mesh API that follows it, with a template per shape and per topology (see the Visualization Guide).

docs.title: Local Arrays
docs.text:
tack.local_array allocates a per-thread private array. It maps to stack memory on CPU and private/register memory on GPU:

@tack.kernel
def cached_interp(cs, ct,
                  array1, array2, out1, out2, n_cells):
    for c in range(n_cells):
        # Compute weights once, reuse for both arrays
        w = tack.local_array(tack.f32, ct.num_points)
        pid = tack.local_array(tack.i32, ct.num_points)
        for v in range(ct.num_points):
            w[v] = ct.weight(v, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)
            pid[v] = cs.get_point_id(c, v)

        v1 = 0.0
        v2 = 0.0
        for v in range(ct.num_points):
            v1 = v1 + w[v] * array1[pid[v]]
            v2 = v2 + w[v] * array2[pid[v]]
        out1[c] = v1
        out2[c] = v2

The size must be known at compilation: a literal, a class constant, a tack.constant, or an expression involving resolved array dimensions and constants, such as CAPACITY * 4. An instance scalar is a runtime parameter and is unsuitable for a portable GPU allocation. Initialize each element before reading it; local scratch storage is not implicitly cleared.

docs.title: local_array_like
docs.text:
When the local array dtype should match an array parameter, use tack.local_array_like instead of hardcoding the type:

@tack.kernel
def generic_process(data, out):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        buf = tack.local_array_like(data, 8)   # inherits the scalar component dtype from data
        buf[0] = data[i]
        out[i] = buf[0]

This works with both f32 and i32 arrays without separate kernels. Only the dtype is inherited: the second argument supplies the size, and no array values are copied. Initialize every scratch element before reading it.

docs.title: Derive a scratch size from an array
docs.text:
Size expressions can combine declared constants and resolved array dimensions. This example reserves two scalars per column, then sums the populated scratch:

PAIR = tack.constant(2)


@tack.kernel
def row_energy(data, out):
    for row in range(data.shape[0]):
        scratch = tack.local_array_like(data, PAIR * data.shape[1])
        for column in range(data.shape[1]):
            x = data[row, column]
            scratch[PAIR * column] = x
            scratch[PAIR * column + 1] = x * x
        total = 0.0
        for column in range(PAIR * data.shape[1]):
            total += scratch[column]
        out[row] = total

For a four-column input, PAIR * data.shape[1] resolves to eight elements. A seven-column input creates a specialization with fourteen. A changing row width changes this allocation size; a scalar argument holding that width would remain a runtime value and would not supply a portable GPU array size.

The scratch is deliberately simple to make the allocation visible; this row calculation could accumulate directly without an array. Download the complete example and check both widths with uv run python docs/examples/array_sizes.py --arch metal --check. The N-body tutorial uses the same constant-expression support for a shared array containing three coordinates per tile entry.

docs.title: Passing Local Arrays to @tack.func
docs.text:
Local arrays can be passed to @tack.func functions, enabling methods that fill an array for the caller. This is useful for cell set abstractions where get_cell_points populates a buffer in one call:

@tack.device_class
class CellSetExplicit:
    points_per_cell = 4  # fixed topology; compile-time allocation size

    def __init__(self, connectivity):
        self.connectivity = connectivity

    @tack.func
    def get_cell_points(self, cell_id, pts):
        for v in range(self.points_per_cell):
            pts[v] = self.connectivity[cell_id * self.points_per_cell + v]

@tack.kernel
def cell_average(cs, data, out, n_cells):
    for c in range(n_cells):
        pts = tack.local_array(tack.i32, cs.points_per_cell)
        cs.get_cell_points(c, pts)      # fills pts in one call
        total = 0.0
        for v in range(cs.points_per_cell):
            total = total + data[pts[v]]
        out[c] = total / float(cs.points_per_cell)

The inliner aliases the local array name directly — no copy, no pointer assignment. The @tack.func body accesses the caller's array in place.

docs.title: Random Numbers
docs.text:
tack.random draws random numbers in kernels from a counter-based generator with explicit state: a kernel seeds a state from the element it works on and a stream number, and every draw returns the value and the next state.

from tack import random

@tack.kernel
def init_particles(pos, vel, n, frame):
    for i in range(n):
        state = random.seed(i, frame)          # element i of this frame
        u, state = random.uniform(state)       # f32 in [0, 1)
        z, state = random.normal(state)        # standard normal
        d, state = random.direction3(state)    # a unit 3-vector; direction2 for 2-D
        pos[i] = d * (0.4 + 0.6 * u)
        vel[i] = d * z

The sequence is a pure function of the integers it was seeded with, so a kernel draws the same numbers on every backend and for any thread order, and a reference written with the module's NumPy mirrors (np_seed, np_uniform, np_normal, ...) over an array of indices draws exactly the same ones; uniform and the states match to the bit, normal and the directions to the rounding of log, sqrt, cos and sin. Unlike Taichi's ti.random(), there is no hidden per-thread state: a different stream number (a frame counter, a pass, a purpose) gives a different sequence, and reusing one repeats it.

docs.title: Atomic Operations
docs.text:
Atomic operations make a single array update indivisible when several iterations contribute to it. Initialize the accumulator before the launch. Atomics do not order arbitrary reads/stores or make a vector update indivisible as a whole; see Gather and scatter.

@tack.kernel
def histogram(data, bins, n):
    for i in range(n):
        idx = int(data[i] * 10.0)
        tack.atomic_add(bins, idx, 1)

Available atomics: - tack.atomic_add(array, index, value) — atomic addition - tack.atomic_min(array, index, value) — atomic minimum - tack.atomic_max(array, index, value) — atomic maximum

Each one is also an expression whose value is the element's value just before the update, which is how threads claim unique slots and append to a shared list:

@tack.kernel
def compact(values, out, count, n):
    for i in range(n):
        if values[i] > 0.0:
            slot = tack.atomic_add(count, 0, 1)    # the old count: this thread's slot
            out[slot] = values[i]

Reset count before each call, allocate enough output capacity, and read it only after the call completes. Slot order depends on execution order. For ordered output and exact allocation, use the count/scan/write tutorial.

For a multi-dimensional array the index is a tuple with one index per dimension, and a vector may supply several of them. On a vector array a vector value updates every component of the element, one atomic per component (and, as an expression, gives the vector of their old values):

@tack.kernel
def scatter(pos, vel, mass, grid_m, grid_v, inv_dx, n):
    for p in range(n):
        cell = int(pos[p] * inv_dx)                     # a 2-vector of cell indices
        tack.atomic_add(grid_m, cell, mass[p])          # grid_m[cell[0], cell[1]] += ...
        tack.atomic_add(grid_v, (cell[0], cell[1]), mass[p] * vel[p])

A plain integer index is the flat, row-major index. On a vector array with a scalar value it is the flat index of one component.

docs.title: Shared Memory
docs.text:
Shared memory is visible to all threads within a workgroup. Use it for cooperative algorithms like parallel reductions.

These kernels require a GPU backend with supports_workgroups=True. CPU rejects shared memory, barriers, thread_id and block reductions. For scratch storage private to each iteration, use tack.local_array or tack.local_array_like; both work on CPU and GPU.

Positive iteration counts must be divisible by 256. Scalar arguments can control collective branches and loops; array-loaded conditions and lane-dependent exits are rejected. See the workgroup contract for the conservative supported domain and unsupported collective expressions.

For example, with fully participating 256-lane workgroups:

@tack.kernel
def block_reduce(data, partial_sums, n):
    for i in range(n):
        smem = tack.shared(tack.f32, 256)
        tid = tack.thread_id()
        smem[tid] = data[i]
        tack.barrier()

        # Tree reduction within workgroup
        stride = 128
        while stride > 0:
            if tid < stride:
                smem[tid] = smem[tid] + smem[tid + stride]
            tack.barrier()
            stride = stride // 2

        if tid == 0:
            tack.atomic_add(partial_sums, 0, smem[0])

For an f32 sum, minimum or maximum over the workgroup, tack.block_sum, tack.block_min and tack.block_max do this in one call; see Reductions and Scans.

  • tack.shared(dtype, size) — allocate threadgroup memory
  • tack.barrier() — synchronize threads in the workgroup
  • tack.thread_id() — thread index within the workgroup

docs.title: shared_like
docs.text:
When the shared memory dtype should match an array parameter, use tack.shared_like instead of hardcoding the type:

@tack.kernel
def generic_reduce(data, partial_sums):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        smem = tack.shared_like(data, 256)   # inherits the scalar component dtype from data
        tid = tack.thread_id()
        smem[tid] = data[i]
        tack.barrier()
        # ... reduction ...

This is especially useful for kernels that need to work with both f32 and i32 arrays without separate implementations. As with local_array_like, only the scalar component dtype is inherited. The size is explicit, and no array values are copied into the shared array.

docs.title: 3D Textures
docs.text:
Wrap an array as a 3D texture for hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation:

# Create texture from an array
data = tack.empty((W * H * D,))
tack.copyto(data, volume_data.ravel())
tex = tack.texture3d(data, shape=(W, H, D))

@tack.kernel
def sample_volume(tex, output, n):
    for i in range(n):
        u = float(i) / float(n)
        output[i] = tex.sample(u, 0.5, 0.5)  # normalized [0,1] coords

Sampling is always trilinear. Which unit does it depends on the backend:

Backend Sampling CPU Software trilinear interpolation, generated in the kernel Metal Hardware texture units, texture3d<float>.sample() CUDA Hardware, tex3D on a texture object HIP Hardware when the device reports image support; software otherwise (for example on CDNA parts such as the MI300) Level Zero Hardware image3d_t when the device has samplers; software on Xe-HPC (Ponte Vecchio)

The texture holds a copy of the array taken by tack.texture3d(), on every backend. Writes to the array afterwards are not visible to it until you call tex.update():

tack.copyto(data, next_frame.ravel())
tex.update()   # sampling now sees next_frame

The array must be f32 and hold W * H * D elements, and interp='linear' is the only interpolation mode. See Backend Implementations.

tex.sample() also works inside @tack.func — texture metadata is propagated through inlining automatically.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text: Vectors are part of the everyday kernel language. See Vectors and matrices for arithmetic, components, array layouts, masks and tack.select.

docs.title: Matrices
docs.text: See Matrices for fixed-size matrix values, products, methods and arrays, and MPM for a worked application.

docs.title: Printing (Debug)
docs.text:
print() works inside kernels on CPU, CUDA, and HIP for debugging:

@tack.kernel
def debug_kernel(data, n):
    for i in range(n):
        if i < 3:
            print("val:", data[i])

This emits printf calls. On Metal, print is a no-op (Metal has no printf). CUDA and HIP launches are queued, so their output may appear only when the host next waits for the device: a read of an array, or tack.sync().

To find an index out of bounds, turn on debug mode instead: it checks every array access and raises IndexError naming the first bad one.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text: Tack compiles the same kernel source to different GPU APIs. Each backend has its own compilation pipeline and memory model.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Backend Platform GPU Compilation Dependencies CPU All None (uses CPU cores) LLVM JIT via llvmlite llvmlite Metal macOS Apple Silicon MSL source → Metal API pyobjc-framework-Metal CUDA Linux/Windows NVIDIA CUDA C → NVRTC → PTX cuda-python>=13.2, NVRTC 13 HIP Linux AMD (ROCm) HIP C → hipRTC hip-python Level Zero Linux Intel OpenCL C → libocloc → SPIR-V Level Zero runtime Warp (prototype) Linux/Windows, Apple silicon NVIDIA through Warp, or Warp's CPU Python @wp.kernel → Warp warp-lang

Every backend keeps what it compiles on disk, so a later process does not compile the same kernel again. See The Kernel Cache.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
A device is where arrays live and kernels run. tack.device("cuda") returns one: the spec is "cpu", "metal", "cuda", "hip" or "level_zero", and the numbered types also take "cuda:1": the second CUDA GPU. Asked for twice, it is the same device, with the kernels it has compiled.

  • tack.set_default_device("cuda") makes it the default device: where arrays are allocated, and where kernels with no array arguments run. With nothing set, the default is the CPU. tack.get_default_device() says which it is.
  • with tack.device("cuda"): makes it the default inside the block, on that thread only. Blocks nest.
  • Every array constructor takes device=, and every array records its device in a.device. a.to_device(d) returns the array itself if its memory is usable on d, else a copy there. empty_like and the other *_like constructors allocate on the prototype's device.
  • A kernel runs where its arrays are: on the default device when that can address them, otherwise on the arrays' own device. Arrays on two devices in one call raise ValueError; move one with to_device first. Copies, reductions and tack.algorithms functions run on their input's device.
  • Switching the default doesn't invalidate anything. Arrays made before the switch keep their device and keep working.
  • tack.sync() waits for every device; d.synchronize() waits for one.

On a machine with several GPUs, tack.device_count("cuda") says how many there are (also for "hip" and "level_zero"), and tack.device("cuda:1") is the second. A bare "cuda" or "hip" is the GPU the thread already uses, as a framework that embeds Tack may have chosen, else the first. Each device compiles its own kernels, and a kernel's arrays must all be on one: b = a.to_device(tack.device("cuda:1")) copies through the host. To split one problem over several devices, or MPI ranks, see Communicate Between Blocks.

Options make a separate device: tack.device("cpu", num_threads=1) is a second CPU device with one thread. It shares memory with the default CPU device, so it runs kernels on CPU arrays made before it.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def scale(x, out, factor):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[i] * factor


x = tack.arange(8, dtype=tack.f32)
out = tack.empty_like(x)            # on x's device
scale(x, out, 2.0)                  # runs where x and out are
assert x.device == tack.get_default_device() and str(x.device) == "cpu"

serial = tack.device("cpu", num_threads=1)
with serial:                        # the default device inside the block
    y = tack.ones(8)
    scale(x, out, 3.0)              # serial can address CPU arrays: runs there
assert y.device == serial
assert x.to_device(serial) is x     # same memory, so no copy
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), np.arange(8) * 3.0)

On a machine with a GPU the same calls move data to it:

gpu = tack.device("cuda")
grid = tack.zeros(1024, device=gpu) # allocated on the GPU
b = x.to_device(gpu)                # a copy of the CPU array
c = tack.empty_like(b)              # on b's device
scale(b, c, 2.0)                    # runs on the GPU, whatever the default

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
Every backend runs the same kernel language, but within its own capabilities. A kernel that uses something a backend lacks is rejected with an error naming the kernel and the missing capability. It is never run with a different meaning.

CPU Metal CUDA HIP Level Zero Warp (prototype) f64 arrays yes no yes yes depends on the device yes Shared memory, barriers, thread_id, block reductions no yes yes yes yes on a CUDA device Atomic array types all ten i32, u32, f32 32- and 64-bit ints, f32, f64 32- and 64-bit ints, f32, f64 i32, u32, f32 32- and 64-bit ints, f32, f64 sum/min/max on the device no (NumPy) f32 f32 f32 f32 no (NumPy) 3D textures software hardware hardware hardware where the device has image support hardware where the device has samplers no Iterations per launch no limit 2^32 device limit (max grid × 256) device limit, at most 2^32 − 256 device limit (max group count × group size) 2^31 − 1

A launch past a backend's limit raises ValueError naming the kernel, the count and the limit; split the work across several calls.

The backend capability contract has the full matrix, what each capability rejects and when, and the subset that is portable to all five supported backends. In code, ask the backend rather than checking its name:

from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend
be = get_backend()
be.supports_f64, be.supports_workgroups, be.supported_atomic_dtypes

docs.title: When a call returns
docs.text: On the CPU a kernel call returns when the kernel has finished. On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero it returns once the launch is queued; the device runs queued launches in order, and fills and host writes take their place in that order. The host waits where it reads an array (numpy(), indexing, reductions, DLPack export) or calls tack.sync(). Most code never needs tack.sync(): it is for timing kernels (see Debugging and timing), and for memory another library reads without Tack. An error in a queued launch is raised at that wait rather than at the call. A launch that uses memory shared with another library (exported through DLPack, or wrapped with tack.array_from_ptr) completes before the call returns. In an asyncio program, await tack.sync_async() and await array.numpy_async() do the waiting in a worker thread, so the event loop keeps running (see Waiting from asyncio).

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
The CPU backend uses LLVM JIT (via llvmlite) to compile kernels to native machine code. Work is split across physical CPU cores using a persistent thread pool. The pool is itself JIT-compiled from LLVM IR, so a fan-out is one call that never enters Python; TACK_CPU_POOL=python uses a ThreadPoolExecutor instead, which is also the fallback on Windows or where the pool cannot be started.

Threading is not free — a fan-out costs a few microseconds when the workers are warm and about a hundred after they have been idle, and the work between launches stays on the calling thread — so the backend only uses it when the serial run would take meaningfully longer than that. It measures both sides: the fan-out cost of the machine it is on, and the per-element cost of each compiled kernel. That matters because the break-even point depends on how much work the kernel does per element, and moves by a factor of a thousand between a memory-bound expression and a compute-heavy one.

Set TACK_CPU_THREADS, or use tack.device("cpu", num_threads=n), to override the thread count. A thread count of 1 runs everything on the calling thread, which is useful when profiling or when Tack is embedded in a host that manages its own threads.

The CPU has no workgroup execution model, and Tack doesn't emulate one. Kernels that use tack.shared, tack.shared_like, tack.barrier, tack.thread_id, tack.block_sum, tack.block_min or tack.block_max are rejected on CPU before anything is compiled or run, even when the primitive sits in a branch that never executes. A call raises RuntimeError, and tack.inspect raises NotImplementedError. For per-iteration scratch storage, use tack.local_array or tack.local_array_like, which work on every backend.

uv sync --extra cpu      # or, in another environment: pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[cpu]'

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

docs.title: Metal
docs.text:
On Apple silicon the GPU buffer and Tack's internal NumPy view share the same allocation. There is no separate device-memory transfer, but the public tack.array, tack.copyto and numpy() calls still copy values. Use the interoperability APIs when you need shared storage.

uv sync --extra metal    # or: pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[metal]'

tack.set_default_device("metal")

Metal has a 31-buffer binding limit per kernel. Tack automatically packs scalar parameters into constant buffers to stay within this limit.

Hardware 3D texture sampling is supported via texture3d<float>.sample().

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
NVIDIA GPUs via the CUDA driver API. Arrays use device memory (cuMemAlloc) with explicit host-device copies.

pip install 'cuda-python>=13.2'

tack.set_default_device("cuda")

Tack works in the device's primary context, the one the CUDA runtime and the libraries on it (PyTorch, CuPy, Warp) use. So Tack and those libraries can take turns on one thread in any order, and arrays pass between them through DLPack without a context switch. If a context is already current when Tack first makes the device (an embedding application's own), Tack adopts that one instead. Tack retains the primary context and, when it is done with it, releases it rather than destroying it, since other libraries may hold it too.

Tack makes the context current on the thread that first asks for the device (tack.device("cuda"), set_default_device or device=). To call kernels from another thread, that thread needs it current too. A thread on which PyTorch, CuPy or the CUDA runtime already used the device has it; otherwise make it current first:

from cuda.bindings import driver

_, cu_device = driver.cuDeviceGet(0)
_, primary = driver.cuDevicePrimaryCtxRetain(cu_device)   # in the other thread
driver.cuCtxSetCurrent(primary)

Calls of one kernel from several threads are safe on every backend: each call runs with its own arguments. On GPU backends calls of the same compiled kernel take turns.

docs.title: HIP
docs.text:
AMD GPUs via ROCm. The codegen extends CUDA — HIP device code uses the same syntax (blockIdx, threadIdx, __global__).

uv sync --extra hip        # hip-python is on PyPI

tack.set_default_device("hip")

ROCm 7.0.2 and 7.1.1 miscompile some integer code. Their device compiler, AMD clang 20 inside hipRTC, can evaluate a 64-bit signed comparison wrongly when it sits inside a long integer expression. The kernel then returns a wrong value with no error. Tack's own tests found one case: a generated expression in which -253 < -1 evaluated false at -O1 and above. The same source is correct on CUDA, as host C++, and under ROCm's clang 23. Whether a kernel is affected depends on the surrounding expression, so Tack can't rewrite around it. Use a ROCm release newer than 7.1 if you can. Go by the ROCm release, not hiprtcVersion(), which reports 9.0 on 7.0.2. On 7.0 and 7.1, check integer-heavy kernels against the CPU backend.

docs.title: Level Zero
docs.text:
Intel GPUs via the Level Zero API. OpenCL C source is compiled to SPIR-V in-process using libocloc, then loaded via zeModuleCreate.

f64 depends on the device. Some Intel GPUs implement double precision and some don't. The backend asks the device when it starts and adds f64 to its supported types only when the device reports it. Level Zero array atomics remain limited to i32, u32 and f32, even on a device with f64 storage. Check tack.device("level_zero")._backend.supports_f64 rather than assuming.

VTK device interop needs a shared context. A Level Zero pointer is meaningful only inside the context it was allocated from, so Tack and VTK must use the same one. Start Tack with tack.interop.vtk.init_level_zero() instead of tack.set_default_device("level_zero"); it returns the Level Zero device, in VTK's context, that it made the default. Arrays on another Level Zero device can't be shared with VTK, and can't be mixed with this device's in one kernel call.

Hardware 3D texture sampling (image3d_t with read_imagef) is used on devices with texture units (Xe-HPG/Xe-LPG). Xe-HPC (Ponte Vecchio) falls back to software trilinear since it has no sampler hardware.

tack.set_default_device("level_zero")

docs.title: Warp (prototype)
docs.text:
A sixth backend runs Tack kernels through NVIDIA Warp, for running Tack, and tack.dataset's filters, inside a program built on Warp. It is a prototype: CI runs its tests on Warp's CPU, and on CUDA its filters matched Tack's CUDA backend bit for bit (a probe to within 2e-7), but it lacks parts of the language (below) and its interface may change. The whole suite runs on it with PYTHONPATH=packages/tack-core/tests uv run pytest -p _warp_default.

uv sync --extra warp       # or: pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[warp]'

tack.set_default_device("warp")

Each kernel variant becomes a @wp.kernel written from Tack's typed IR, which Warp compiles and caches; helpers keep Tack's semantics where Warp's differ (wrapping integers, floor // and %, NaN-preferring min/max, signed zeros, no fused multiply-add across statements). The device is Warp's default device when Tack first makes it: its first CUDA device, else its CPU. Arrays are wp.array buffers, and launches are queued on Warp's current stream, so a wp.ScopedStream around Tack calls applies.

What works: every array type including f64; atomics on 32- and 64-bit integers, f32 and f64; workgroups (shared memory, barriers, thread_id, block reductions) on a CUDA device; array_from_ptr; DLPack both ways (CUDA memory on Warp's device, or host memory on Warp's CPU); debug mode's bounds checks.

What it lacks:

  • tack.inspect: there is no backend source to show; inspect the kernel with arrays on another device.
  • 3D textures: a kernel that samples one raises RuntimeError.
  • Device reductions: sum, min, max and mean reduce through NumPy, as on the CPU.
  • Disk-cached variants: Warp's own kernel cache keeps the compiled code; Tack's disk cache keeps only the lowered IR.
  • Launches above 2^31 − 1 iterations (Warp's 32-bit thread index).

tack.interop.warp (in tack-vis, uv sync --extra warp, which adds warp-simdata) shares arrays with Warp both ways (from_warp, to_warp) and exchanges datasets with warp-simdata (from_simdata, to_simdata), most models without copies. See its reference.

docs.title: Error Messages
docs.text:
If a backend is unavailable, tack.device() gives a clear error:

RuntimeError: Cannot start the 'hip' device: missing dependency.
  No module named 'hip'
  Requires an AMD GPU with ROCm, plus hip-python; in a clone:
    pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[hip]'   (or: uv sync --extra hip)
  ...

Kernel compilation errors show the kernel name, backend, and the relevant error lines without dumping the full generated source. To see the generated code on any backend, use tack.inspect(kernel, *args, mode="source"). On Metal, TACK_DUMP_MSL=1 also writes each compiled kernel's MSL to /tmp. Other backends ignore it.

docs.title: Type Checking
docs.text:
Tack validates array dtypes at dispatch time before compilation. If an array uses a dtype not supported by the target backend, you get a clear error:

TypeError: Kernel 'my_kernel': parameter 'data' has dtype tack.f64, which is
not supported on Metal. Supported dtypes: tack.f32, tack.i16, tack.i32,
tack.i64, tack.i8, tack.u16, tack.u32, tack.u64, tack.u8

tack.inspect applies the same check.

Supported dtypes per backend:

Backend Supported dtypes CPU i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, f64 Metal i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32 (no f64) CUDA i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, f64 HIP i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, f64 Level Zero i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, plus f64 on devices that report it

docs.title: Reductions and Scans
docs.text:
Tack has five ways to combine many values into a few:

Family Entry points Where it runs Array reductions array.sum(), .min(), .max(), .mean() Called from Python; the array's device or NumPy, depending on backend and dtype Statistics var, std, norm, absmax, count_nonzero, dot, histogram in tack.algorithms Called from Python; terms formed on the inputs' device and reduced as arrays are Prefix scans exclusive_scan, inclusive_scan (plus copy, fill_value) in tack.algorithms Called from Python; a sequence of kernels on the inputs' device Sorting and segmented reductions argsort, sort_by_key, gather, unique, reduce_by_key in tack.algorithms Called from Python; a sequence of kernels on the inputs' device Segmented operations segment_reduce, segment_scan, segment_broadcast, segment_ids in tack.algorithms Called from Python; a sequence of kernels on the inputs' device Block reductions tack.block_sum, block_min, block_max Inside a kernel; GPU backends only

Every family runs on all five backends except block reductions, which need a workgroup execution model and are rejected on CPU. A call that returns a Python value (an array reduction, a statistic, a scan's total) waits for the work it reads. On GPU backends launches are queued, so a scan without its total, a sort, or a kernel using block reductions may return before the device has finished; the next read of an array waits for it (see When a call returns).

The behavior below is stated per backend. Where it is the current implementation rather than a promise, the page says so; the reduction contract is the normative text.

docs.title: Array reductions
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")   # or a configured GPU backend

data = tack.array(np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32))

total = data.sum()       # Python float
lo = data.min()
hi = data.max()
average = data.mean()    # data.sum() / data.size
assert (total, lo, hi, average) == (28.0, 0.0, 7.0, 3.5)

Each method reduces every scalar component, whatever the array's shape or element dtype. A reshape preserves the result; there is no axis argument. For a (n,) array with dtype vec3(f32), size is n, but the reduction includes 3 * n components. The result is always a Python float, including for integer arrays.

Where it runs. CPU always reduces with NumPy. Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero reduce f32 arrays on the device with a 256-lane tree per group and an atomic combine of the group results. Every other dtype is copied to the host with numpy() and reduced with NumPy. Two further host fallbacks exist for f32: Metal reduces arrays of 2^32 or more elements with NumPy over its shared buffer, and Level Zero uses NumPy when the device cannot run 256-lane groups.

Accumulator and result.

Input dtype sum() accumulates in min() / max() f32 f32 exact f32 value f64 (not Metal) f64 exact f64 value i8 … i64 i64, wrapping modulo 2^64 exact integer value u8 … u64 u64, wrapping modulo 2^64 exact integer value

The accumulated value is then converted to a Python float, so integer results beyond 2^53 can round. mean() divides the returned sum by array.scalar_size in Python (binary64); it does not use a wider accumulator, and an integer mean inherits any wrapping of the integer sum.

NaN, infinities and zeros. A NaN anywhere makes sum(), min() and max() return NaN. Sums combine infinities by ordinary floating addition: inf + 1 is inf, inf + -inf is NaN. min() of 0.0 and -0.0 is -0.0, max() is 0.0, whatever their order.

Empty arrays. sum() returns 0.0, mean() returns NaN, and min() and max() raise ValueError ("min reduction requires a nonempty array"). None of these launches anything. Every backend allocates a zero-element array.

Run-to-run repeatability.

CPU Metal / CUDA / HIP / Level Zero f32 sum() / mean() NumPy Low bits can differ between calls: group results are combined atomically in whatever order the groups finish other dtypes, sum() / mean() NumPy NumPy min() / max() Order-independent Order-independent integer sum() Exact (with wrapping) Exact (with wrapping)

The NumPy paths currently give the same answer on every call, but the contract does not promise that floating sums are reproducible on any backend. The accuracy that is promised is an absolute error budget, stated in the reduction contract.

What crosses to the host

On a GPU backend an f32 reduction reads back one value. Any other dtype copies the whole array to the host first, on every call.

The implicit arrays of tack.arrays reduce the same way, with the same semantics: tack.arrays.CountingArray(8).sum() is 28. Their values are computed into a temporary array first, which is then reduced as a stored array is. The algorithms below also take implicit arrays as inputs, read in their kernels without a temporary: exclusive_scan(CountingArray(n), offsets, n) scans 0, 1, 2, ... without storing them.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
from tack.algorithms import var, std, norm, absmax, count_nonzero, dot, histogram

v = var(data)                         # population variance
s = std(data)                         # sqrt(var(data))
l1 = norm(data, ord=1)                # sum of |x|
l2 = norm(data)                       # ord=2: Euclidean norm
linf = norm(data, ord=float("inf"))   # max |x|
m = absmax(data)                      # same as norm(data, ord=float("inf"))
nz = count_nonzero(data)
d = dot(data, data)
counts, edges = histogram(data, bins=8, range=(0.0, 8.0))

These functions live in the tack.algorithms package, which import tack does not load. Import them as above, or import tack.algorithms before writing tack.algorithms.var(...).

Each statistic forms its terms -- |x|, x², (x − mean)², a·b -- in a temporary array of the inputs' precision, f64 if any input is f64 and otherwise f32 (an integer input converts before any arithmetic), and reduces that array with Array.sum() or Array.max(). So the array-reduction rules apply to them: their accuracy, repeatability and host traffic are those of array reductions. count_nonzero scans its 0/1 flags into i64 on the device and reads only the total. histogram bins with tack.atomic_add, which gives exact counts in any order.

docs.title: What each function computes
docs.text:
Function Accumulator Returns Notes var(data, n=None) the data's precision, Array.sum() Python float Mean of the first n values, then Σ(x − mean)² / n; integers convert to floating point first; NaN when empty std(data, n=None) as var Python float math.sqrt(var(data, n)) norm(data, ord=2, n=None) the data's precision; Array.sum() for ord 1 and 2, Array.max() for infinity Python float ord must equal 1, 2 or float("inf"); anything else raises ValueError: Unsupported norm order before any launch. 0.0 when empty absmax(data, n=None) as norm(data, float("inf")) Python float 0.0 when empty; a NaN propagates, as in Array.max() count_nonzero(data, n=None) i64, a scan of 0/1 flags Python int Tests x != 0.0: -0.0 counts as zero, NaN as nonzero. Exact past 2^31 dot(a, b, n=None) f64 if either input is f64, otherwise f32; Array.sum() Python float Σ a[i]·b[i]; 0.0 when empty histogram(data, bins=10, range=None, n=None) i32 per bin, atomic_add (counts, edges): an i32 array of bins counts, still on the device, and a NumPy float64 array of bins + 1 edges See below

n is the number of elements to read, in flat (row-major) order, so multi-dimensional arrays work. n=None means data.size (for dot, a.size). Every function checks n against each array it reads and raises ValueError when n is negative or larger than an array, so dot(a, b) with a shorter b is refused rather than reading past it.

With an n smaller than the array, everything covers the first n elements only: var and std take the mean of those elements, and histogram without range takes its range from them. To do that they copy the first n elements into a temporary array and reduce it with Array.sum(), min() and max(), so the mean and range follow the array-reduction rules.

docs.title: Dtypes on each backend
docs.text:
Every input dtype the backend can allocate works. var, std, norm, absmax and dot form terms in a temporary array, then use array reductions. They do not require floating-point atomics in the input's dtype.

Input CPU CUDA / HIP Metal Level Zero f32 supported supported supported supported f64 f64 terms and sums f64 terms and sums; host reduction no f64 arrays f64 terms and sums where supported; host reduction integers runs runs runs runs

Integer inputs convert to the accumulation precision before products, subtraction or absolute values. This avoids integer overflow in a product such as 100000 * 100000, though large integers can round on conversion to floating point. dot uses f64 if either input is f64; otherwise these statistics use f32.

docs.title: Complete example: check accumulation precision
docs.text:
This CPU example checks both conversion before multiplication and double-precision accumulation. Save it as a .py file:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import absmax, dot

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
integers = tack.array(np.array([100000], dtype=np.int32))
assert dot(integers, integers) == 10_000_000_000.0

precise = tack.array(np.array([1.0, 1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-4], dtype=np.float64))
actual = dot(precise, precise)
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, 1.00000003, rtol=0, atol=1e-15)
print(actual)                              # approximately 1.00000003

with_nan = tack.array(np.array([1.0, np.nan], dtype=np.float32))
assert np.isnan(absmax(with_nan))

The same f64 calculation requires a backend that supports f64 arrays. On a GPU it currently copies the temporary f64 terms to the host for the sum, as described under array reductions.

docs.title: NaN, infinity and empty inputs
docs.text:
Function NaN in input Infinity in input n == 0 var, std NaN NaN NaN, as Array.mean() of an empty array norm(ord=1), norm(ord=2), dot NaN inf, or NaN when opposite infinities are added or, in dot, an infinity meets a zero 0.0 norm(ord=inf), absmax NaN inf 0.0 count_nonzero counted as nonzero counted 0 histogram not supported (see below) not supported (see below) all-zero counts with an explicit range; ValueError without one

absmax and norm(ord=inf) reduce absolute values with Array.max(), including its NaN propagation. Histogram inputs still need finite, representable bin coordinates. With no explicit range, a nonfinite autodetected range raises ValueError; passing a finite range does not make a NaN input valid.

An empty array (data.size == 0) behaves like n == 0.

docs.title: Histogram binning
docs.text:
The bin of each value is int((x - lo) * (1 / width)), computed in f32 (f64 for an f64 array), where width = (hi - lo) / bins, then clamped into [0, bins - 1]:

  • values below lo are counted in the first bin and values above hi in the last — unlike numpy.histogram, which drops them;
  • a value equal to hi is counted in the last bin, as in NumPy;
  • range=None uses the minimum and maximum of the first n elements; if they are equal, hi becomes lo + 1;
  • a value whose offset (x - lo) / width does not fit a 32-bit integer, and a NaN, is outside the kernel language's float-to-integer domain. Its bin is backend-dependent: a value of 1e12 with range=(0, 1) lands in the first bin on CPU and in the last on CUDA. Filter such values first.

Use an integer bins of at least 1. bins=0 raises ValueError, as does a range with a nonfinite endpoint or lo > hi. Equal endpoints are expanded by setting hi = lo + 1. For an f32 input the bin arithmetic uses f32 while edges is float64, so a value lying exactly on an interior edge can land on either side of it. counts stays on the device; call counts.numpy() to read it. Counts must fit in each bin's i32 accumulator.

docs.title: Accuracy and repeatability
docs.text:
The sum's order and error budget are those of array reductions. On GPUs, the f32 tree sums combine group results atomically, so their low bits can vary. The current CPU and f64 host reductions use NumPy; portable code should still compare floating sums with a suitable tolerance.

The reduction budget covers summing the terms. Rounding when forming products, squares or deviations from a mean also contributes to a statistic's error. Check against an independent reference in the precision appropriate for the problem. count_nonzero is exact, and histogram counts are exact while they fit their i32 bins. Extrema are order-independent and propagate NaNs as above.

docs.title: Prefix scans
docs.text:
from tack.algorithms import exclusive_scan, inclusive_scan

counts = tack.empty((n,), tack.i32)
offsets = tack.empty((n,), tack.i32)
# ... a kernel fills counts ...

total = exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, n)  # offsets[i] = counts[0] + ... + counts[i-1]
total = inclusive_scan(counts, offsets, n)  # offsets[i] = counts[0] + ... + counts[i]

The classic use is stream compaction: one kernel counts how many outputs each item produces, an exclusive scan turns the counts into write offsets, and the returned total sizes the output array. When the output can exceed 2^31 − 1 elements, keep the counts i32 but make the offsets i64: the scan runs in the output's dtype, so the running sums are formed in i64 and the total comes back exact.

offsets = tack.empty((n,), tack.i64)
total = exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, n)  # i32 counts, i64 offsets and total

Both functions run on every backend, by chunks: each chunk is copied into the output and totalled, the chunk totals are scanned the same way, recursively, and each chunk then writes its running sums from its offset. That is two launches per level, and a level small enough for one thread -- 4096 elements on the CPU, one tile on GPU backends -- is one launch that scans it in order. On the CPU a chunk is 256 elements, one thread each: a million elements take a chunked level and a serial one, three launches. On GPU backends a chunk is a tile of 2048 elements scanned by one workgroup -- eight elements to each of its 256 lanes, the lane totals scanned in shared memory -- so a million elements take a tiled level and a serial one. Launches on the CPU complete before returning; Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero queue them and wait when the host next reads an array. For small arrays, copying to NumPy, calling np.cumsum and copying back can still be faster.

Return value. Both return the sum of the first n inputs, in the output array's dtype, as a Python int (integer outputs) or float (floating outputs). It is read as one element from the device, so only that element comes back to the host, not the whole output.

Behavior.

  • Any dtype the backend allocates works. The scan runs in the output array's dtype; input values convert to it on the copy, as numpy.cumsum does with an output dtype (an i32 input scanned into an f32 output gives f32 sums). Integer sums wrap at the output's width, and so does the returned total.
  • The input is not modified (unless it is also the output). Both functions work in place: exclusive_scan(f, f, n) and inclusive_scan(f, f, n) are correct.
  • Only the first n elements are read and written; later output elements are left alone. n must be at most the size of both arrays; a larger or negative n raises ValueError. n = 0 writes nothing and returns 0, the empty sum.
  • Returning the total means reading it to the host, which waits for the device (on GPU backends, for every launch queued so far). A caller that needs only the offsets passes total=False: the scan returns None, reads nothing, and stays queued with whatever follows.
  • Each call allocates two arrays of the output's dtype per chunked level, the chunk totals and their offsets, one element per chunk: about n / 128 elements in all on the CPU, n / 1024 on GPUs, not a copy of the input, and a one-element array for the total.
  • Integer results are exact (modulo wrapping) and identical on every backend and every run.
  • Floating results are deterministic for a given n and backend. Through the serial level's size -- 4096 elements on the CPU, 2048 on GPUs -- they are added in np.cumsum's order and match it bit for bit; beyond it a chunk starts from the sum of the earlier chunks' totals rather than from the previous element's running sum (on GPUs a tile's lanes from their predecessors' totals, combined in tree order), so results can differ from np.cumsum in the last bits.

docs.title: Copy and fill utilities
docs.text:
from tack.algorithms import copy, fill_value

copy(src, dst, n)          # dst[i] = src[i] for i < n
fill_value(dst, 0, n)      # dst[i] = 0 for i < n

Both are single kernels on their arrays' device and return None. They work on the first n elements in flat order and do not check n against either array.

  • copy converts on store into dst's dtype with the kernel language's rules: floats truncate toward zero (2.7 → 2, -2.7 → -2) and must fit the target; integers wrap. Unlike array.copy(), it writes into an existing array rather than allocating one.
  • fill_value passes value as a kernel scalar argument (a Python float is f32, or f64 when dst is f64; an int is i32, or i64/u64 by magnitude) and converts it on store: 2.5 fills an i32 array with 2, and 300 fills a u8 array with 44. Unlike array.fill(value), which converts the value as NumPy's ndarray.fill does and fills the whole array, it fills a prefix.
  • copy_with_offset(src, dst, dst_offset, n) writes dst[dst_offset + i] = src[i]. It is not re-exported from tack.algorithms; write from tack.algorithms.copy import copy_with_offset. (The attribute tack.algorithms.copy is the copy function, not the submodule, so tack.algorithms.copy.copy_with_offset does not work.)

docs.title: Sorting and segmented reductions
docs.text:
from tack.algorithms import argsort, gather, reduce_by_key, sort_by_key, unique

perm = argsort(keys)                           # index array: keys[perm] ascending, stable
skeys, svals = sort_by_key(keys, values)       # new arrays, values carried along
ukeys, counts = unique(skeys)                  # each distinct key once, and its run length
ukeys, sums = reduce_by_key(skeys, svals)      # one value per distinct key; op="sum"|"min"|"max"
picked = gather(values, perm)                  # picked[i] = values[perm[i]]

These are the building blocks for everything on unstructured data that is free on a structured grid: inverting a connectivity array into the cells around each point, finding the external faces of a mesh (sort the faces, keep the ones that appear once), merging duplicate points. The pattern is always make a key per item, sort, then walk the runs of equal keys:

# The cells around each point, as a CSR structure. conn holds the point
# ids of each cell's corners; cell_of holds the cell id of each entry.
points, cells = sort_by_key(conn, cell_of)     # entries grouped by point
upoints, counts = unique(points)               # each point and its cell count
offsets = tack.empty((upoints.size,), tack.i32)
exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, upoints.size)  # cells[offsets[p]:offsets[p]+counts[p]]

All five functions allocate and return new arrays rather than writing into the caller's, and take an optional n (default: the whole array) with the same bounds check as the scans: n past any array involved raises ValueError, and n = 0 returns empty arrays.

Sorting (argsort, sort_by_key). Keys are i32, u32, i64 or u64 arrays; any other key dtype raises TypeError.
