The sort is stable, so equal keys keep their original order, and sort_by_key's values keep theirs. Values can be any dtype; they are gathered once by the final permutation, so sort_by_key(keys, values) costs an argsort plus two gathers. The permutation is i32 up to 2^31 − 1 elements and i64 beyond; argsort(keys, index_dtype=tack.i64) asks for i64 at any size, as a mesh with 64-bit ids does. unique's counts follow the same rule.

The implementation is a least-significant-digit radix sort over 8-bit digits, built from kernels and the exclusive scan. On the CPU, one thread per chunk of 256 elements counts digits into a private histogram, a scan turns the counts into output slots, and a second kernel scatters each chunk in order. On GPU backends, which have workgroups, each pass instead sorts tiles of 4096 keys in shared memory by their digit (eight stable one-bit splits), scans the tiles' digit counts, and scatters each digit's run; a private histogram per thread is slow on a GPU. Both give the same permutation. The number of passes follows the spread of the keys, not their width: the smallest key is subtracted on the fly, so point ids below 2^16 take two passes whatever the key dtype, and all-equal keys take none. Results are identical on every backend and every run.

Runs of equal keys (unique, reduce_by_key). Both take keys that are already grouped — sorted, or merely with equal keys adjacent — and work on any key dtype that supports !=, floats included. They return the first key of each run in order of appearance, so an unsorted input such as [7, 7, 2, 2, 7] gives [7, 2, 7]; sort first for a true set of distinct keys. unique returns the run lengths as an i32 array. reduce_by_key reduces each run's values with "sum", "min" or "max" into an array of the values' dtype, running one thread per run serially in element order: integer sums are exact modulo the values' width, and floating results are reproducible and equal to a sequential sum of the run. The cost is load imbalance when a few runs are very long; that is the price of not using atomics, whose floating sums would vary between runs.

docs.title: Segmented operations
docs.text:
from tack.algorithms import segment_broadcast, segment_ids, segment_reduce, segment_scan

# Segment k is values[offsets[k]:offsets[k + 1]]: CSR offsets, empty segments allowed.
sums = segment_reduce(values, offsets)               # one per segment; op="min"|"max"|"mean"
prefix = segment_scan(values, offsets)               # running sums, restarting per segment
before = segment_scan(values, offsets, inclusive=False)
spread = segment_broadcast(sums, offsets, n)         # each segment's value on its elements
ids = segment_ids(offsets, n)                        # each element's segment, -1 outside

A collection of variable-length segments -- each cell's points, each point's cells, the degrees of freedom of each element, the rows of a sparse matrix -- is flat values and CSR offsets, size(offsets) - 1 segments. These are its reductions, prefix sums and broadcasts, where reduce_by_key needs keys and gives one thread to each run.

Shapes. A segment of up to 256 elements is one thread's, in element order; a longer one is cut into chunks of 256, each a thread's, and a segment over several chunks is combined a level up, the same way. So many short segments cost one pass, and one enormous segment a few launches rather than one thread walking it. On an M1 Max's GPU, a 10M-element segment reduces in 4 ms where a thread per segment takes 1.2 s; 2.5M segments of about 4 elements take the same 0.6-0.7 ms either way.

Results. Integer sums wrap at the values' width; min and max are exact. Floating sums group by those fixed chunks, so they are the same bits on every backend and every run, though a long segment's sum is not the sequential one; segment_reduce(..., ordered=True) sums each segment in element order, one thread a segment, as reduce_by_key does. An empty segment reduces to empty=, by default 0 for a sum, NaN for a floating mean and the type's greatest or least (an infinity for floats) for min and max; empty="keep" leaves its output as it was. tack-vis averages over each point's cells this way (point gradients, cell-to-point projection, surface normals), reading the values through the point links without gathering them: a point at the apex of 403,200 tetrahedra took 294 ms on an M1 Max's GPU, one thread walking its links, and takes 5.7 ms. Vectors reduce componentwise. Elements outside every segment (offsets need not start at 0 or end at the last value) are left alone. In debug mode (tack.set_debug) the offsets are checked to be non-decreasing and within the values.

docs.title: Block reductions inside kernels
docs.text:
tack.block_sum(v), tack.block_min(v) and tack.block_max(v) combine one f32 value from every lane of a 256-lane workgroup and give every lane the result. Use them to reduce within a kernel without a separate pass:

@tack.kernel
def group_sums(data, partial, n):
    for i in range(n):
        s = tack.block_sum(data[i])     # every lane of the group gets the same s
        if tack.thread_id() == 0:
            partial[i // 256] = s       # one lane writes the group's result

n = 1 << 20                             # a multiple of 256
data = tack.empty((n,))
partial = tack.empty((n // 256,))
group_sums(data, partial, n)
total = partial.sum()

With for i in range(n), group g holds iterations 256*g to 256*g + 255, and tack.thread_id() is the lane's position in it.

Backends. Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero. CPU has no workgroups and rejects any kernel that contains a block reduction, even in a branch that never runs: calling it raises RuntimeError ("Kernel 'group_sums' failed on CPUBackend: CPU backend does not support workgroup execution required by block_sum, thread_id ..."), and tack.inspect raises NotImplementedError. Check get_backend().supports_workgroups to choose a path, and use the array reductions or statistics above on CPU.

Rules. The workgroup contract has the full conservative domain; in short:

  • f32 only. The argument must be f32 and the result is f32. Anything else raises TypeError ("block_sum requires f32 input; use an explicit f32 cast") on the first call. Write tack.block_sum(tack.f32(x)) for an integer or f64 value.
  • Complete groups. A positive iteration count must be a multiple of 256, including stepped ranges and the total of a tack.ndindex. Otherwise the call raises ValueError ("... require complete 256-lane groups; iteration count 1000 would create a partial workgroup") before anything runs. A count of zero runs nothing. Tack does not pad; pad the data to a multiple of 256 with the reduction's identity (0.0 for a sum, inf for a minimum, -inf for a maximum).
  • Every lane participates. The reduction must be reached by all lanes of the group: not under a condition that depends on the loop index, an array value or thread_id(), not after a lane-dependent break or continue, and not in a conditional expression, the second operand of and/or, or a while condition. Conditions on scalar arguments and on earlier block-reduction results are fine. Violations raise ValueError naming the kernel and IR location. To reduce a subset, have every lane contribute, using the identity where it should not count: tack.block_sum(x if x > 0.0 else 0.0).
  • The generated reduction includes its own barriers, including one after the result is read, so no extra tack.barrier() is needed around it.

Values. block_min and block_max follow the array-reduction rules: a NaN in the group gives NaN, and zero ties give -0.0 for the minimum and 0.0 for the maximum. block_sum adds in a tree whose order may vary, with the same error budget as array sums over the group's terms. Combining the group sums with tack.atomic_add adds in arrival order, so such a total can change in its low bits from run to run.

docs.title: From Python to a Tack program
docs.text:
A Tack application contains two kinds of code. Host code is ordinary Python: it allocates arrays, prepares data, chooses which kernels to run, repeats timesteps, and displays the results. Device code is the body of a @tack.kernel or @tack.func: Tack reads that source and compiles its supported numerical operations for the selected backend. On the CPU, device code still means compiled code.

Understanding that boundary makes it much easier to turn a NumPy calculation into a program that runs on a GPU.

docs.title: Start with one operation per element
docs.text:
Suppose you want out = alpha * x + y. NumPy expresses the whole array operation at once. A Tack kernel expresses what happens to one element and provides the iteration space:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
x = tack.array(np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32))
y = tack.array(np.ones(8, dtype=np.float32))
out = tack.empty((8,))

@tack.kernel
def saxpy(x, y, out, alpha):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = alpha * x[i] + y[i]

saxpy(x, y, out, 2.0)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(out.numpy(), np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32) * 2 + 1)

The allocation, call and assertion run in Python. The arithmetic in saxpy runs as compiled code. The loop has eight independent iterations. Tack may schedule them in any order; the program is correct because iteration i owns out[i].

docs.title: A call describes a whole launch
docs.text:
A kernel has one parallel for directly in its body. Nested loops run sequentially within an iteration. For a row sum, assign one iteration to a row and let that iteration walk its columns:

@tack.kernel
def row_sums(matrix, sums, rows, columns):
    for row in range(rows):
        total = 0.0
        for column in range(columns):
            total += matrix[row, column]
        sums[row] = total

Here total belongs to one iteration. A local variable does not communicate between threads. Sequential statement order inside an iteration is preserved; it does not establish an order between rows.

For a serial recurrence, use for _ in range(1) with an ordinary loop inside it. For multidimensional work, use tack.ndindex. See Kernels for stepped ranges, interior ranges and variable-length inner loops.

docs.title: Separate stages into separate kernels
docs.text:
Consider particle motion: first compute every force from the old positions, then update every position. Writing positions while other iterations still read them mixes old and new state. Put the two stages in separate kernels:

@tack.kernel
def compute_force(pos, force, n):
    for i in range(n):
        force[i] = -pos[i]                 # independent restoring force

@tack.kernel
def integrate(pos, vel, force, dt, n):
    for i in range(n):
        vel[i] += dt * force[i]
        pos[i] += dt * vel[i]

for step in range(100):                    # Python controls the simulation
    compute_force(pos, force, n)
    integrate(pos, vel, force, 0.01, n)

Every launch sees the results of the launches before it, and every host access to an array -- numpy(), tack.copyto, indexing, reductions -- sees the results of every launch before it. So the second kernel sees the completed force array, and so does a read after the loop. On the CPU a call completes before Python continues; on CUDA, HIP, Metal and Level Zero it is queued and returns at once, and the host access waits. The program above behaves the same either way, and there is no stream or event to manage. tack.sync() waits for everything launched so far on every device, for timing kernels or for memory another library reads without Tack.

docs.title: Waiting from asyncio
docs.text:
A host access that waits blocks its thread. In an application with an event loop -- a trame or web server, a Jupyter kernel -- that thread is the loop, and nothing else runs while the device works. Two coroutines wait in a worker thread instead:

async def frame():
    advance(state, dt)                        # queued; returns at once
    await tack.sync_async()                   # the loop runs while it works
    pixels = await image.numpy_async()        # wait, then copy, off the loop
    return pixels

tack.sync_async() waits for the launches made on every device before the call, not for ones another task queues while it waits. numpy_async returns every write queued before the call; one queued later by another task may or may not be in it, so order the two with await if it matters. A launch's error is raised at the await. On CUDA, HIP, Metal and Level Zero the wait runs in a worker thread; on the CPU, whose launches complete before returning, both return at once.

A tack.barrier() synchronizes only a GPU workgroup. It cannot turn two stages over a whole grid into one ordered launch. Use completed kernel calls for that. The memory chapter explains stencil buffers, scatter operations, and the cases where atomics are appropriate.

docs.title: Choose what changes between calls
docs.text:
There are three common ways to give device code a numerical value:

Kind of value How to supply it Example A coefficient changing each call Scalar argument advance(pos, vel, dt, n) A fixed model parameter tack.constant GRAVITY = tack.constant(9.8) An array of state Array argument or device-class attribute Particle positions, a grid, a counter

An ordinary Python global such as gravity = 9.8 is not captured in device code. Declare a constant or pass it. Changing a runtime argument changes the next call without changing the kernel source. Constants are fixed when the specialization is first lowered; rebinding a Python name later does not update cached code.

@tack.device_class gathers arrays and parameters into an object. Its instance scalars are runtime arguments; its class constants and method structure help define the compiled specialization. The Templates chapter shows how to use this to organize a solver.

docs.title: Shapes, values and compilation
docs.text:
The first call includes compilation. Later compatible calls reuse the compiled variant. Changing a scalar value usually reuses it. Changing the scalar's dtype, array dtype, vector width, template structure or a baked-in dimension may create another variant.

This distinction matters for a grid. A 1-D length used only as the launch bound can vary without recompilation; multidimensional indexing uses row strides that depend on the shape. Two grids with different shapes may need different code even when the Python kernel is identical. Prefer fixed working arrays during a simulation; allocate once and update them each frame.

See Kernel Caching for examples and Debugging and timing for how to measure warm calls.

docs.title: The kernel language uses Python syntax
docs.text:
Many familiar constructs work: arithmetic, if, sequential for and while, vectors, matrices and device-function calls. Arbitrary Python objects, NumPy calls and file operations do not run inside a kernel. For example, generate an initial state with NumPy on the host, upload it, then work on the array:

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
initial = rng.normal(size=1024).astype(np.float32)  # Python / NumPy
data = tack.array(initial)

Use tack.random for random draws within a kernel. Use @tack.func for reusable compiled helpers. Such helpers can be called from kernels and other device functions, rather than as ordinary host functions.

Write complete examples in a .py file: Tack needs the decorated function's source to compile it. Dynamically generated functions and interactive contexts that cannot supply their source are poor starting points for learning the API.

Before tackling a larger program, run Heat diffusion. It combines allocation, a multidimensional kernel, a Python timestep loop and a NumPy reference in one small script.

docs.title: Memory and parallel correctness
docs.text: The most useful question when writing a parallel kernel is: which iteration owns each output, and what can it read while other iterations are writing? Start with independent writes. Add sharing only when the algorithm requires it.

docs.title: Describe your layout explicitly
docs.text:
A scalar array with shape=(height, width) stores height * width values in row-major order: the last index varies fastest. image[row, column] is the same scalar as image[row * width + column] in a kernel.

For a two-row, three-column array, the last index runs fastest:

flowchart TB
    A["Logical grid: shape = (2, 3)"] --> B["Row 0: a[0,0] · a[0,1] · a[0,2]"]
    A --> C["Row 1: a[1,0] · a[1,1] · a[1,2]"]
    B --> D["Flat storage: row 0, then row 1"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["Scalar offsets: 0 · 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5"]

A vector array adds components to each logical element:

Allocation Logical element numpy() tack.empty((h, w)) One f32 scalar per pixel (h, w) tack.empty((h, w), tack.vec3()) One RGB vector per pixel (h, w, 3) tack.empty((n,), tack.mat2()) One 2×2 matrix per particle (n, 2, 2)

Every row uses the same constructor and download method. The dtype determines the component dimensions, which are appended to the array shape in NumPy. Host indexing reads a logical element; flat component indexing is an internal storage convention.

For an RGB array, the flat order is R00, G00, B00, R01, G01, B01, …: components stay together, then the column advances, then the row.

The introductory grid examples use (height, width) and [row, column]. The dye tutorial instead uses (width, height) and [x, y] to match its coordinate arithmetic; it transposes for image output. Both conventions are valid, but conversions must respect which one was used. Uniform-grid visualization uses x-fast flat indexing: i + nx_points * (j + ny_points * k). That is a different convention from a scalar array with shape (nx_points, ny_points, nz_points); do not interchange the layouts without arranging the data accordingly.

docs.title: One writer per output
docs.text:
This kernel is safe even when it updates its input in place:

@tack.kernel
def scale(data, factor):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        data[i] *= factor

Iteration i only accesses its own element. The same reasoning applies to per-particle velocity updates when each iteration reads completed forces and writes only its own particle.

Tack does not establish race freedom for you. A kernel compiling successfully does not mean two iterations cannot interfere. Array accesses are not bounds-checked either: keep indices within the storage you allocated. Debug mode (tack.set_debug(True) or TACK_DEBUG=1) checks every array index and raises IndexError naming the access, for finding such a bug. Negative host indices count from the end; do not assume that rule for kernel array loads.

docs.title: Neighbour reads need a stable input
docs.text:
A smoothing stencil reads the old values around every cell. Updating the same array allows one iteration to see a neighbour already changed by another. Use distinct input/output arrays:

@tack.kernel
def smooth(old, new, n):
    for i, j in tack.ndindex(n, n):
        if 0 < i < n - 1 and 0 < j < n - 1:
            new[i, j] = 0.25 * (old[i - 1, j] + old[i + 1, j]
                               + old[i, j - 1] + old[i, j + 1])
        else:
            new[i, j] = 0.0

for step in range(steps):
    smooth(old, new, n)
    old, new = new, old

The swap changes Python references and costs no array copy. Both buffers must have the same layout. Write every output that the next step will read, including the boundary. When using an interior-only ndindex, initialize or explicitly maintain the unwritten border of both buffers: a new array's contents are unspecified, and tack.zeros is the allocation that starts at zero.

The heat tutorial develops this pattern. In-place numerical schemes can be valid when they have an explicit ordering strategy, such as red-black updates in separate calls, but that needs an algorithm-specific argument.

docs.title: Views still share storage
docs.text:
reshape is a view; copy makes independent storage:

grid = tack.empty((8, 8))
view = grid.reshape((64,))                 # same allocation
independent = grid.copy()                 # another allocation

Passing grid and view as two arguments does not provide two independent buffers. Tack preserves valid aliasing within each iteration; overlapping arguments do not make concurrent conflicting accesses safe. Use a separate allocation for a stencil output.

docs.title: Gather and scatter
docs.text:
In a gather, one iteration reads several inputs and owns its destination. A row sum or a particle interpolating a completed grid is a gather. No atomic is needed for its output.

In a scatter, several iterations may contribute to the same destination. Particles depositing mass to a grid need atomic addition:

@tack.kernel
def deposit(cell_ids, mass, grid_mass, n):
    for p in range(n):
        tack.atomic_add(grid_mass, cell_ids[p], mass[p])

grid_mass.fill(0.0)                        # reset once on the host
deposit(cell_ids, mass, grid_mass, n)

Plain grid_mass[cell_ids[p]] += mass[p] can lose contributions. An atomic makes that one update indivisible. It does not make a whole algorithm ordered. A vector atomic performs one update per component, rather than one indivisible update of the vector as a whole. Floating additions can arrive in different orders, so their low bits may differ between runs.

Finish depositing before starting a kernel that reads the grid. The Physarum and MPM tutorials show this separation explicitly. Check the backend's supported atomic dtypes; f64 storage support alone does not imply f64 atomic support.

docs.title: Claiming slots and allocating output
docs.text:
An atomic return value can claim a unique slot in a preallocated buffer:

@tack.kernel
def append_positive(values, out, count, n):
    for i in range(n):
        if values[i] > 0.0:
            slot = tack.atomic_add(count, 0, 1)
            out[slot] = values[i]

count.fill(0)
append_positive(values, out, count, n)      # out needs capacity for at least n items
length = count[0]

The order of appended items is unspecified. The counter must be initialized, and capacity is the caller's responsibility. An atomic does not allocate storage or check the resulting index.

When order matters or capacity is unknown, count → scan → write gives each input its own output interval and tells Python the exact allocation size. See Marching squares for a complete example.

docs.title: Host access and ownership
docs.text:
Every array belongs to the device it was allocated on (a.device), and a kernel runs on its arrays' device. Changing the default device does not move existing arrays; they keep working where they are. Use a.to_device(d) to copy one to another device. See Devices.

tack.copyto and numpy() transfer complete arrays. On CPU and Metal storage is host-addressable, but these calls still copy values. A host read array[i] reads one logical element; CUDA, HIP and Level Zero copy just that range, one transfer per read. Avoid making it the inner loop of an application. On GPU backends launches are queued, and each of these reads first waits for the launches before it; see When a call returns.

For shared storage, array_from_ptr and DLPack have distinct lifetime and writability rules. Keep an external pointer's owner alive for as long as its Tack view is used. See Interoperability.

docs.title: Vectors and matrices
docs.text: Particles, colours, directions and local deformation all have several components. Tack lets you express their arithmetic as small values instead of maintaining one scalar name per component. A value lives inside an iteration; a vector or matrix array stores one such value per element across iterations and launches.

docs.title: Start with positions and velocities
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
pos = tack.empty((3,), tack.vec2(tack.f32))
vel = tack.empty((3,), tack.vec2(tack.f32))
tack.copyto(pos, np.array([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1]], dtype=np.float32))
vel.fill([1.0, 0.0])

@tack.kernel
def advance(pos, vel, dt):
    for i in range(pos.shape[0]):
        pos[i] += dt * vel[i]

advance(pos, vel, 0.5)
print(pos.numpy())    # [[0.5, 0.0], [1.5, 0.0], [0.5, 1.0]]

Each iteration loads a two-component velocity and updates its own position. dt broadcasts to both components. Multiplying two vectors with * multiplies corresponding components; use dot or @ for a dot product.

A local assignment p = pos[i] loads a value. Changing p.x changes that local; write pos[i] = p to store it back. Writing pos[i].x targets the array directly. Vectors have a fixed width for each compiled specialization. There are no runtime-length vector values or swizzle constructors such as v.rgb/tack.vec4(v, 1.0); construct the components explicitly.

docs.title: Vectors
docs.text:
Choose a vector element dtype through vec2, vec3, vec4, or vec(n). The component dtype defaults to f32, the default float type. The ordinary array constructors allocate its storage, and vector operations are scalarized at the IR level:

v = tack.empty((n,), tack.vec3(tack.f32))

@tack.kernel
def normalize_vectors(v, n):
    for i in range(n):
        vec = v[i]                   # loads 3 components
        length = sqrt(vec[0]**2 + vec[1]**2 + vec[2]**2)
        v[i] = vec / length          # stores 3 components

Arithmetic works on whole vectors, component by component, and a scalar operand is applied to every component. So do the math builtins, the casts and conditional expressions:

@tack.kernel
def step(pos, vel, grid, out, dt, n):
    for i in range(n):
        v = vel[i]
        v = min(max(v, -10.0), 10.0)        # clamp each component
        cell = int(floor(pos[i] / 0.25))    # a vector of i32 cell indices
        v = v if pos[i].y > 0.0 else -v     # one condition, whole vectors
        speed = v.norm()                    # methods are listed below
        vel[i] = v
        pos[i] += v * dt                    # augmented store to an array element
        out[i] = grid[cell] * speed         # grid[cell] is grid[cell[0], cell[1], cell[2]]

In a kernel the element-type names build vector values: tack.vec3(x, y, z) from three scalars, tack.vec3(s) with every component s, and tack.vec3(v) from a 3-vector (vec2 and vec4 likewise). A list of scalars is also a vector, of any width, so it can stand wherever a vector is expected: pos[i] = [x, y], v = [0.0, 0.0], w.dot([1.0, 0.0]), p - [1.0, 0.0].

The vector methods are norm(), norm_sqr(), dot(w), cross(w) (3-vectors), normalized(), and the reductions over components sum(), min() and max(). norm(eps) is sqrt(norm_sqr() + eps), a length that is never zero. normalized(eps) divides by norm() + eps, for a vector that may be zero. min and max as functions take two or more values, as in Python: min(a, b, c).

Comparing vectors compares component by component and gives a mask, a vector of 0/1. any and all reduce a mask to one truth value, and tack.select(mask, a, b) picks per component:

@tack.kernel
def confine(pos, vel, alive, n):
    for i in range(n):
        p = pos[i]
        inside = -1.0 <= p <= 1.0                  # a mask, every link evaluated
        if not all(inside):
            alive[i] = 0
        vel[i] = tack.select(inside, vel[i], -vel[i])    # reflect the components outside
        pos[i] = tack.select(p > 1.0, 1.0, p)             # a scalar arm fills every component
        hits = (p > 0.9) and (vel[i] > 0.0)              # and/or act per component on masks
        if any(hits):
            alive[i] += hits.sum()

A mask is an ordinary integer vector, so mask.sum() counts. if and while take a scalar condition: a mask there is rejected with the hint to reduce it with any or all.

A device function can return several values, vectors among them, to be unpacked at the call:

@tack.func
def closest_hit(origin, direction):
    ...
    return distance, normal, color        # a scalar and two vectors

distance, normal, color = closest_hit(o, d)

A vector array's shape excludes its component dimension. A vector array of shape (n,) and dtype tack.vec3(tack.f32) downloads as (n, 3) with numpy(), and tack.copyto takes values of that shape, or values that broadcast to it (one (3,) vector, say), not the flat storage shape. size is n; scalar_size is 3 * n. scalar_dtype gives the component type. Copies and reshapes preserve the element type; reshaping changes only the array dimensions, without copying storage.

Two vectors in one operation must have the same number of components. An assignment evaluates its whole right side before it stores anything, so v = v.cross(w) and pos[i] = pos[i].cross(axis[i]) read the old components. A tuple assignment does the same and then assigns its targets from left to right, and its targets may be array elements: pos[i], vel[i] = p, v, or a[i], b[i] = b[i], a[i] to swap two.

A store to an array element must match the array: a vector of the array's width, or a scalar, which sets every component (vel[i] = 0.0). A vector of another width, or a vector stored into an array of scalars, is rejected.

Components are scalars. vec[0] and vec.x read one (x, y, z, w name the first four); vec[1] = x, vec.y = x and vec[1] += x write one. The same forms work on an array element without naming the vector first: v[i][2] and v[i].z read a component, v[i][2] = x and v[i].z += x store one. The index may be a runtime value (vec[k] for a loop variable k), which lowers to a chain of selects rather than a branch; a typed or integer tack.constant read that way is instead one load from a constant array. A runtime index must be in [0, n): outside it, on either side, a read gives the last component and a write does nothing, since a kernel cannot raise. Only a literal index counts from the end (vec[-1]), and a literal out of range is rejected at lowering.

docs.title: Matrices
docs.text:
Matrices are small and fixed-size, up to 4×4. Like vectors they are scalarized: a matrix is its entries, and every operation expands to scalar arithmetic at lowering.

F = tack.empty((n,), tack.mat2(tack.f32))    # a 2x2 matrix per particle
C = tack.empty((n,), tack.mat2(tack.f32))

@tack.kernel
def update(F, C, x, dt, n):
    for p in range(n):
        F[p] = (tack.identity(2) + dt * C[p]) @ F[p]   # '@' multiplies
        J = F[p].determinant()
        stress = (F[p] - F[p].inverse().transpose()) * J      # '*' is entry by entry
        x[p] += stress @ tack.vec2(0.0, -1.0) * dt        # matrix @ vector
  • Building one. tack.mat2([a, b], [c, d]) from rows of scalars, tack.mat2(u, v) from vectors as rows, tack.mat2(a, b, c, d) from four scalars in row-major order (mat3, mat4 likewise); tack.mat(row, ...) for any shape up to 4×4, such as three rows of two; tack.identity(n) for a literal n, as np.identity; or u.outer_product(v).
  • Products. A @ B for matrices; A @ v and v @ A take a vector as a column and as a row and give a vector; u @ v is the dot product. Shapes must agree. +, -, *, /, the math builtins and scalar operands work entry by entry, as for vectors.
  • Methods. transpose(); for square matrices trace(); for 2×2 and 3×3 determinant() and inverse(). inverse() divides by the determinant without checking it. norm() and sum() run over all entries.
  • Entries. A[i, j] reads one and A[i, j] = x or A[i, j] += x writes one, on a matrix variable or directly on an array element (F[p][0, 1]). The indices may be runtime values, which must then be in range.
  • Arrays. A matrix array stores each matrix in row-major order. tack.copyto takes (*shape, n, m) and numpy() returns it. F[p] = A, F[p] += A, F[p] *= s and tack.atomic_add(F, p, A) work as they do for vector arrays.
  • Device functions take and return matrices, alone or among several values.

A matrix and a vector with the same number of entries are different things: storing one where the other belongs, or adding them, is rejected.

The statistics in tack.algorithms (dot, norm, var, ...) accept a vector array and reduce over all its components in storage order.

docs.title: Matrices in a real computation
docs.text:
In MPM, each particle stores a 2×2 affine velocity matrix. A matrix-vector product predicts a velocity contribution at a nearby grid node; an outer product reconstructs the affine matrix during interpolation. The example shows why * and @ mean different operations, and why a matrix array is clearer than a four-component vector used as a matrix by hand.

The dye tutorial reuses one interpolation function on RGB vectors. N-body accumulates three-component directions. Use those examples after the small position update above.

The same names serve both sides: on the host tack.vec3() and tack.mat2() are element dtypes that allocate arrays of vectors and matrices, and in a kernel tack.vec3(x, y, z) and tack.mat2(...) build values.

docs.title: Debugging, numerical checks and timing
docs.text: Start a new kernel with a small input and a result you can calculate independently. Once it agrees, increase the problem size and change the backend. This makes layout errors, unsupported operations and numerical differences much easier to separate.

docs.title: Compare a complete calculation
docs.text:
The first check should include input upload, execution and output download:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
host_x = rng.normal(size=32).astype(np.float32)
x = tack.array(host_x)
out = tack.empty(host_x.shape)

@tack.kernel
def transform(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = sqrt(abs(x[i]))

transform(x, out)
actual = out.numpy()
expected = np.sqrt(np.abs(host_x))
assert np.isfinite(actual).all()
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=2e-6, atol=1e-7)

An independent reference should express the mathematics directly. Copying the same indexing expressions into a second kernel can reproduce the same mistake. For a stencil, a NumPy slice expression is a useful contrast with the kernel's per-cell loads. For a surface, check that vertices lie near the analytic level set and that connectivity indices are valid.

The tutorials include such checks, executable without image dependencies:

uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch cpu
uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch metal  # on an Apple GPU

These commands require the selected backend; they do not silently fall back to another one. The CPU run checks the portable algorithms, while a GPU run also executes N-body's shared-memory path.

docs.title: Choose a tolerance for the computation
docs.text:
Use exact comparisons for small integer results where arithmetic does not overflow. Floating computations need a tolerance that accounts for precision, operation order and the problem's sensitivity.

assert_allclose accepts an element when abs(actual - expected) <= atol + rtol * abs(expected). Absolute tolerance is particularly useful around zero. Keep reference and input dtypes explicit; an accidental float64 reference may answer a different precision question.

Transcendentals can differ slightly across vendor libraries. Multiply-add contraction can alter rounding. Parallel floating reductions and atomic scatters can change summation order even between runs on one backend. A simulation may amplify those differences over many steps. Check an early timestep as well as the final result, and consider physical properties such as mass conservation, residuals or bounded temperatures when a long trajectory is sensitive.

Do not increase a tolerance merely to hide a discrepancy. First check array layout, boundaries, initialization, dtype conversions and cross-iteration races. Use Arrays and Types for literal precision and integer rules, and Reductions and Scans for accumulator precision. Statistics such as dot form their terms in f64 if either input is f64, and otherwise in f32, then use array reductions. For f32 inputs, a float64 reference is useful for measuring accumulated error; it is not a promise that the f32 result will agree in every bit.

docs.title: Diagnose the failing stage
docs.text:
Symptom First thing to inspect Unknown name in device code Pass a runtime value or declare tack.constant; check the defining namespace Array has unexpected values or shape Compare NumPy shapes and dtype; distinguish vectors from flat components Results change between runs Conflicting stores, missing atomics, or floating atomic summation Only boundary cells are wrong Bounds and initialization of both timestep buffers: run in debug mode (below) A crash, or garbage that moves with the input size An index out of bounds: run in debug mode (below) Kernel rejected on CPU Workgroup primitives need a GPU; use a portable path or local arrays Kernel rejected on Metal Look for f64, unsupported atomic types, or a runtime array size Every call seems slow Compilation/specialization, allocation, readback after every launch, or many small launches

print in a kernel is useful on CPU, CUDA and HIP. Limit it to a few iterations and remove it when timing. Metal does not provide this printing facility. For portable inspection, write diagnostic values to an array and read it after the call.

docs.title: Check every index with debug mode
docs.text:
An index out of bounds is the usual cause of a kernel that crashes, or that gives wrong values near the edges of an array. Kernels do not check indices, so a[i, j + 1] at the last column quietly reads the first element of the next row. Turn on debug mode to find it:

tack.set_debug(True)    # or run with TACK_DEBUG=1 in the environment

Every array index is then checked, one dimension at a time. An access out of bounds is skipped (a load gives 0) and the call raises IndexError naming the first one:

IndexError: Kernel 'blur': a[i, j + 1] at blur.py:14, column 19: index 64 of
dimension 1 is outside [0, 64). The access was skipped (a load gives 0).
63 more out-of-bounds accesses in the launch were skipped too.

An access in a @tack.func names the device function and its line. Debug mode works on every backend and compiles kernels anew, so it is for finding bugs, not for timing: each launch waits for its result. tack.set_debug(False) turns it off again. TACK_DEBUG is read once, when Tack is imported.

To inspect compilation without running the kernel:

print(tack.inspect(transform, x, out, mode="ir"))
print(tack.inspect(transform, x, out, mode="source"))

Pass the actual argument types and shapes. Inspection uses them to prepare the same specialization and applies the backend's capability checks. mode="optimized" shows optimized LLVM IR on CPU only. See Inspecting Generated Code.

docs.title: Measure first-call and warm time separately
docs.text:
On the CPU a call returns when the kernel has finished. On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero it returns once the launch is queued, and the host waits only when it reads an array or calls tack.sync(). Call tack.sync() before reading the clock, or a GPU time measures only the launch. The first call also includes compilation, unless an earlier process left the kernel in the disk cache; run with TACK_CACHE=off to time a cold compile. Record these separately:

from time import perf_counter

@tack.kernel
def timed_transform(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = sqrt(abs(x[i]))

start = perf_counter()
timed_transform(x, out)                    # this kernel has not been called yet
tack.sync()                                # wait for a queued GPU launch
first_call = perf_counter() - start

for _ in range(5):
    timed_transform(x, out)                 # warm compilation and CPU scheduling
tack.sync()

times = []
for _ in range(30):
    start = perf_counter()
    timed_transform(x, out)
    tack.sync()
    times.append(perf_counter() - start)

print(f"First call: {first_call * 1e3:.3f} ms")
print(f"Warm median: {np.median(times) * 1e3:.3f} ms")

The 32-element diagnostic example is intentionally small; use a larger array when studying throughput. Keep its shape and dtype fixed during measurement. On CPU the scheduler measures whether worker threads help; several warm calls allow that policy to settle. A single-thread run can help distinguish scheduling cost from compiled arithmetic: tack.set_default_device("cpu", num_threads=1).

Measure end-to-end application time separately, including upload, preprocessing, kernel stages and readback. Allocate working arrays outside the timed loop when studying kernel execution, and describe which costs a reported number includes. There is no portable speedup factor for all problem sizes and machines.

docs.title: Improvements to try in order
docs.text:
Keep intermediate data in arrays, reuse allocations, swap timestep buffers, and read back only at checkpoints. Combine independent per-element operations in one kernel when that avoids launches and temporary arrays. Keep dependent global stages separate. After measuring a clear memory bottleneck, consider tiling; N-body shows how to preserve both barriers and a CPU path.

Compare a change using identical inputs, backend, shape and measurement procedure. Re-run the numerical check too. The repository's performance page contains historical measurements, while the design pages explain specialization and CPU scheduling in more detail.

docs.title: Sharing arrays with other libraries
docs.text: There are two choices when another library produces your data: copy its values into a Tack array, or share compatible storage. A copy gives Tack an independent allocation. A shared view needs agreement on the device, layout, lifetime and permission to write.

docs.title: NumPy: an independent array
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
host = np.arange(12, dtype=np.float32).reshape(3, 4)
data = tack.array(host)
host[:] = -1                              # does not change the Tack array
np.testing.assert_array_equal(data.numpy(), np.arange(12, dtype=np.float32).reshape(3, 4))
tack.copyto(data, host)                   # now it does
np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.asarray(data), host)

tack.array allocates and copies. tack.copyto replaces the values in an existing array and converts to its dtype. numpy() and np.asarray produce a NumPy copy. These are simple boundaries for a first program or for data that arrives infrequently.

docs.title: External pointers: borrowed storage
docs.text:
On CPU, a contiguous NumPy array can be wrapped directly:

array = np.zeros(8, dtype=np.float32)
view = tack.array_from_ptr(array, (8,), tack.f32, writable=True)

@tack.kernel
def fill_indices(out):
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        out[i] = float(i)

fill_indices(view)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(array, np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32))

The external allocation must remain alive. The supplied dtype and shape must describe its actual storage, and the address must meet the dtype's alignment requirements. Tack does not take ownership of a raw pointer. The default view is read-only; request writable=True only when the owner permits writes.

Metal wraps an MTLBuffer, while CUDA, HIP and Level Zero wrap device addresses. Those addresses must belong to the selected device/runtime. Selecting the same kind of backend does not prove that two separately initialized contexts can share an allocation. Keep context lifetimes aligned with the view. On CUDA, Tack works in the device's primary context, as PyTorch, CuPy and Warp do, so their allocations and Tack's are in one context and each library's calls can follow the other's on one thread (Backends).

docs.title: DLPack: exchange a tensor description
docs.text:
For a compatible library that implements DLPack, start with its object:

# producer is a tensor from another library, on a compatible device.
view = tack.from_dlpack(producer)

Tack reads the producer's device, dtype and shape and retains the managed tensor while its array uses the storage. A DLPack import cannot represent arbitrary strided layouts: contiguous storage is required. Device support is backend-dependent, and an imported read-only tensor remains read-only.

Metal currently has no zero-copy DLPack import. Use tack.from_dlpack(host_tensor, copy=True) to copy a NumPy-readable host tensor into a Metal array. Export from a Metal array describes its shared host storage as kDLCPU, so it does not exchange an MTLBuffer handle with another GPU API.

Tack arrays implement the DLPack protocol too. Pass an array to a consumer that supports its device. For a CPU array, NumPy offers a compact example:

data = tack.array(np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32))
shared_array = np.from_dlpack(data)

This shares compatible CPU storage; it does not request migration to the host from an arbitrary GPU backend. Do not interpret a GPU address as a NumPy pointer. A raw DLPack capsule can be consumed only once. Passing producer objects is usually clearer than managing capsules yourself.

On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero a kernel call returns once its launch is queued (see When a call returns), so memory another library reads is kept in step for it. Exporting an array through DLPack waits for the launches queued before it; from then on, every launch that uses that array completes before the call returns, and so does every launch that uses a wrapped pointer or a DLPack import. The other library can read the results as soon as the Tack call returns; the cost is a wait on each such launch.

See the runtime contract for supported device types, copy requests, read-only behavior and errors. The interoperability design explains the lifetime mechanism.

docs.title: VTK: tuple and component layout
docs.text:
With tack-vis and a compatible VTK build:

from tack.interop.vtk import array_to_vtk, vtk_to_array

data = vtk_to_array(vtk_array)              # VTK tuples × components become the array shape
vtk_array = array_to_vtk(data)

For a flat interleaved coordinate array, specify the component count when exporting: array_to_vtk(points, n_components=3); an array of vec3 elements needs no count. vtk_to_array(array, flatten=True) gives a flat array of tuples * components values.

Level Zero sharing with VTK needs a shared context. Call tack.interop.vtk.init_level_zero() before creating arrays, using a VTK build that exposes the necessary handles. The Visualization chapter describes that setup; a system VTK wheel does not necessarily offer every device-interoperability path.

docs.title: A complete CPU exchange
docs.text:
The VTK image example creates a vtkImageData, wraps its scalar array with Tack, fills it in a kernel, and exports the Tack array back to VTK. Each image point stores its squared distance from the centre. VTK image indices are x-fast, so the kernel decomposes the flat index accordingly:

@tack.kernel
def radius_squared(values, nx, ny):
    for i in range(values.shape[0]):
        x = float(i % nx) - float(nx - 1) * 0.5
        y = float((i // nx) % ny) - float(ny - 1) * 0.5
        z = float(i // (nx * ny)) - 2.0
        values[i] = x * x + y * y + z * z

The two conversions below share the allocation and retain its owners:

    image = vtkImageData(dimensions=(9, 7, 5))
    initial = vtkFloatArray(number_of_tuples=image.number_of_points)  # VTK allocates it
    initial.Fill(0.0)
    image.point_data.SetScalars(initial)  # attribute data has no settable scalars property
    values = vtk_to_array(initial)  # shares VTK's allocation; retains its owner
    radius_squared(values, 9, 7)
    result = array_to_vtk(values, name="radius_squared")  # shares the Tack field
    image.point_data.SetScalars(result)

The script compares VTK's values against a NumPy reference and checks that a write through Tack appears in both VTK arrays. It uses the CPU backend; Metal cannot import this VTK host allocation without copying. A GPU exchange needs compatible device arrays and the context rules described above.

Tack's VTK interop needs VTK 9.7.1 or later, for VTK's pythonic API (uv sync --extra interop installs it). Zero-copy array exchange also needs a VTK build exposing vtkmodules.util.dlpack_support. Its Python version must match the interpreter running Tack. Add the build's Python site-packages directory to PYTHONPATH if it is not installed in that environment. A VTK wheel sufficient for the tutorial figures may lack this DLPack module. The PyPI wheel that uv sync --extra interop installs (VTK 9.7.1) lacks it; it is enough for vtk_to_dataset and dataset_to_vtk, which copy the arrays.

uv run python docs/examples/vtk_interop.py --output radius.vti
uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch cpu --vtk

radius.vti can be read by VTK or ParaView. The validator's VTK option is explicit because the usual CPU and GPU numerical checks do not need VTK.

# Copyright (c) 2026 Kitware, Inc.
# SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause
"""Share a VTK image's scalars with Tack on CPU, update them, and export to VTK.

Requires a VTK build with vtkmodules.util.dlpack_support. Rendering is not needed.
"""

import argparse

import numpy as np
from vtkmodules.vtkCommonCore import vtkFloatArray
from vtkmodules.vtkCommonDataModel import vtkImageData

import tack
from tack.interop.vtk import array_to_vtk, vtk_to_array


@tack.kernel
def radius_squared(values, nx, ny):
    for i in range(values.shape[0]):
        x = float(i % nx) - float(nx - 1) * 0.5
        y = float((i // nx) % ny) - float(ny - 1) * 0.5
        z = float(i // (nx * ny)) - 2.0
        values[i] = x * x + y * y + z * z


def run():
    tack.set_default_device("cpu")
    image = vtkImageData(dimensions=(9, 7, 5))
    initial = vtkFloatArray(number_of_tuples=image.number_of_points)  # VTK allocates it
    initial.Fill(0.0)
    image.point_data.SetScalars(initial)  # attribute data has no settable scalars property
    values = vtk_to_array(initial)  # shares VTK's allocation; retains its owner
    radius_squared(values, 9, 7)
    result = array_to_vtk(values, name="radius_squared")  # shares the Tack field
    image.point_data.SetScalars(result)
    # A VTK structured image's x index varies fastest.
    z, y, x = np.mgrid[:5, :7, :9]
    expected = ((x - 4) ** 2 + (y - 3) ** 2 + (z - 2) ** 2).ravel().astype(np.float32)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.asarray(initial), expected)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.asarray(result), expected)
    # The exported array still aliases the original: an edit crosses both views.
    values.fill(123.0)
    assert np.asarray(initial)[0] == 123 and np.asarray(result)[0] == 123
    radius_squared(values, 9, 7)
    return image


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--output", help="Write the updated VTK image as a .vti file")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    image = run()
    if args.output:
        from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLImageDataWriter

        writer = vtkXMLImageDataWriter(file_name=args.output)
        image >> writer
        # Write(), not writer(image): the call returns None and only logs a failure.
        if writer.Write() != 1:
            raise RuntimeError("VTK could not write the image")
    print("VTK interop: check passed")

docs.title: The Kernel Cache
docs.text:
A kernel compiles the first time it is called with a new combination of argument types and shapes. Most of that time is Tack's own front end, and the rest is the backend's compiler. Tack keeps what it compiles on disk, so a later process starts warm. On an M1 Max, the first contour of a 21³ grid in a new process took 445 ms on the CPU and 1.1 s on Metal; with the cache warm, 31 ms on both. On an RTX 6000 Ada it took 1.15 s on CUDA, 0.88 s with only the lowered kernels stored, and 72 ms with their PTX stored too. On an Intel Max 1100 it took 5.1 s on Level Zero, nearly all of it Intel's offline compiler, so storing only the lowered kernels saved little; with their compiled code stored too, 145-190 ms. On an MI210 (HIP), where hipRTC is likewise nearly all of a first call, it took 6.9 s, 6.8 s with only the lowered kernels stored, and 37 ms with their code objects stored too.

The cache is on by default and needs no code. This page covers where it lives, how to turn it off, and how to use it in MPI jobs on a shared file system.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Three environment variables, read when the first kernel compiles:

Variable Meaning TACK_CACHE_DIR Where entries are kept. Default: ~/Library/Caches/tack on macOS, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/tack or ~/.cache/tack on Linux, %LOCALAPPDATA%\tack\Cache on Windows. TACK_CACHE write: look up and store (the default). read: look up, never store. bundle: only the directory's bundle file (the default under MPI, below). off: no cache. TACK_CACHE_SIZE The most the entries may take, such as 500M or 2G (binary units), or unlimited. Default: 1G. See below.

The same from Python, before the first kernel compiles:

import tack.cache

tack.cache.configure(directory="/scratch/me/tack-cache", mode="write")
tack.cache.configure(max_size="4G")
tack.cache.configure(mode="off")

The directory must belong to you and be writable by nobody else, since its entries hold code. Tack refuses one that is not, with a warning, and compiles without it.

docs.title: What is kept, and when it is not used
docs.text:
Two things are stored for each kernel:

  • The lowered kernel, before it is specialized for argument types. Its key is the kernel's source and specialization, Tack's own version, and whether debug mode is on: a kernel lowered with bounds checks is a different kernel, and so are the variants compiled from it. Every name the kernel and its device functions resolve (another @tack.func, a tack.constant, a module) is recorded with what it was bound to, and the entry is used only if each still resolves to the same thing.
  • Each compiled variant: object code on the CPU, generated source on Metal, and the compiled code on CUDA, HIP and Level Zero (below). Its key adds the argument types, the shapes compiled in, and what the code depends on: the LLVM version and host CPU, or the GPU and system.

So editing a kernel, a device function it calls, a constant it reads or a template class it is given makes the next process compile again, as does upgrading Tack or moving to another machine. A damaged or partly written entry is ignored and the kernel compiled.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
The entries of every Tack version share one limit, TACK_CACHE_SIZE (1 GiB by default): each Tack version, and each edit of a Tack checkout, keeps its own entries, and those of a version no longer run would otherwise stay forever. Past the limit, a process that stores entries deletes the least recently used, until 90% of the limit is left. Loading an entry marks it used (to the hour), so the kernels you run stay. The directory is checked at most once an hour by all processes together, never per kernel, so the cache can briefly exceed the limit. Bundles are neither counted nor deleted: they are made, and removed, by hand.

python -m tack.cache info                  # settings, entries and size
python -m tack.cache prune                 # keep to the limit now
python -m tack.cache prune --max-size 200M # ...or to another one
python -m tack.cache clear                 # this Tack version's entries
python -m tack.cache clear --all           # every version's

clear --all deletes only what the cache made (version directories, bundles), so the directory may hold other files.

docs.title: MPI jobs on a shared file system
docs.text:
Thousands of ranks looking up a file per kernel on Lustre or GPFS is the same metadata storm as thousands of ranks importing Python. Tack avoids it with a bundle: one file that holds every entry, which each rank reads once.

  1. Warm up with a run that compiles the kernels the job uses: one rank, or a small job, with TACK_CACHE=write and TACK_CACHE_DIR set to a directory of your own, on scratch.
  2. Pack the directory into a bundle:
TACK_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/me/tack-cache python -m tack.cache pack
  1. Run the job with the same TACK_CACHE_DIR. Under MPI the default mode is bundle: each rank reads the bundle once and never looks up or writes a per-kernel file. A kernel the bundle lacks compiles in memory, as it would without a cache.

Tack recognizes MPI from the launcher's rank variables (Open MPI, MPICH, Intel MPI, MVAPICH2, Cray PALS and ALPS, Slurm's srun). A launch of one task counts as no MPI, and so does a Slurm batch script itself: a warm-up run on the script's own line, without srun, stores entries as it would on a workstation.

To have only rank 0 read the bundle, and broadcast it to the others, call this on every rank before the first kernel (with mpi4py's communicator):

from mpi4py import MPI
import tack.cache

tack.cache.load_bundle(comm=MPI.COMM_WORLD)

It returns the number of entries read. If rank 0 cannot use the bundle (there is none, it is damaged, or it is not your own), rank 0 warns why and every rank compiles its kernels, as it would without a cache.

With TACK_CACHE=write under MPI, only rank 0 stores entries; the other ranks read. Entries are written to a temporary file and renamed into place, so a reader never sees a partial one. Concurrent writers are safe, but the bundle is the better path for a large job.

docs.title: Measuring compile time
docs.text: To time a cold compile, turn the cache off (TACK_CACHE=off), or the first call in a process may be a disk hit rather than a compile. See Debugging and Timing.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text: Every backend stores both levels. CUDA stores PTX, which the driver compiles for the device at load. HIP stores the code object, machine code for the device's architecture. Level Zero stores the device's native code, which loads without compiling, and the SPIR-V it was made from, compiled at load if a driver update or another stepping of the device refuses the native code.

docs.title: Communicate between blocks
docs.text:
A problem too large for one device is cut into parts, each with its own arrays on its own device, and the parts need each other's data: a stencil's neighbouring cells, the owner of a point, every copy of a key. Part of tack itself, tack.communication is a small layer for moving Tack arrays between such parts, called blocks, and for combining values over them. This chapter shows how to write an algorithm on it.

The model is DIY's (blocks, links, exchanges, collectives), with Tack arrays as the messages and plain dictionaries in place of callbacks. It runs the same in one process, with blocks on any of its devices, and over MPI ranks: an algorithm written on Blocks never asks which. tack.dataset's algorithms over a dataset in pieces are written on it too; the Visualization Guide's Pieces and Blocks shows how they use it.

docs.title: Blocks and worlds
docs.text:
A block is a unit of work on one device, with a global id: a part of a domain, a share of particles, a piece of a dataset. Blocks(devices, world) makes this process's blocks, one per device given (several may share a device); global ids run over every rank's blocks, contiguous by rank. blocks.local is the range of this rank's, blocks.count the number in all, blocks.rank_of(g) and blocks.device(g) where a block lives.

A world is the transport. World() is this process alone; World(comm) spans the ranks of an mpi4py communicator (Tack imports no MPI module itself). Every method takes and returns dictionaries keyed by global id, holding an entry for each of this rank's blocks. Every call is collective: each rank makes it, in the same order, even a rank with nothing to send -- the Blocks, Plan and Routing constructors included, which gather what every rank has.

Collectives combine small host values (numbers, NumPy arrays, anything picklable for all_gather) over every block: all_reduce by "sum", "min" or "max", all_gather into a list by global id, and exclusive_scan, each block's offset in a global numbering. They combine in order of global id, whichever rank holds which block, so a floating-point sum has the same bits however the blocks are shared out.

exchange sends messages -- each a dict of names to Tack arrays, on the sending block's device -- from any block to any block. It takes {source: {destination: message}} and returns {destination: {source: message}} for every block on this rank (an empty dict where nothing came), each message's arrays on the destination block's device. A sent array belongs to the receiver afterwards: where the receiver can address its memory, it gets that array itself, so the sender must not write to it again. link_by_bounds finds each block's neighbours by their boxes, touching or within a margin.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

world = tc.World()                                   # tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD) under mpiexec
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu", "cpu"], world)            # two blocks on this rank

# Block g holds g + 3 values: 10 g, 10 g + 1, ...
values = {g: tack.array(10.0 * g + np.arange(g + 3)) for g in blocks.local}

total = blocks.all_reduce({g: values[g].sum() for g in blocks.local})
largest = blocks.all_reduce({g: values[g].max() for g in blocks.local}, op="max")
sizes = blocks.all_gather({g: values[g].size for g in blocks.local})
starts, count = blocks.exclusive_scan({g: values[g].size for g in blocks.local})

every = [10.0 * g + np.arange(g + 3) for g in range(blocks.count)]
assert total == sum(v.sum() for v in every) and largest == every[-1].max()
assert sizes == [g + 3 for g in range(blocks.count)] and count == sum(sizes)
assert all(starts[g] == sum(sizes[:g]) for g in blocks.local)

# Each block sends its first value to the block before it, and its last to
# the block after it: neighbours from boxes, one exchange for every block.
boxes = {g: ((float(g),), (g + 1.0,)) for g in blocks.local}       # unit intervals
neighbours = blocks.link_by_bounds(boxes)                          # {g: [g - 1, g + 1]}
outgoing = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    first, last = values[g].numpy()[[0, -1]]
    outgoing[g] = {n: {"edge": tack.array([first if n < g else last])} for n in neighbours[g]}
incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)                 # {destination: {source: message}}

for g in blocks.local:
    for source, message in incoming[g].items():
        expected = every[source][-1] if source < g else every[source][0]
        assert message["edge"].numpy()[0] == expected
print(blocks, "total", total, "of", count, "values")

docs.title: Plans: ghosts refreshed
docs.text:
Most exchanges repeat: the same elements of the same blocks, every step. A Plan keeps one: for each pair of blocks, the element indices the sender reads and those the receiver writes, in matching order (checked across ranks when the plan is made). plan.run(values) gathers, exchanges and scatters in place; {g: {name: array}} moves several arrays in one exchange. A block may send to itself, as a block in a periodic domain is its own neighbour.

Here a line of cells is cut into blocks of m cells, each held with a ghost cell at either end, and diffused by a kernel that reads a cell's two neighbours. Before each step, the plan copies each block's edge cells into its neighbours' ghosts; the blocks then give exactly the whole line's values. To sample the result, Routing sends points to the block that holds them and their answers back:

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def diffuse(u, out):
    for i in range(1, u.shape[0] - 1):
        out[i] = u[i] + 0.25 * (u[i - 1] - 2.0 * u[i] + u[i + 1])


world = tc.World()                                   # tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD) under mpiexec
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 2, world)
m = 50                                               # cells per block
n = m * blocks.count                                 # cells in all

# Block g owns cells [g m, (g + 1) m), held at 1 .. m with a ghost each side:
# 0 and m + 1, the neighbours' edge cells (or a fixed zero at the ends).
start = np.exp(-((np.arange(n) - n / 3) / 8.0) ** 2)
u = {g: tack.array(np.pad(start[g * m:(g + 1) * m], 1)) for g in blocks.local}
v = {g: tack.zeros(m + 2, tack.f64) for g in blocks.local}

# The ghost exchange: each block sends its edge cells, and the neighbour
# writes them into its ghost. Indices match in order, sends to receives.
sends = {g: {} for g in blocks.local}
receives = {g: {} for g in blocks.local}
for g in blocks.local:
    if g > 0:
        sends[g][g - 1], receives[g][g - 1] = [1], [0]
    if g < blocks.count - 1:
        sends[g][g + 1], receives[g][g + 1] = [m], [m + 1]
ghosts = tc.Plan(blocks, sends, receives)

for step in range(100):
    ghosts.run(u)                                    # ghosts from their owners
    for g in blocks.local:
        diffuse(u[g], v[g])
    u, v = v, u

# The same steps over the whole line, one array: the same bits.
whole, other = tack.array(np.pad(start, 1)), tack.zeros(n + 2, tack.f64)
for step in range(100):
    diffuse(whole, other)
    whole, other = other, whole
whole = whole.numpy()
for g in blocks.local:
    assert np.array_equal(u[g].numpy()[1:m + 1], whole[1 + g * m:1 + (g + 1) * m])

# Sample the result at points each block chooses: each point goes to the
# block whose cells hold it, which answers with its value there.
rng = np.random.default_rng(blocks.local.start)
points = {g: rng.uniform(0.0, n, (5, 1)) for g in blocks.local}
boxes = {g: ((g * m,), ((g + 1) * m,)) for g in blocks.local}


def holds(g, x):                                     # cells [g m, (g + 1) m)
    return (x[:, 0] >= g * m) & (x[:, 0] < (g + 1) * m)


routing = tc.Routing(blocks, points, boxes, holds)
arrived = routing.send()                             # {g: (points, values)}
answers = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    x, _ = arrived[g]
    cells = (np.floor(x[:, 0]) - g * m + 1).astype(np.int64)  # local index, after the ghost
    answers[g] = {"u": tack.array(u[g].numpy()[cells])}
sampled = routing.reply(answers, like={"u": tack.f64})          # in each block's order

for g in blocks.local:
    assert np.array_equal(sampled[g]["u"].numpy(), whole[1 + np.floor(points[g][:, 0]).astype(int)])
print("max", whole.max(), "sampled", sampled[blocks.local.start]["u"].numpy()[:3])

docs.title: Routing: points to their blocks
docs.text:
Routing(blocks, positions, boxes, holds) sends each point to the block that holds it. Each block gives its points (an (n, d) host array), its box (None if it holds nothing), and a function holds(g, x) that block g is asked with the points inside its box: 0 where it does not hold a point, or a rank, True being 1. The point goes to the block of the highest rank, the lowest block on a tie -- so a block that holds a point exactly beats one that holds it only within a tolerance, and a point on a boundary two blocks share goes to the lower block. routing.destination[g] is each point's block, -1 where none holds it.

send(values) moves the points, and any values with them, and returns what arrived at each block, in order of origin block and then of the points there. reply(answers, like) sends an answer for each arrived point back, in that order, and returns one per original point (zero where the point went nowhere). Coordinates travel as the bits of f64 values, so the block decides on exactly the point it was given. Run in rounds, routing each particle after every stretch it takes, it moves particles between blocks.

docs.title: Sorting over blocks
docs.text:
sort_by_key(blocks, keys, values) sorts every block's integer keys together, carrying values along: block 0 ends with the smallest keys and the last block with the largest, each ascending, and every copy of a key ends on one block. That last property is what it is for: matching. Give each item a key -- a hash of a point's exact position, a grid cell, a cluster label, a global id -- sort, and the copies of each key meet on one block, which matches or reduces them there; the values say where each came from. It is a stable sample sort (DIY's): equal keys keep the order of their blocks, then their order within a block. Heavily repeated keys can leave blocks uneven.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

world = tc.World()                                   # tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD) under mpiexec
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 3, world)

# Each block's keys, some on several blocks; the value says where each came
# from: (block << 40) | index.
keys, origin = {}, {}
for g in blocks.local:
    k = np.random.default_rng(g).integers(0, 40, 25 + 5 * g)
    keys[g] = tack.array(k, tack.i64)
    origin[g] = {"origin": tack.array((g << 40) | np.arange(k.size), tack.i64)}

ordered, carried = tc.sort_by_key(blocks, keys, origin)

# Block 0 has the smallest keys, the last block the largest, each ascending,
# and every copy of a key is on one block: count them where they landed.
mine = {g: ordered[g].numpy() for g in blocks.local}
every = blocks.all_gather(mine)
given = [np.random.default_rng(g).integers(0, 40, 25 + 5 * g) for g in range(blocks.count)]
assert np.array_equal(np.concatenate(every), np.sort(np.concatenate(given)))
held = [set(part.tolist()) for part in every]
assert all(not (held[a] & held[b]) for a in range(len(held)) for b in range(a))

# Each value still names its key's block and index.
for g in blocks.local:
    o = carried[g]["origin"].numpy()
    came = [given[s][i] for s, i in zip(o >> 40, o & ((1 << 40) - 1))]
    assert np.array_equal(came, mine[g])
    print("block", g, "holds", mine[g].size, "keys,", mine[g].min(), "to", mine[g].max())

docs.title: Over MPI
docs.text:
The examples above run under mpiexec unchanged but for the world:

from mpi4py import MPI

world = tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD)

mpiexec -n 3 python plan.py

Each rank makes only its own blocks (here two each, so three ranks give six blocks and a longer line); the checks pass on any number of ranks. MPI is optional: uv sync --extra mpi builds mpi4py against the system's MPI. Messages between ranks are staged through host memory, or, with World(comm, gpu_aware=True) and an MPI that reads device memory, handed to MPI as the device arrays themselves. Make each rank's device (tack.device(f"cuda:{local_rank}")) before importing mpi4py.MPI, which starts MPI on the device current then. World(comm) communicates on a duplicate of comm, so its messages never meet the application's; make one per run.

docs.title: Run and check
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch cpu
uv run pytest packages/tack-core/tests/test_communication.py

validate.py runs this chapter's three examples in one process. The test suite runs every pattern on threads that stand in for ranks, and under mpiexec -n 3 staged and GPU-aware (--extra mpi); the reference for each call is the API page, and what it guarantees is in the Runtime API contract.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Use this page while writing a kernel. For a first complete program, start with Getting Started.

docs.title: Host code and device code
docs.text:
Task In Python, outside a kernel In a kernel or @tack.func Allocate storage tack.empty, tack.zeros, tack.full, tack.array Fixed-size scratch with tack.local_array Choose a device tack.set_default_device("cuda"), with tack.device("cuda"):, device= on a constructor, data.to_device(d) Runs on its arrays' device Access values data.numpy() or np.asarray(data) (copies), or data[i] for one element data[i], grid[row, column] Write values tack.copyto(data, host_values) or tack.copyto(data, other_array), data.fill(value) data[i] = value Repeat work Python timestep loop calling kernels One parallel for in a kernel; sequential nested loops Reuse an operation Ordinary Python function Helper decorated with @tack.func Change a parameter Pass a scalar argument Read that argument Fix a model parameter Declare DT = tack.constant(0.01) Read DT Sum a whole array data.sum() or tack.algorithms statistics Write contributions, or use an atomic where appropriate Wait for the GPU tack.sync(); host array reads also wait tack.barrier() waits only within a workgroup

Device code supports a numerical subset of Python. NumPy calls, file operations and arbitrary Python objects belong on the host. Save decorated functions in a .py file so Tack can read their source. See the execution model.

docs.title: Choose storage
docs.text:
Need Allocation NumPy result Uninitialized scalar array tack.empty((h, w)) (f32) numpy() → (h, w) Zero-filled integer array tack.zeros((h, w), tack.i32) numpy() → (h, w) Allocate without copying tack.empty_like(prototype) Same array shape and element type; unspecified values Copy an existing NumPy array tack.array(a) Same shape and dtype (float64 stays f64) One RGB vector per pixel tack.empty((h, w), tack.vec3()) numpy() → (h, w, 3) One 2×2 matrix per particle tack.empty((n,), tack.mat2()) numpy() → (n, 2, 2)

Initialize every value before reading it. Shape comes first, then dtype, as in NumPy; the dtype defaults to f32 (tack.set_default_float(tack.f64) changes that). Array shape counts elements; the dtype describes one scalar, vector or matrix element. numpy() appends component dimensions, and tack.copyto expects them. reshape preserves the element type and shares storage; copy allocates independent storage. See Arrays and Types.

docs.title: Choose an execution pattern
docs.text:
Calculation Pattern Example Independent element update One iteration owns each output First kernel Neighbourhood stencil Read an old array, write a new array, swap Heat diffusion Many inputs contribute to one output Initialize an accumulator, then use atomics Particle-to-grid simulation Unordered append with known capacity Claim slots with the old value from atomic_add Kernel results Ordered or exactly sized output Count, exclusive scan, allocate, write Marching squares Reuse data within a GPU workgroup Shared memory and barriers, with complete groups Tiled N-body

Separate globally dependent stages into separate kernel calls. The device runs them in order. A workgroup barrier cannot synchronize the whole grid. See Memory and Parallel Correctness.

docs.title: Choose a dataset operation
docs.text:
Need Start with Build discontinuous nodal coefficients Construct an L2 field Initialize quadratic nodal values Construct a quadratic H1 field Continuous, per-cell or discontinuous values Fields and Spaces Select whole cells or cut a region Filter and Analyze Work per cell or face without hard-coding connectivity Write Mesh Algorithms Evaluate a field at physical positions Probing Trace a steady velocity field or render extracted geometry Pipelines Filter and reduce a dataset in pieces, with ghost cells Work with Data in Pieces

tack.Array describes storage. tack.dataset.Field associates values with a topology through a space. A field's association must be correct before a filter can interpolate or propagate it.

docs.title: Keep these numerical choices explicit
docs.text:
• Use f32 for a portable starting point. Metal has no f64; on Level Zero, check get_backend().supports_f64 after importing get_backend from tack.runtime.dispatch.
  • int(x) truncates toward zero. Use int(floor(x)) for the cell containing a possibly negative coordinate.
  • Vector * is component-wise; vector dot and matrix @ form products.
  • Integer / produces f32. Cast both operands to tack.f64 for a double-precision quotient on a backend that supports it.
  • Floating parallel sums can differ in their low bits. Compare against an independent result with a tolerance chosen for the calculation.

See Control Flow and Math, numerical details, and reductions.

docs.title: Check, then time
docs.text:
Use tack.set_debug(True) to find invalid indices. Compare a small case with a NumPy reference before increasing the input size. For timing, disable debug mode, warm the kernel, reuse allocations, and call tack.sync() before stopping the clock. Measure transfers separately when studying kernel execution.

Debugging and Timing has complete examples and a symptom table. Backends explains capabilities and setup.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
These examples develop a complete application from its data layout to the host loop and a check of the result. Start with the data examples below for scientific analysis, or heat diffusion for a first simulation. Every script is included with its explanation and available as a download; it needs no separate examples repository.

The scripts target the current Tack checkout. They use NumPy and the selected backend. The simulation tutorials use VTK for optional figures; the new data comparisons use Matplotlib. Install from source as in Getting Started, then run from the repository root:

uv run python docs/examples/heat.py --arch cpu --check
uv run --with vtk python docs/examples/heat.py --output heat.png

In a checkout, uv sync --extra cpu --extra interop (with your other extras) installs VTK from the lock instead, and uv run python ... --output then needs no --with vtk.

With an installed Tack environment, download a script and use python heat.py. Install VTK separately if you want its figure. --check uses smaller inputs and checks a numerical reference or independent properties; it is not a performance benchmark. --arch requires the named backend to initialize.

If you use a local VTK build, make its Python site-packages directory available through PYTHONPATH and use uv run python ... without --with vtk. The build must match your Python version. These figures use ordinary VTK image, geometry, rendering and PNG-writing modules; they do not require DLPack support. Offscreen geometry and image-panel rendering needs a working VTK rendering backend.
