Do not infer a function space from an array class. A CartesianProduct describes a way to compute 3-vectors; H1 describes how coefficients are associated and interpolated on a topology. td.Field couples these two choices, with a check that the value count matches the space.

docs.title: Other implicit coefficient arrays
docs.text:
data.fields["constant"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.arrays.ConstantArray(5.0, data.num_points))
    explicit = tack.arrays.materialize(data.fields["constant"].values)
    snapshot = tack.arrays.to_host(data.fields["constant"].values)

Here ConstantArray stores the constant and count, not 12 separate values. materialize computes storage on the default device. to_host evaluates and downloads a snapshot. Neither changes the original field's representation.

Implicit array Useful when UniformCoordinates, CartesianProduct Coordinates follow a uniform or rectilinear grid ConstantArray, CountingArray Values are constant or a sequence Permutation, View, Strided Values are selected or reorganized without a new value buffer ExtractComponent, Components Scalar components and vector values need to be connected Transform, Function, Cast A device function or conversion can compute values on demand

Operands can themselves be implicit arrays. This keeps intermediates out of storage, but the expression still does work whenever it is read. Materialize an expensive expression if reuse makes that worthwhile, then measure the whole pipeline. An implicit wrapper around a mutable buffer observes its current values; a materialized result is a previous computation until recomputed.

docs.title: Know the present higher-order limits
docs.text: Cell Types and Bases lists which spaces, orders and bases each shape takes. Filters that keep whole cells (extract_cells, split, remove_ghosts) keep higher-order fields and a curved geometry at their order, and extract_surface keeps a solid's fields and geometry on its surface. The cutting filters (contour, slice, clip, threshold) cut curved and high-order cells on linear sub-cells, their crossings at the field's roots; subdivide gives those sub-cells. The reference records the supported layouts and filter propagation rules.

docs.title: Run and reproduce the figure
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/data_fields.py --check
uv run --with matplotlib python docs/examples/data_fields.py --check --output spaces.png

Download the complete program. Continue with Filtering and Analysis.

docs.title: Filter and analyze datasets
docs.text:
Choose a filter by what should happen to the cells. Keeping a whole cell, cutting a cell, and extracting its intersection with a surface answer different questions, even when all three use the same scalar threshold.

The running example samples x and the velocity [-y, x, 0] on a grid covering [-1, 1]³. The simple analytic fields make the results independently checkable.

docs.title: Prepare named inputs
docs.text:
@tack.kernel
def sample(xyz, scalar, velocity):
    for p in range(scalar.shape[0]):
        x = xyz.get(p)
        scalar[p] = x.x
        velocity[p] = [-x.y, x.x, 0.0]

    data = td.uniform_grid((9, 5, 5), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.25, 0.5, 0.5))
    x = tack.empty((data.num_points,))
    velocity = tack.empty((data.num_points,), tack.vec3(tack.f32))
    sample(data.geometry.values, x, velocity)
    data.fields["x"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), x)
    data.fields["velocity"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), velocity)

The complete script supplies the imports and initializes the backend. All following fragments use this dataset. A field argument can be its name or the td.Field itself; a raw value buffer needs a space wrapper first.

docs.title: Select cells, cut cells, or extract a surface
docs.text:
Goal Operation Output Keep cells whose scalar lies in an interval threshold Whole cells, preserving their shapes Keep cells inside a region described by a function extract_geometry Whole cells Keep a named or explicit cell selection extract_cells Whole cells in input order Keep a box of a structured grid, every n-th point extract_extent A structured grid of the same kind (VTK's vtkExtractGrid/vtkExtractVOI); a one-point-thick box is a grid of one dimension less Normals of a surface, its polygons wound alike surface_normals The surface with normals on points and cell_normals on cells (VTK's vtkPolyDataNormals without splitting) Keep the part on one side of a level clip Whole cells and pieces of cut cells Extract a scalar level set, or several contour Triangles in 3D; line cells in 2D; vertices on lines; dimension= picks which cells of a mixed mesh (the highest by default, never mixed); with several values, all of them, each cell's in contour_value Intersect with a plane or another implicit function, or several parallel ones slice_plane, slice Intersection geometry Keep original points by scalar or region threshold_points, extract_points Vertex cells, without cell connectivity

For point data, threshold checks every corner by default. With all_points=False, one in-range corner suffices. Neither option interpolates a cut boundary. For cell data, the cell's one value makes the selection.

    whole = td.threshold(data, "x", 0.125, 1.0)                  # all corners in range
    touching = td.threshold(data, "x", 0.125, 1.0, all_points=False)
    plane = td.Plane(origin=(0.125, 0, 0), normal=(1, 0, 0))
    clipped = td.clip(data, plane, fields=["x"])                # keep x >= 0.125
    surface = td.contour(data, "x", 0.125, fields=["velocity"])
    section = td.slice_plane(data, origin=(0.125, 0, 0), normal=(1, 0, 0))

At x = 0.125, no grid plane coincides with the requested boundary. The threshold keeps 48 cells starting at x = 0.25, with total volume 3. The clipped region starts at x = 0.125 and has volume 3.5. The contour is a plane of area 4. all_points=False keeps 64 whole cells, including a layer that crosses the threshold. These different measures are intentional.

docs.title: Understand the sign of an implicit function
docs.text:
Plane, Sphere, Cylinder, Box and Planes expose a value(position) that is negative inside, zero on the boundary and positive outside. For the plane in the example it is x - 0.125. Union, Intersection and Difference combine them (Difference(box, sphere) is the box with a ball taken out), as VTK's vtkImplicitBoolean does, on the device.

clip(data, plane) keeps values at or above zero, here the positive-x side. Pass inside=True to keep the other side, inside the function's region. extract_geometry instead defaults to inside=True, the negative side, and keeps whole cells. State which region you mean before choosing flags; the words “inside” and “keep” do not by themselves specify the same default for both functions.

docs.title: Decide which fields follow the geometry
docs.text:
Filters creating datasets accept fields=: all named fields by default, a name or list to select them, and [] for geometry alone. Geometry is always handled separately. An unknown requested name raises KeyError.

Input association Typical propagation Floating point data Gathered for kept points; interpolated onto edge crossings Cell data Copied to each retained cell or each piece of an input cell L2 data Retained cell by cell when whole cells survive on a shape-based output Face values Retained only when the filter has a face map; on an extracted surface, mapped to output cells where supported Side traces or entities with no propagation map Left behind

For example, the contour above carries only velocity, interpolated at its new points; the clip carries only x. Computing a derived field does not automatically name it: put it in data.fields before extraction if it should travel with the result.

Integer point labels are not interpolated as continuous data. Use cell labels when that is the intended association. To preserve provenance of cell pieces, attach td.cell_ids(data) as a named cell field before filtering; its ids then refer to the source mesh, while output cell ids refer to the new mesh.

docs.title: Sets follow provenance, not geometric guesses
docs.text:
Cell sets survive selections and follow pieces of selected cells. A face set can become a cell set when its faces become surface cells. Newly generated points do not automatically inherit a point set merely because they lie near an old selected point. The result follows the filter's entity maps.

The mixed-mesh example names a roof cell and a boundary face set, then filters:

    mesh.sets["boundary"] = td.boundary_faces(mesh)  # a face Set
    mesh.sets["roof"] = td.Set(mesh, "cells", [1])   # a cell Set
    kept = td.threshold(mesh, "material", 1.5, 3.0)  # sets come along
    print(f"boundary: {len(mesh.sets['boundary'])} faces; the roof is cell "
          f"{kept.sets['roof'].numpy()} of the threshold")

Its returned roof id is zero after thresholding because the output cells have been renumbered. Use the returned set with the returned dataset.

docs.title: Derived fields and summaries
docs.text:
speed = td.magnitude(data, "velocity")
    data.fields["speed"] = speed                               # keep the returned field
    velocity_gradient = td.gradients(data, "velocity")
    flow = td.flow_quantities(data, velocity_gradient)
    summary = td.statistics(data, "x")

magnitude returns a field in the velocity's space. gradients returns cell gradients by default; at="points" evaluates and averages onto points. For a 3-vector field its gradient has nine components, in row order d(u_i)/d(x_j). flow_quantities derives divergence, vorticity and Q from it. The solid rotation in this example has divergence 0, vorticity [0, 0, 2] and Q = 1 in every cell.

statistics summarizes stored field samples, not a volume integral. An arithmetic mean of point temperatures is not a volume-weighted mean on a stretched mesh. Choose cell measures and a suitable quadrature when the quantity you need is a physical integral. The function returns Python values and therefore waits for the device work it reads.

docs.title: Cell quality
docs.text:
cell_quality(data, measures) measures how well shaped each cell is, a cell field per measure, each 1 on the ideal cell of its shape (equilateral; a cube, a regular tetrahedron):

Measure What it says scaled_jacobian the worst corner's edges' determinant, edges scaled to unit length, relative to the ideal cell's: 1 ideal, 0 flat, negative inverted jacobian_ratio the least corner determinant over the greatest: 1 for every simplex, below 1 as a cell tapers condition the worst corner's condition number against the ideal cell's: 1 ideal, growing as it distorts, the largest float when inverted edge_ratio, min_edge, max_edge the longest edge over the shortest; the shortest and longest, in the spatial unit

They are Verdict's definitions (VTK's vtkMeshQuality), matched to VTK where it defines them, and extended to every shape Tack has: the corners' edges are the geometry's Jacobian applied to the reference cell's edge directions, so order-2 cells are measured along their curved edges, and wedges and pyramids get every measure. Polyhedra and polygons, which have no reference cell, are measured by the fan tetrahedra and triangles Tack evaluates them in.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

mesh = td.tetrahedralize(td.uniform_grid((4, 4, 4)))
quality = td.cell_quality(mesh, ["scaled_jacobian", "condition", "edge_ratio"])
sj = quality["scaled_jacobian"].values.numpy()
print(f"scaled Jacobian {sj.min():.3f} to {sj.max():.3f}")
mesh.fields["sj"] = quality["scaled_jacobian"]
worst = td.threshold(mesh, "sj", -1.0, 0.75)          # the right-corner tetrahedra
assert np.isclose(sj.max(), 1.0) and np.isclose(sj.min(), 1 / np.sqrt(2))
assert worst.num_cells == np.count_nonzero(sj < 0.75)

docs.title: Feature edges
docs.text:
feature_edges(data, angle=30.0) finds a surface's edges by how many cells meet there and at what angle, as VTK's vtkFeatureEdges: boundary edges (one cell), feature edges (two cells whose normals are at least angle degrees apart), non-manifold edges (three or more cells) and, if asked, manifold edges (the rest of the two-cell edges). The result is line cells on the same points with a kind cell field (EdgeKind), point fields carried. A volume mesh's surface comes from extract_surface first.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

box = td.uniform_grid((4, 3, 3))
surface = td.extract_surface(box, td.boundary_faces(box))
edges = td.feature_edges(surface)                 # the box's 12 edges, in segments
kinds = edges.fields["kind"].values.numpy()
print(edges.num_cells, "feature edges")
assert (kinds == td.EdgeKind.FEATURE).all() and edges.num_cells == 4 * 3 + 4 * 2 + 4 * 2
open_top = td.uniform_grid((4, 4))
assert td.feature_edges(open_top).num_cells == 12           # its boundary

docs.title: Check algorithm support before building a pipeline
docs.text:
Task Shape-based Polyhedral / polygonal Polyline Select whole cells; measure cells Yes Yes Yes Extract boundaries Yes, subject to line-cell limitations Yes Chain ends Contour or slice Yes, of order-1 and L2 fields; above order 1, or on a curved geometry, on linear sub-cells of segments, quads, hexahedra, triangles, tetrahedra and wedges (subdivision=, tolerance=); an order-2 H1 field on pyramids is refused Yes Contour: vertices, of point data Clip cells H1 geometry required; above order 1, or on a curved geometry, whole cells kept as they are and the others cut on linear sub-cells (a PartitionedDataSet; threshold too) Polyhedra: yes, into polyhedra (faces clipped, iso-polygons as caps); polygons not yet Currently unsupported Project between point and cell data Yes Yes Yes Gradients and flow quantities Yes (2D cells in their plane) Yes: Green–Gauss over each polyhedron's faces, and over each polygon's edges in its plane (exact for linear fields) Yes (zero) Locate cells and probe Yes Yes: in sub-tetrahedra or fanned triangles; cells must be star-shaped from their points' mean Yes, on segments Advection and streamlines Yes, 2D and 3D cells Yes, as probing locates Currently unsupported Carry ghost marks over pieces Yes Yes Yes

An empty supported filter result is a valid dataset. Check num_cells before assuming an extraction contains visible geometry. Algorithms requiring a reference element reject unsupported topologies; storing H1 values alone does not change that support. The reference matrix has the details.

docs.title: Run and check
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/data_analysis.py --arch cpu --check
uv run --with matplotlib python docs/examples/data_analysis.py --check --output filters.png

The checks include counts, independently calculated volumes and areas, interpolated velocity, flow derivatives, probe validity and analytic rotation. Download the complete program.

Continue with Mesh Kernels to implement an operation, or Sample and Connect Simulations to connect stages.

docs.title: Write mesh algorithms
docs.text:
Use td.for_each when an operation is naturally expressed per cell, face or edge. Tack supplies a view of the mesh and compatible views of its fields; Views explains what they are and where they come from. Your kernel can use geometry and interpolation without manually switching on cell type or maintaining a connectivity parser for every representation.

An operation on each value of a field alone, such as scaling it, needs no mesh: pass field.values to an ordinary kernel and loop over range(len(values)). That is also how to loop over points.

Read Device Functions and Templates when the kernel syntax is new. The built-in filters use the same dataset API as the examples here.

docs.title: Separate an algorithm from storage layout
docs.text:
This kernel computes each cell's mean corner temperature:

@tack.kernel
def corner_mean(cells, temperature, out):
    for c in cells:
        total = 0.0
        for j in range(cells.NUM_POINTS):
            total += temperature.corner_value(c, j)
        out[cells.entity_id(c)] = total / cells.NUM_POINTS

cells is a domain view. temperature is a field view, so temperature.corner_value(c, j) resolves through that field's space and storage. It can read a stored value or evaluate an implicit array.

The dispatcher launches once per compatible group: usually each cell shape, with further grouping for varying space order or size buckets. NUM_POINTS is consequently a constant for this kernel specialization. It is eight for a hex and five for a pyramid; the source stays the same.

This corner mean is a teaching algorithm. It is not a general quadrature rule for integrating a field over an arbitrary cell.

docs.title: Use global ids for global output
docs.text:
The loop variable c belongs to its view. On structured cells it can represent several indices rather than an ordinary integer. Pass it to view methods; use cells.entity_id(c) when indexing output storage allocated for the entire mesh. A group-local index is not an output cell id on a mixed mesh.

td.for_each(kernel, data, "cells", *args) supplies the domain view as the first argument. Each td.Field in the remaining arguments becomes a matching field view. A raw Tack array stays a raw buffer; the kernel is responsible for indexing it correctly.

docs.title: Run over a selection and initialize unwritten output
docs.text:
On the two-cell mesh, select just the right cell:

    data.sets["right"] = td.Set(data, "cells", [1])
    means = tack.zeros((data.num_cells,))
    td.for_each(corner_mean, data, "right", data.fields["temperature"], means)
    # Only cell 1 is written. Cell 0 retains its initialized zero.

The output has room for all cells because the kernel writes global ids. tack.zeros initializes the cell that this selected launch will not visit. The result is [0, 3.25]. Uninitialized allocation would be appropriate when every element is written before anything reads it.

A cell or face set's name is a domain. For a point set, iterate its ids in an ordinary kernel; point sets do not currently supply a dataset domain view. Sets belong to their topology, so a set from an earlier filter input cannot be substituted for a set on its renumbered output.

docs.title: Visit a space's nodes
docs.text:
td.for_each(kernel, data, space, *arrays) runs a kernel over a space's nodes, each once, where td.interpolate evaluates its function: an order-2 H1 space's points, edge middles, quad face centers and cell interiors, an L2 space's corners per cell. Each node has nodes.node_dof(i, j), where its value goes in the space's array, and nodes.node_position(i, j):

@tack.kernel
def sample(nodes, values):
    for i in nodes:
        for j in range(nodes.node_count(i)):
            x = nodes.node_position(i, j)
            values[nodes.node_dof(i, j)] = x[0] * x[1]

docs.title: Work at a field's nodes
docs.text:
A field view numbers its own cell's nodes, whatever its space, order or shape: NODES of them (a constant, so a loop over them unrolls), node k at parametric coordinates node_parametric(k), its value dof(c, k), stored at dof_index(c, k) in the field's array. That is enough to compute a field of one space from fields of others without projecting first. To add an order-1 field p to an order-2 field q into a new order-2 field, read p through its own basis at each of q's nodes:

@tack.kernel
def add_at_nodes(cells, p, q, out):
    for c in cells:
        for k in range(q.NODES):
            out[q.dof_index(c, k)] = p.value(c, q.node_parametric(k)) + q.dof(c, k)


p, q = data.fields["p"], data.fields["q"]      # H1 of order 1 and of order 2
space = q.space
out = tack.empty((space.size,), tack.f32)
for group in data.launch_groups("cells", [p, q]):
    add_at_nodes(data.domain_view("cells", group), p.view(group), q.view(group), out)
s = td.Field(space, out)

The same kernel runs on every shape and every space: a hexahedron's 27 quadratic nodes, a segment's 3, an order-3 tetrahedron's 20, an L2 cell's own, a Constant cell's one at its centre. Cells that share a node write the same value to the same place, so the result does not depend on which one writes last. Here it equals td.project(data, p, space) plus q, since p lies in the order-2 space.

NODES is the field's, not the shape's. The shape's NUM_QUADRATIC and quadratic_node(k), which a view also has, are the quadratic element's nodes whatever the field: an order-1 field has fewer, an order-3 field more, and a segment none, so a loop over them writes nothing. A serendipity field's NODES are the corners and edges it stores, which come first; it computes the rest. In a Bernstein basis (basis="bernstein"), dof(c, k) is a coefficient, not the field's value at node_parametric(k) (the Greville point), so a kernel that writes values there writes a Lagrange interpolant's values into a Bernstein field: right only where they agree, as they do for multilinear fields.

for_each over a space (above) visits each stored value once; a loop over a field view's nodes visits a shared node once per cell holding it, but has the cell's other fields at hand.

docs.title: Parametric and world coordinates have different meanings
docs.text:
cells.parametric_center() returns a location in the cell's reference element. temperature.value(c, pc) evaluates the field there, and cells.position(c, pc) maps it into physical space. A parametric coordinate is not a world-space [x, y, z] query point.

Likewise, temperature.parametric_gradient(c, pc) differentiates with respect to the reference coordinates. A physical gradient also needs the geometry's Jacobian mapping. Use td.gradients for the built-in physical calculation; use probing when query positions are given in world coordinates.

docs.title: Compute one oriented flux per face
docs.text:
A face has side 0 and possibly side 1. Its normal points out of side 0; faces.num_sides(f) == 1 identifies a boundary face. Reading a neighbouring cell must be guarded when that side is absent.

For the vector field v(x,y,z) = (x,y,z), the following kernel computes its integrated normal flux, dot(v, normal) * area, at each face's center:

@tack.kernel
def integrated_flux(faces, centers, normals, areas, out):
    for f in faces:
        e = faces.entity_id(f)
        velocity = centers[e]                   # v(x,y,z) = (x,y,z)
        out[e] = velocity.dot(normals[e]) * areas[e]

Geometry, centers and output values are raw device fields here, indexed by the face's global id. Each iteration owns one output, so it needs no atomic. The normal and center fields use the same topology's face numbering.

    faces = data.topology.faces()               # derive incidence once
    geometry = td.face_geometry(data)
    centers = td.face_centers(data)
    flux_values = tack.empty((faces.num_faces,))
    td.for_each(integrated_flux, data, "faces", centers.values,
                geometry.normal.values, geometry.area.values, flux_values)
    flux = td.Field(td.Values(data, "faces", oriented=True), flux_values)
    net_outflow = td.net_flux(data, flux)       # integrated flux, per cell
    divergence = td.divergence(data, flux)    # net_outflow / volume: 3 for v = (x,y,z)

td.net_flux is an outward sum of the supplied face values: a face adds to its side-0 cell and subtracts from its side-1 cell. It does not divide by cell volume. With integrated face flux as input, its result is integrated net outflow. td.divergence divides it by each cell's volume, the finite-volume divergence.

Each example cell has volume 0.5, net outflow 1.5, and therefore average divergence 3. The sum of both cells' outflows is the boundary outflow 3; the internal face cancels. This independent balance catches orientation and association errors that a plausible image might hide.

For a scalar transported by a constant velocity, td.upwind_flux provides the face calculation and returns an oriented field. Its boundary convention uses the one existing cell's value; a solver needing prescribed inflow must supply its own boundary treatment.

docs.title: Share face-based code with polyhedra
docs.text:
Shape-based cells have compile-time corner counts. Polyhedra instead expose runtime num_points(c) and num_faces(c) counts. The following surface-area kernel walks each cell's outward faces and works on both paths:

    @tack.kernel
    def surface_areas(cells, out):
        # Every face of every cell, walked outward from the cell: the same code
        # for a hexahedron, a pyramid or a polyhedron.
        for c in cells:
            total = 0.0
            for k in range(cells.num_faces(c)):
                a = cells.side_position(c, k, 0)
                n = a - a
                for j in range(1, cells.side_num_points(c, k) - 1):
                    n += (cells.side_position(c, k, j) - a).cross(
                        cells.side_position(c, k, j + 1) - a)
                total += 0.5 * n.norm()
            out[cells.entity_id(c)] = total

    mesh.topology.faces()                            # the faces kernels walk
    areas = tack.empty((mesh.num_cells,))
    td.for_each(surface_areas, mesh, "cells", areas)

    polyhedra = td.as_polyhedra(mesh)                # every cell a polyhedron
    same = tack.empty((polyhedra.num_cells,))
    td.for_each(surface_areas, polyhedra, "cells", same)

The complete program compares its shape-based and polyhedral results. The triangle fan is appropriate for the example's planar convex faces; general nonplanar or nonconvex faces require a deliberate geometric interpretation. For supported built-in measures, prefer td.cell_geometry and td.face_geometry.

docs.title: Keep parallel ownership explicit
docs.text:
The safe pattern is one writer per cell or face output. A face kernel that adds to both neighbouring cells is a scatter; concurrent faces can target the same cell and require atomics or a separate gather pass. A barrier cannot order all mesh groups. Keep globally dependent stages in separate launches.

Allocate and derive topology before the repeated calculation. Time first-use group construction and compilation separately from warm calls. Scalar model parameters can change between calls without changing the source, but a new cell shape or space layout can require another specialization.

docs.title: Run and check
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/data_mesh_kernels.py --arch cpu --check
uv run python docs/examples/datasets.py --arch cpu --check

Download the cell/face kernel program. The reference lists the full view methods. Continue with Write a Filter to turn kernels like these into filters, or Sampling, Rendering and Simulation Pipelines.

docs.title: Sample and connect simulations
docs.text:
A useful visualization pipeline connects a simulation's fields to a scientific question and an output. Keep the data's space and lifetime explicit at each stage: a streamline needs an interpolated velocity, and a file writer needs host-accessible data in its format.

flowchart LR
    A[Simulation or reader] --> B[Dataset and named fields]
    B --> C[Derived fields and selections]
    C --> D[Contour, slice or boundary]
    D --> G
    C --> F[Probe or integrate trajectories]
    C --> G[Export a dataset]

docs.title: Sample at physical positions
docs.text:
probe evaluates a source dataset's fields at positions in world coordinates. The example asks for two points in the mesh and one outside it:

    locator = td.CellLocator(data)
    query = np.array([[0.2, 0.3, 0.0], [-0.4, 0.1, 0.0], [2.0, 0.0, 0.0]], np.float32)
    sampled = td.probe(data, query, fields=["x", "velocity"], locator=locator)
    valid = to_host(sampled.fields["valid"].values).astype(bool)
    samples = to_host(sampled.fields["x"].values)
    # Use valid before interpreting samples: zero also denotes a missing sample.

The returned dataset contains the query positions as vertex cells, sampled fields as point data, and valid as a point attribute. Invalid samples are zero-filled. Always consult valid: zero may also be a valid physical result. The example checks that valid scalar samples equal the query x coordinates.

Passing a target dataset instead of a point array preserves that target's topology and geometry, samples at its point positions, and adds the source fields. This is a way to resample onto another grid. A name collision is resolved by the sampled field replacing the target's field of that name.

Without a locator, probe uses the one the mesh's topology keeps, so probing the same mesh again does not rebuild its search bins. A CellLocator of your own serves any dataset of the same cells and positions. Both follow the positions: after Tack writes them (a kernel, fill or copyto), the kept one is rebuilt, and one of your own is refused, since its bins describe the mesh as it was. Positions changed through memory shared with another library (DLPack) are not seen: make a new locator then. Where a query lies in more than one cell, the smallest cell id wins (a query on a face, edge or vertex that cells share is in all of them); a cell the query is only within the tolerance of counts only where no cell holds it. At a discontinuity that choice can determine which side is sampled; it is not an average across the interface.

Probing takes shape-based cells, polyhedra (located in sub-tetrahedra), polygons (in the triangles fanning each from its points' mean) and polylines (on their segments). A Values field on faces is not a continuous field that can be sampled arbitrarily through the volume.

docs.title: Voxelize onto a uniform grid
docs.text:
probe onto an image samples one point per image point. voxelize(data, grid) gives each voxel (an image cell) the share of its volume the data covers, fraction, and each field's mean over that share, as cell data: what a simulation's fields are on a uniform grid, for analysis or for learning. Each voxel is sampled at samples points a side (4 by default, so 64 in 3D) through probe, so fraction is right to about one sample's share and a mean is the samples' mean; voxels the data does not reach are hidden. It takes anything probe takes: datasets, pieces over MPI ranks, AMR hierarchies and octrees.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# A ball of tetrahedra, cut from a cube, with a temperature rising along x.
mesh = td.tetrahedralize(td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1)))
x = mesh.positions().astype(np.float64)
mesh.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(mesh), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(x - 0.5, axis=1)))
mesh.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(mesh), tack.array(300.0 + 10.0 * x[:, 0]), unit="K")
ball = td.clip(mesh, "r", 0.4, inside=True)

voxels = td.uniform_grid((6, 6, 6), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
v = td.voxelize(ball, voxels, samples=6)
covered = v.fields["fraction"].values.numpy().sum() * 0.2 ** 3
volume = td.cell_geometry(ball).measure.values.numpy().sum()
print(f"covered {covered:.4f} of the ball's {volume:.4f}")
assert abs(covered - volume) < 0.02 * volume
assert v.fields["T"].unit == "K"

docs.title: Integrate a steady velocity field
docs.text:
seeds = np.array([[0.5, 0, 0], [0, 0.75, 0]], np.float32)
    paths = td.streamlines(data, "velocity", seeds, step_size=0.05, steps=20, locator=locator)
    particles = td.advect(data, "velocity", seeds, step_size=0.05, steps=20, locator=locator)

advect returns the particles where they stop, with steps, time and status. streamlines returns the paths as a polyline per seed that moved, with seed on cells and time on points. It also keeps a point for a seed that did not move, without inventing a line.

The default integrator is fixed-step RK4; Euler is also available. The step is in the integration parameter for dx/dt = velocity, so its spatial length depends on speed.

integrator="rk45" adapts the step to the flow, as VTK's vtkStreamTracer does with its RK45 (Cash-Karp): step_size is the first step, a step whose error estimate passes tolerance (a distance, 1e-6 by default) is tried again smaller, and each step taken proposes the next, between min_step and max_step (by default a fiftieth of step_size and twice it, VTK's ratios). Smooth stretches take long steps and sharp turns short ones; on a swirl, at VTK's settings, it takes about half of fixed RK4's points and lies as close to the path as VTK's RK45. Where the flow turns back at a wall, a particle whose step cannot get past it ends there (SPATIAL_BOUNDS), as in VTK. Its step control makes yes-or-no choices, so where paths diverge (a recirculation, a wall) a rounding-sized change can send two runs, or two devices, along paths of other lengths, each within the tolerance; a looser tolerance makes that rarer (on the aneurysm in f64, paths of other lengths from seeds 1e-13 apart: 4,899 of 20,000 at 1e-7, 721 at 1e-6, none at 1e-5). max_length stops a path that has gone that far, whatever the integrator.

streamlines(..., step_unit="length") steps a fixed arc length instead, following the velocity's direction as VTK's vtkStreamTracer does by default: slow flow takes steps as long as fast flow, and steps * step_size is the longest path. time on the points is still the time the particle takes. Where speeds vary widely, a time step sized for the fastest makes tiny steps elsewhere, so length steps reach as far in far fewer steps.

Choose the device by the number of seeds. Each particle is one thread that takes all its steps, so a few seeds use a few threads of a GPU built for thousands, and a single GPU thread is slower than a CPU core. Below a few thousand seeds the CPU is usually faster; above, the GPU. On a 28-core EPYC against an RTX 6000 Ada (ms, warm):

mesh seeds CPU CUDA aneurysm, 8.7M tetrahedra 25 8.4 32.0 2,000 57.2 75.8 20,000 871 331 ONERA M6 wing, 46.9M cells 17 41.7 84.4 1,024 92.9 149 16,384 1,190 108

On an Intel Data Center GPU Max 1100 the gap is wider: the M6's 17 seeds took 708 ms against its host CPU's 24.5. For a few seeds on a mesh that lives on a GPU, advect a CPU copy of it (data.to_device("cpu")); the locator is built where the mesh is.

Choose the locator by the mesh. Each step finds the particle's cell among the candidates its bin holds. The default locator bins the cells on two levels, as Viskores' CellLocatorTwoLevel does, so a mesh graded toward a body in a large far field (the M6 wing's cells span a millionfold in size) is not all in a few bins. On a small mesh of cells of about one size, one uniform grid of bins, as Viskores' CellLocatorUniformBins and VTK's vtkStaticCellLocator have, holds fewer candidates a bin: in tack-examples' fire room (10,462 hexahedra) a search scans 6.6 cells against 12. Build it and pass it in:

locator = td.CellLocator(data, levels=1)
paths = td.streamlines(data, "velocity", seeds, 0.02, 2500, locator=locator)

probe and advect take it the same way. Both locators find the same cells, so the paths are the same bit for bit; only the time differs.

The example's [-y, x, 0] velocity rotates a point at unit angular speed. Twenty steps of 0.05 reach time 1. The program checks the final positions against sine and cosine, and checks path lengths against the radii times elapsed time, allowing for polyline chord approximation.

Particles stop at the step limit, zero velocity, or domain bounds; an outside seed does not move. Inspect status and time before treating a short path as evidence of low speed. These functions sample one steady field. A pathline through a changing simulation requires a time-dependent integration strategy; repeating a steady streamline calculation does not by itself provide one.

docs.title: Keep a simulation's state in the pipeline
docs.text:
A common pattern is to retain topology and geometry, attach each working field once, update its values with simulation kernels, and run the analysis stages at selected timesteps. Intermediate datasets hold results of those stages; they are not a graph that recomputes automatically when an input changes.

What changed What needs attention Values in an existing simulation field Re-run dependent filters, samples and summaries A field was replaced by a new buffer Update the named td.Field attachment Point positions changed Rebuild locators Connectivity changed Construct a corresponding topology, spaces and associations

Prefer kernels that compute through data.geometry.values to downloading all positions just to form a derived field on the host. Keep readback at checkpoints or output boundaries. A named field holding simulation storage can share its allocation: follow the same ownership and synchronization rules as any other shared buffer.

docs.title: Exchange whole datasets with VTK
docs.text:
With tack-vis and VTK installed, vtk_to_dataset reads VTK image, rectilinear, structured, unstructured or polygonal (vtkPolyData) data. Point fields become H1, cell fields Constant; geometry and connectivity are converted into the dataset model. dataset_to_vtk creates the matching VTK dataset for visualization or writing to a file.

For a contour, the VTK result is an unstructured triangle mesh. The following fragment assumes surface was produced by td.contour:

from tack.interop.vtk import dataset_to_vtk
from vtkmodules.vtkIOXML import vtkXMLUnstructuredGridWriter

vtkXMLUnstructuredGridWriter(file_name="surface.vtu")(dataset_to_vtk(surface))

Tack uses VTK's pythonic API (VTK 9.7.1 or later) in its interop and examples: keyword constructors, properties, a writer or filter called on its input. A contour's cells come across as VTK's own implicit arrays: its cell types a vtkConstantArray, its offsets a vtkAffineArray.

These whole-dataset conversions copy arrays and provide a straightforward host boundary. Zero-copy array exchange is a separate route using array_to_vtk, vtk_to_array and a DLPack-enabled VTK build. A standard VTK wheel sufficient for file I/O may not expose that route. Level Zero sharing also needs a shared allocation context. See Sharing Arrays.

MFEM meshes and grid functions enter through tack.interop.mfem; supported spaces include H1 orders 1 and 2 and L2 orders 0 and 1 on every shape it maps, and H1 and L2 of any order with curved geometry of any order on quads, hexahedra, triangles, tetrahedra and wedges; mfem_grid_function gives a field back. Check the interop reference for signatures and the current mapping limits.

docs.title: Measure the boundaries you actually use
docs.text:
Stage Host interaction to account for Construct from NumPy or a reader Input upload and topology setup Derive faces, edges or a locator First-use work and retained auxiliary storage Extract variable-size geometry Count readbacks and output allocation Return a scalar summary Device wait and result readback Probe or integrate Locator setup, query upload; streamlines also read path lengths for output allocation Export to VTK or a file Array copies and writer time

Queued GPU launches preserve Tack's program order, but host reads synchronize. Call tack.sync() before stopping a timer when the next operation is not a readback. Separate first-use compilation from repeated work, and include the output stage when reporting application time. See Debugging and Timing.

docs.title: Complete programs to run next
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/data_analysis.py --arch cpu --check
uv run python docs/examples/datasets.py --arch cpu --check

The analysis program covers probing and flow, and the dataset tour connects mixed meshes, spaces, sets and streamlines.

docs.title: Work with data in pieces
docs.text:
Large data often arrives in pieces: a reader's partitions, a simulation's blocks, the share of each GPU or MPI rank. Tack keeps each piece a whole DataSet and adds three things: a container for the pieces, marks saying which cells and points another piece owns, and reductions that combine the pieces into the whole's answer.

  • A PartitionedDataSet is an ordered list of datasets, as VTK's vtkPartitionedDataSet. Each piece has its own topology, numbering, geometry, fields, sets and device. Iterate over it, index it, take its length.
  • Work on one piece takes the piece. Filters, analyses and for_each take a DataSet, as everywhere else, and you loop over the pieces. There is no "apply to every piece" wrapper: the loop says what it does.
  • Only algorithms whose answer needs every piece take the container: statistics and entropy, given a field's name, here; probing, particles, connected regions and the point-cloud filters in Algorithms Across Pieces.

docs.title: Cut a grid into pieces
docs.text:
split cuts a structured grid by index ranges. ghost_layers=1 adds a layer of each neighbour's cells around every piece:

    whole = td.wavelet(10)                                   # 21^3 points, 8000 cells
    pieces = td.split(whole, 4, ghost_layers=1)              # a PartitionedDataSet
    for piece in pieces:
        marks = piece.ghosts
        print(piece.topology.point_dims,
              owned(marks.cells, piece.num_cells), "cells owned of", piece.num_cells,
              owned(marks.points, piece.num_points, td.Ghosts.SKIPPED_POINTS),
              "points owned of", piece.num_points)

Each piece of this 20 × 20 × 20-cell grid owns 2000 cells and holds 420 more from its neighbours. Every cell and point that several pieces hold has exactly one owner; in every other piece its copy is a ghost. The owned cells of the four pieces are the grid's 8000 cells, and the owned points its 9261 points.

An unstructured mesh is cut by VTK or by the application that made it (see Pieces from VTK).

docs.title: Ghost marks
docs.text:
data.ghosts is a tack.dataset.Ghosts, or None for data with no pieces. It holds one u8 per cell (ghosts.cells) and one per point (ghosts.points), either of which may be None, with VTK's vtkGhostType bits:

Bit Value Meaning Ghosts.DUPLICATECELL 1 a copy of a cell another piece owns Ghosts.REFINEDCELL 8 a cell a finer AMR level covers: valid data, superseded (AMR Hierarchies) Ghosts.HIDDENCELL 32 a cell whose data is not valid here: a blanked cell Ghosts.DUPLICATEPOINT 1 a copy of a point another piece owns Ghosts.HIDDENPOINT 2 a point whose data is not valid here Ghosts.REFINEDPOINT 8 a point at whose location a finer AMR level has one (Tack's; VTK has no such bit)

The other cell bits (HIGHCONNECTIVITYCELL, LOWCONNECTIVITYCELL, EXTERIORCELL) are carried along unread. Filters that make cells leave Ghosts.MASKED_CELLS (hidden and refined) out. Ghosts.SKIPPED_CELLS and Ghosts.SKIPPED_POINTS are the bits a reduction leaves out. The marks are kept apart from the fields, as the geometry is, so no algorithm mistakes them for data. to_device moves them; vtk_to_dataset and dataset_to_vtk map them to and from vtkGhostType arrays. Set them yourself with data.ghosts = td.Ghosts(cells=..., points=...); marks of the wrong length or type are refused.

docs.title: Work on each piece
docs.text:
Loop over the pieces:

    surfaces = []
    for piece in pieces:
        piece.fields["grad"] = td.gradients(piece, "RTData")
        surfaces.append(td.contour(piece, "RTData", 160.0))
    surfaces = td.PartitionedDataSet(surfaces)

The ghost layer is why this works near a piece's edge. A point gradient at the edge of a piece averages over every cell around the point, and the ghost layer supplies the cells across the cut, so each piece's gradients at its own points are the whole grid's.

Filters process the ghost cells too, and carry the marks to what they make, as VTK's do. What a filter makes takes the owner of what it came from:

Output Owner a cell (a contour's triangles, a clip's pieces, a kept cell) its source cell's a point a filter keeps its own a point on an input edge (a contour's, a clip's crossings) the edge's: the owner of its smallest point a point inside a cell (a clip's centroids) the cell's a surface face the cell it is a side of a face two cells share, an edge, a vertex the owner of its smallest point

"Smallest" goes by position, so every piece that holds a shared edge or face decides alike, with no communication. With a ghost layer, the piece that owns a point holds every cell around it. So the owned part of a filter's output, over all pieces, is the whole's output, cell for cell and point for point. That holds for every filter that makes cells or points, chained filters included. The ghost output itself is what the next step near the edge needs: point normals, smoothing, a second filter that looks at neighbours.

docs.title: Reduce over the pieces
docs.text:
grid_stats = td.statistics(pieces, "RTData")             # each point counted once
    surface_stats = td.statistics(surfaces, "RTData")        # each surface point once
    triangles = sum(owned(s.ghosts.cells, s.num_cells) for s in surfaces)

statistics(pieces, name) takes each piece's moments on its own device and combines them pairwise; entropy(pieces, name, bins) sums each piece's histogram over the whole's range. Both count only what each piece owns (cells and points not marked duplicate or hidden), on a single dataset too. So the statistics of the pieces' isosurfaces are the whole grid's isosurface's, and so is the owned triangle count.

An L2 field goes by its cells' marks. A field on faces or edges, or of order 2, is refused on a dataset with marks, since who owns those values is not decided yet.

docs.title: Remove the ghosts at the end
docs.text:
Before rendering, writing one file, or handing a piece to code that does not know ghost marks, take the ghost output away:

    finished = td.PartitionedDataSet(td.remove_ghosts(s) for s in surfaces)

remove_ghosts drops the duplicate and hidden cells, and the points no remaining cell uses, as VTK's vtkRemoveGhosts. The points it keeps keep their marks: a point a piece shares is still its owner's, so reductions over the result are unchanged. A point the piece owns stays even when only ghost cells used it. A contour point on an edge belongs to the owner of the edge's smallest point, and that piece's triangles around the edge may all be ghosts. A structured piece whose remaining cells form a block stays a structured grid. dataset_to_vtk keeps the marks, so pieces with ghosts can also go to VTK as they are; VTK leaves ghosts out when it renders.

docs.title: Pieces need ghost cells
docs.text:
Without ghost cells, a piece cannot tell what its neighbours make or keep from the cells, faces and edges they share. Take a contour point on an edge in the cut: it belongs to the owner of the edge's smallest point, and that piece may have no cell containing the edge. Or a shared point only a neighbour's kept cells use: it disappears from its owner's threshold. Tack does not guess:

    bare = td.split(whole, 4)                                # no ghost cells
    cut = td.PartitionedDataSet(td.contour(piece, "RTData", 160.0) for piece in bare)
    try:
        td.statistics(cut, "RTData")
    except NotImplementedError as error:
        print("refused:", str(error).split(":")[0])

Such outputs record that they lost the marks, and statistics and entropy refuse them with NotImplementedError, naming the cause. What does not depend on neighbours still works on pieces without ghost cells:

  • reductions of the pieces themselves;
  • filters that keep the cells and points (warp, transform, cylindrical, spherical, shrink, as_polyhedra, as_polygons, and probe's target);
  • points chosen by their own values (threshold_points, extract_points, mask_points).

Setting an output's ghosts clears the record.

docs.title: Hidden cells
docs.text:
Filters never process hidden cells: their data is not valid there. Every filter that makes cells or points leaves them out, as if they were not there:

  • contour, slice, clip, threshold, extract_cells, extract_geometry, mask, extract_surface, extract_edges, triangulate, tetrahedralize;
  • the source dataset of probe, advect and streamlines.

A field passed as an object rather than by name follows along. Two things cannot leave hidden cells out yet and are refused on such data: faces or edges chosen by id, and a reused CellLocator. Algorithms whose output is on the same cells (gradients, projections, calculators) still compute there, and the marks stay on those cells.

docs.title: Run and check
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/data_partitioned.py --check
uv run python packages/tack-vis/examples/44_partitioned_data.py --pieces 8

The checks compare the pieces against the whole grid: owned cells and points, statistics of the grid and of its gradients, and the isosurface's triangles and points, before and after remove_ghosts. Download the complete program.

Continue with Algorithms Across Pieces: pieces from VTK, generated ghost cells, global ids, several devices and MPI ranks, and the algorithms whose answer crosses pieces.

docs.title: Point clouds and particles
docs.text:
A point cloud is a dataset whose cells are its points: one vertex cell per point, stored nowhere. LiDAR surveys, SPH particles, N-body particles and tracers from a simulation are all point clouds, with fields per point. The filters that work on points (threshold_points, probe's target, statistics, transform) work on them as on any dataset, and a point locator adds the filters that need each point's neighbours: cleaning and thinning, normals, clusters, deposition onto a grid, SPH interpolation and cosmology halos.

Task Algorithm Make a cloud from positions and fields point_cloud Find the points within a radius, or the k nearest PointLocator Mark noise outliers (radius or statistical) Thin to one point per voxel voxel_downsample Estimate surface normals point_normals Group points closer than a distance connected_components(radius=) Count, sum, average, or take the extremes on a grid deposit Density and kernel-weighted values of SPH particles sph_density, sph_interpolate Halos of dark matter particles connected_components(radius=, periodic=), halo_catalog

The reference has every argument. Each filter is deterministic, with no atomics in its sums: the same input gives the same values every run.

docs.title: Far from zero: the origin
docs.text:
A survey in projected coordinates sits hundreds of kilometres from zero, and single precision has about seven digits: at 4,580,000 m its spacing is half a metre. So a dataset's positions are an origin, three doubles on the host, plus values in the geometry's type. point_cloud given double-precision positions picks the lower corner of their box, in whole units, as the origin; the values are then offsets of at most the tile's size, and keep millimetres in single precision. Kernels see only the offsets. positions() gives them; world_positions() gives the world coordinates back in double precision.

Filters keep the origin, and anything given in world coordinates (a probe point, a seed, an implicit function, a viewpoint) is moved to it in double precision. A grid to deposit onto is rebased to the same origin, as below. Pieces whose positions meet share one origin.

docs.title: Clean, thin and grid a LiDAR tile
docs.text:
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# A 100 m survey tile in UTM coordinates: terrain, a building, and noise.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 40000
east, north = rng.uniform(0.0, 100.0, n), rng.uniform(0.0, 100.0, n)
height = 0.02 * east + rng.normal(0.0, 0.02, n)
roof = (np.abs(east - 50.0) < 10.0) & (np.abs(north - 50.0) < 10.0)
height[roof] += 8.0
height[:40] += rng.uniform(20.0, 40.0, 40)                 # birds and spurious returns
world = np.stack([east + 431000.0, north + 4580000.0, height + 120.0], axis=1)
tile = td.point_cloud(world, fields={"z": world[:, 2],
                                    "classification": np.where(roof, 6, 2).astype(np.uint8)})
print(tile.origin)                     # the box's lower corner in whole metres
assert np.abs(tile.world_positions() - world).max() < 1e-3  # millimetres, in f32

# Mark the outliers, keep the rest, thin to 0.5 m voxels.
marked = td.outliers(tile, radius=1.0, min_neighbors=3)
kept = td.threshold_points(marked, "outlier", 0, 0)
thin = td.voxel_downsample(kept, 0.5)
print(kept.num_points, "kept,", thin.num_points, "after thinning")
assert tile.num_points - kept.num_points >= 40

# Normals point up on the ground and the roof.
normals = td.point_normals(thin, k=12).fields["normals"].values.numpy()
assert np.median(normals[:, 2]) > 0.99

# A surface model: the highest return in each 2 m cell of a 2D image.
image = td.uniform_grid((51, 51), origin=(431000.0, 4580000.0), spacing=(2.0, 2.0))
image = image.rebased(tile.origin)                         # its corner exact, near zero
dsm = td.deposit(kept, image, "z", reduce="max").values.numpy().reshape(50, 50)
print(f"roof {dsm[25, 25]:.1f} m, ground {dsm[5, 5]:.1f} m")
assert abs(dsm[25, 25] - 129.0) < 0.2 and abs(dsm[5, 5] - 120.2) < 0.2

outliers marks points (outlier, 1 for noise) rather than removing them, as PDAL does: threshold_points keeps the rest, and the marks stay for inspection. The radius test marks points with fewer than min_neighbors others within radius, as VTK's vtkRadiusOutlierRemoval; outliers(data, k=8) is the statistical test instead, a mean distance to the k nearest more than deviations standard deviations above the mean, as VTK's vtkStatisticalOutlierRemoval and PCL.

voxel_downsample keeps one point per occupied voxel, of exactly the size asked: the voxel's centroid (floating-point fields averaged, integer ones such as a classification taken from its first point), its first point, or its point nearest the centroid (keep=). point_normals fits each point's neighbourhood, its k nearest or those within a radius, and signs the normal upward or toward a viewpoint.

deposit puts each point in the image cell holding it (method="nearest", a field on the cells), or spreads it over the cell's corners by trilinear weights ("cic", cloud in cell, on the points). Without a field it counts; with one it takes the "sum", "mean", "min" or "max": the highest return per cell is a surface model, the lowest ground return a terrain model. Cells nothing reaches hold 0 for counts and sums, NaN otherwise.

An image's own coordinates are in the geometry's type too, so one cornered at 431,000 m would be half a metre coarse in single precision at 4,580,000 m. rebased(tile.origin) keeps it an image and moves its corner next to zero in double precision, in the tile's frame.

docs.title: Neighbours, directly
docs.text:
The filters above share one structure, which you can use yourself:

locator = td.PointLocator(tile)                      # uniform bins, sorted by bin
offsets, ids = locator.neighbors(1.0)                # within 1 m of each point (CSR)
nearest, d2 = locator.nearest(8)                     # the 8 nearest, nearest first

neighbors and nearest take other query points too, world positions or offsets. A filter given no locator uses the one the dataset's topology keeps, so several filters on one cloud bin it once; a locator is refused once the positions change. Its device class (locator.grid()) gives your own kernels the bins.

docs.title: SPH particles
docs.text:
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Particles of equal mass on a jittered lattice filling the unit cube: density 1.
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
side = np.arange(0.0, 1.0, 0.05) + 0.025
x = np.stack(np.meshgrid(side, side, side, indexing="ij"), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3)
x += rng.uniform(-0.005, 0.005, x.shape)
particles = td.point_cloud(x.astype(np.float32), origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
                           fields={"h": np.full(len(x), 0.06), "mass": np.full(len(x), 0.05**3),
                                   "T": 300.0 + 10.0 * x[:, 0], "one": np.ones(len(x))})
particles = td.sph_density(particles)                       # adds "density"
inner = np.all((x > 0.2) & (x < 0.8), axis=1)
rho = particles.fields["density"].values.numpy()
assert abs(np.median(rho[inner]) - 1.0) < 0.02

# Resample onto an image. The Shepard sum says how well the particles cover
# each point; normalize divides by it, which keeps a constant exact out to the
# particles' edge, where the plain sum falls off.
image = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
out = td.sph_interpolate(particles, image, fields=["T", "one"], normalize=True)
T, one = (out.fields[name].values.numpy() for name in ("T", "one"))
shepard = out.fields["shepard"].values.numpy()
print(f"coverage {shepard.min():.2f} at a corner, {np.median(shepard):.2f} inside")
assert np.abs(one - 1.0).max() < 1e-5
inside = np.all((image.positions() > 0.15) & (image.positions() < 0.85), axis=1)
assert np.abs(T - (300.0 + 10.0 * image.positions()[:, 0]))[inside].max() < 0.05

sph_interpolate sums (m_j / rho_j) A_j W(|x - x_j|, h_j) over the particles reaching each target point (the scatter form, each particle out to its kernel's support), onto any dataset's points: an image, a slice, another cloud, or an array of world positions. kernel is "cubic" (the default), "quartic", "quintic" or "wendland", VTK's, normalized in dimension dimensions; the results agree with VTK's vtkSPHInterpolator to float rounding. Smoothing length, mass and density are point fields, by name, or one number for all. sph_density computes the density (the gather form, SPLASH's) when a code does not write it.

docs.title: Halos in a periodic box
docs.text:
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Dark matter particles in a periodic box of side 50: three halos, one of them
# across a face of the box, and a smooth background.
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
box = 50.0
centres = np.array([[10.0, 10.0, 10.0], [30.0, 25.0, 40.0], [49.5, 20.0, 20.0]])
parts = [c + rng.normal(0.0, 0.4, (n, 3)) for c, n in zip(centres, (3000, 1500, 800))]
x = np.concatenate(parts + [rng.uniform(0.0, box, (20000, 3))]) % box
v = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, x.shape)
particles = td.point_cloud(x.astype(np.float32), fields={"v": v}, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))

# Friends of friends: particles closer than the linking length are one halo.
linking = 0.2 * box / len(x) ** (1 / 3)
fof = td.connected_components(particles, radius=linking, min_size=100, periodic=box)
catalog = td.halo_catalog(fof, mass=1.0e10, velocity="v", periodic=box)
counts = catalog.fields["count"].values.numpy()
print(catalog.num_points, "halos of", sorted(counts.tolist()), "particles")
print(catalog.positions())                                  # their most bound particles
assert catalog.num_points == 3 and counts.min() > 700
gap = catalog.positions()[:, None, :] - centres[None, :, :]
gap -= box * np.round(gap / box)                            # across the box's faces
assert (np.linalg.norm(gap, axis=2).min(axis=1) < 0.5).all()

With periodic (a box's side, its three sides, or two corners), distances are to the nearest image, so a halo across a face is one halo. Friends of friends is connected_components with the linking length as radius; min_size drops the small groups, renumbering the rest. halo_catalog gives one point per halo, at its most bound particle (center="com" for the centre of mass), with its count, mass, centre of mass, the most bound particle's index and potential, the mass-weighted mean velocity and the velocity dispersion, and its radius. The most bound particle is exact for every halo: large halos are pruned by bounds, not estimated. On ParaView's HACC test data the halos, their counts and their most bound particles are those of ParaView's ANL halo finder, which counts the halos across a face of the box twice.

docs.title: Point clouds in pieces
docs.text: A cloud cut into pieces, by a simulation's ranks or a survey's tiles, needs each piece's neighbours from the others. ghost_points gives them, and clusters, catalogues, outliers, voxels and deposits take the pieces: see Point clouds in pieces.

docs.title: Algorithms across pieces
docs.text: Work with Data in Pieces cuts a grid, marks the ghosts and loops over the pieces in one process. This chapter gets pieces from elsewhere -- VTK, a partitioner, other devices, other MPI ranks -- and covers the algorithms whose answer crosses pieces: ghost generation, global ids, particles, probes, connected regions and point clouds.

docs.title: Pieces from VTK
docs.text:
vtk_to_dataset turns a vtkPartitionedDataSet into a PartitionedDataSet, and a vtkPartitionedDataSetCollection into a dict of names to partitioned datasets; dataset_to_vtk does the reverse. To cut an unstructured mesh with ghost cells, use VTK's filters (no MPI needed):

from vtkmodules.vtkFiltersParallelDIY2 import (
    vtkGhostCellsGenerator,
    vtkRedistributeDataSetFilter,
)

from tack.interop.vtk import vtk_to_dataset

cut = (vtkRedistributeDataSetFilter(number_of_partitions=4,
                                    preserve_partitions_in_output=True)
       >> vtkGhostCellsGenerator(number_of_ghost_layers=1, build_if_required=False))
pieces = vtk_to_dataset(cut(mesh))                 # mesh: any vtkDataSet

The filters' rules hold over these pieces as over split's.

docs.title: Generate ghost cells
docs.text:
Unstructured pieces without ghost cells, from VTK's redistribution, a reader or your own partitioner, get a layer from ghost_cells, as VTK's vtkGhostCellsGenerator would give them, marks and values alike:

plain = vtk_to_dataset(vtkRedistributeDataSetFilter(number_of_partitions=4,
                                                    preserve_partitions_in_output=True)(mesh))
pieces = td.ghost_cells(plain)                     # one layer, marked
deeper = td.ghost_cells(plain, layers=2)           # two, for two neighbour filters in a row

Structured pieces, split's or VTK's image pieces, stay structured: each becomes its block grown by the layers, with the right offset and coordinates.

Pieces neighbour where they share points at exactly the same position, and a shared point belongs to the lowest piece holding it. The pieces may be on different devices, or on different MPI ranks (each rank passes its own pieces and a tack.communication.World; see the API reference).

A filter that needs each entity's neighbours is right on what a piece owns but wrong on the rim of the ghost layer, whose neighbours the piece lacks. Before a second such filter reads those values, copy them from their owners:

for piece in pieces:
    piece.fields["p"] = td.project(piece, "c", td.H1(piece))  # a cell field "c" to points
td.update_ghosts(pieces, "p")                      # ghost values from their owners
for piece in pieces:
    piece.fields["grad"] = td.gradients(piece, "p", at="points")   # right where owned

ghost_cells keeps the exchanges, so each update_ghosts is one copy per neighbour, not a new matching.

docs.title: Global ids
docs.text:
Each piece numbers its points and cells from 0. Global ids number them across all the pieces, one id per point and per cell wherever it is held: piece.global_ids.points and .cells, i64 arrays (td.GlobalIds). VTK's GlobalIds arrays come in as them, and generate_global_ids makes them, as vtkGenerateGlobalIds does:

pieces = td.generate_global_ids(td.ghost_cells(plain))
ids = pieces[0].global_ids.points                  # the same at a shared point

Filters keep the ids of the points and cells they keep (threshold, extract_cells, remove_ghosts); what they make has none.

docs.title: Pieces on several devices
docs.text: A piece is a dataset, so it can live on any device: td.PartitionedDataSet(piece.to_device(f"cuda:{i % 2}") for i, piece in enumerate(pieces)) spreads them over two GPUs. Each piece's work runs on its own device, and statistics and entropy reduce each piece where it is. packages/tack-vis/examples/44_partitioned_data.py does this when there are several devices of the chosen type.

docs.title: Across MPI ranks
docs.text:
Over MPI each rank holds its own pieces, and the container says where the others are: a tack.communication.World made from an mpi4py communicator. The algorithms that take the container then communicate; the per-piece loops do not change.

from mpi4py import MPI

import tack.dataset as td
from tack import communication as tc

world = tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD)
every = td.split(data, 8, ghost_layers=1)                  # or each rank reads its own
mine = [every[i] for i in range(world.rank, 8, world.size)]
pieces = td.PartitionedDataSet(mine, world)
print(td.statistics(pieces, "RTData").mean)                # over all eight pieces

mpiexec -n 4 python script.py

Tack imports no MPI module: you make the communicator, and mpi4py must be built against your MPI (uv sync --extra mpi). Results that sum over pieces add in the pieces' global order, so they have the same bits however the pieces are shared out. With an MPI that reads device memory, tc.World(comm, gpu_aware=True) sends device arrays without staging them through the host; make the rank's device (tack.device("cuda:N")) before importing mpi4py.MPI, which starts MPI.

Every algorithm here is written on tack.communication, and so can one of your own: Pieces and Blocks.

docs.title: Particles across pieces
docs.text:
advect and streamlines take a partitioned dataset too, and particles cross from piece to piece:

pieces = td.split(data, 8, ghost_layers=1)
particles = td.advect(pieces, "velocity", seeds, 0.01, 500)  # a dataset per piece
paths = td.streamlines(pieces, "velocity", seeds, 0.01, 500) # each piece's stretches

With a ghost layer wider than a step (step_size times the speed), the paths are the whole mesh's up to rounding: a particle that ends a step in a ghost cell is handed to the cell's owner, which goes on with whole steps. Without ghost cells it crosses at the boundary by a shortened step. Each particle is in one piece of the result, with its seed; a path's stretches are in the pieces that traced them, each after the first starting at a point marked DUPLICATEPOINT.

docs.title: Probing pieces
docs.text:
probe takes a partitioned source: each point is evaluated by the piece that holds it, and the values come back in your points' order, equal to probing the whole dataset. Ghost cells are not needed for it.

values = td.probe(pieces, points)                  # points: an array or a dataset
values.fields["RTData"], values.fields["valid"]    # valid 0 outside every piece

docs.title: Connected regions across pieces
docs.text:
connected_components labels cells connected through shared points; given pieces, it numbers the regions across all of them, so a region that crosses a cut has one number everywhere:

regions = td.connected_components(pieces)          # region, point_region on each piece

With global ids on the pieces, regions are numbered as on the whole dataset. min_size drops regions of fewer points, each point counted once.

docs.title: Point clouds in pieces
docs.text:
A point cloud's pieces share no points, so a filter over a point's neighbours needs copies of the points near it that other pieces hold. ghost_points appends them, marked as ghosts: every point within a radius of the piece (radius=), or exactly those among its owned points' k nearest (k=). The neighbour filters then run per piece, as mesh filters do after ghost_cells, and each owned point gets the whole's answer. Clusters, statistical outliers, voxel downsampling, deposition onto a grid and halo catalogues need every piece, so they take the pieces:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Clumps in a periodic box, and the same cloud cut into four pieces.
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
box = 10.0
x = np.concatenate([c + rng.normal(0.0, 0.3, (400, 3)) for c in rng.uniform(1, 9, (12, 3))]
                   + [rng.uniform(0.0, box, (2000, 3))]) % box
x = x.astype(np.float32)
whole = td.point_cloud(x, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
pieces = td.PartitionedDataSet([td.point_cloud(part, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
                                for part in np.array_split(x, 4)])

# Per piece, after copying in each owned point's 10 nearest from elsewhere.
ghosted = td.ghost_points(pieces, k=10)
normals = np.concatenate([td.point_normals(piece, k=10).fields["normals"].values.numpy()
                          [:len(own)] for piece, own in zip(ghosted, np.array_split(x, 4))])
expected = td.point_normals(whole, k=10).fields["normals"].values.numpy()
assert np.abs(normals - expected).max() < 1e-3

# Over the pieces: the whole's clusters, numbered as the whole numbers them.
groups = td.connected_components(pieces, radius=0.15, min_size=50, periodic=box)
labels = np.concatenate([p.fields["point_region"].values.numpy() for p in groups])
assert np.array_equal(labels, td.connected_components(
    whole, radius=0.15, min_size=50, periodic=box).fields["point_region"].values.numpy())
print(labels.max() + 1, "clusters")

After a filter that is right only where a piece owns its points, update_ghosts brings the copies' values from their owners: SPH densities before an interpolation that reads them, for instance.

ghosted = td.ghost_points(pieces, radius=2 * h_max)        # an SPH kernel's reach
for piece in ghosted:
    piece.fields["density"] = td.sph_density(piece).fields["density"]
td.update_ghosts(ghosted, "density")                       # the copies' from their owners

deposit of pieces gives every rank the whole grid, and halo_catalog of pieces a catalogue piece per piece, the halos in label order across them. In a periodic box the copies across a face are images, moved by the box's side, so run the per-piece filters on ghost_points' pieces without periodic.

docs.title: One dataset again
docs.text:
merge_pieces gives the pieces back as one dataset, each cell and point once, ghosts dropped: to write one file, or to hand to code that knows no pieces. Structured pieces come back as one structured grid; across MPI ranks the result is on the root rank.

whole = td.merge_pieces(pieces)                    # None on the other ranks

docs.title: Not here yet
docs.text: Asynchronous exchange, should particles across MPI ranks need it, and rebalancing pieces are not planned for now.

docs.title: Run and check
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch cpu
uv run python packages/tack-vis/examples/44_partitioned_data.py --pieces 8

validate.py runs the point-cloud example above, comparing the pieces' normals and clusters with the whole cloud's; the test suite compares every algorithm here with the whole, on two devices and on two and three MPI ranks.

docs.title: AMR hierarchies
docs.text:
Block-structured adaptive mesh refinement covers a domain with boxes, and some regions with finer boxes, level after level. An AMRDataSet holds the levels, each a PartitionedDataSet of structured boxes, and the refinement ratio between them. It follows VTK's vtkOverlappingAMR and AMReX's design: the hierarchy is defined in index space alone -- a box is its first cell's index in its level (its topology's offset) and its cell counts -- so a box can be an image, a rectilinear grid or a curvilinear grid.

Making the hierarchy marks what a finer level supersedes:

  • REFINEDCELL on each cell a finer box covers;
  • REFINEDPOINT on each point at whose location a finer level has a point, the edge of a refined region included;
  • DUPLICATEPOINT on points two sibling boxes share, owned by the first.

So every region and location belongs to one box, at the finest level holding it, and reductions over the hierarchy count it once. Filters run per box, and those that make cells leave refined cells out.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td
from tack.dataset import Ghosts

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


def box(lo, cells, spacing):
    """An image box of ``cells`` cells, its first cell at index ``lo`` of its level."""
    corner = tuple(i * spacing for i in lo)
    grid = td.uniform_grid(tuple(n + 1 for n in cells), origin=corner, spacing=(spacing,) * 2)
    topology = td.StructuredTopology(tuple(n + 1 for n in cells), offset=lo)
    data = td.DataSet(topology, grid.geometry.values)
    x = data.positions()
    data.fields["f"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(
        np.exp(-((x[:, 0] - 4) ** 2 + (x[:, 1] - 4) ** 2) / 4).astype(np.float32)))
    return data


# A root of two 4 x 8 boxes, and a box at level 1 across their seam (ratio 2).
amr = td.AMRDataSet([[box((0, 0), (4, 8), 1.0), box((4, 0), (4, 8), 1.0)],
                     [box((4, 4), (8, 8), 0.5)]], ratios=[2])
for level, piece in amr:
    refined = (piece.ghosts.cells.numpy() & Ghosts.REFINEDCELL) != 0
    print(f"level {level}: {piece.num_cells} cells, {refined.sum()} refined")

# Each location once, at the finest level holding it.
assert td.statistics(amr, "f").n == sum(
    ((p.ghosts.points.numpy() & Ghosts.SKIPPED_POINTS) == 0).sum() for _, p in amr)

# Filters run per box and leave refined cells out. The 0.5 contour lies where
# the fine box refines the root, so only the fine box gives segments.
lines = [td.contour(piece, "f", 0.5) for _, piece in amr]
print([line.num_cells for line in lines], "segments")
assert lines[0].num_cells == lines[1].num_cells == 0 and lines[2].num_cells > 0

The root boxes' contours are empty: the 0.5 level lies where the fine box refines them. Pieces of a contour at different levels do not join at level boundaries; crack-free contouring is not part of Tack yet.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Boxes of a level may not overlap, and each fine box, coarsened, must lie within its coarser level's boxes (proper nesting). A level's image boxes share one spacing and lie on one lattice, as VTK's model has it; rectilinear and curvilinear boxes have no such constraint. Ratios may differ per axis.

docs.title: VTK
docs.text: vtk_to_dataset takes a vtkOverlappingAMR, and dataset_to_vtk gives one back for images and rectilinear grids; a hierarchy with curvilinear boxes goes to VTK as a vtkPartitionedDataSetCollection of a partitioned dataset per level. amr_gaussian_pulse makes VTK's Gaussian pulse hierarchy, for tests.

docs.title: Ghost cells
docs.text:
ghost_cells(amr, layers=1) grows every box by a layer within its level's domain. A ghost a sibling box holds is copied from it; one no sibling holds comes from the coarser level, the coarse cell's value for a cell and an interpolation of the coarse cell's corners for a point. A grid's positions are filled the same way, so curvilinear and rectilinear boxes grow as images do. A ghost neither holds is hidden. Afterwards, update_ghosts(amr, "name") refreshes the ghosts after a filter changed the owned values, and average_down(amr, "name") puts the fine levels' data into the coarse cells and points they cover:

grown = td.ghost_cells(amr)                # every box a layer wider
for level, box in grown:
    box.fields["g"] = td.gradients(box, "f", at="points")   # right where owned
td.update_ghosts(grown, "g")               # the ghosts' from their owners
td.average_down(grown, "g")                # coarse cells under fine ones: the fine average

docs.title: Probe and resample
docs.text:
probe(amr, where) evaluates each point in the finest level's cell holding it, so probing onto an image resamples the hierarchy, as VTK's vtkAMRResampleFilter does:

image = td.uniform_grid((64, 64), origin=(0.0, 0.0), spacing=(8 / 63, 8 / 63, 1.0))
resampled = td.probe(amr, image)           # each point from the finest level holding it

docs.title: In pieces
docs.text: The boxes of a hierarchy may be on several devices and spread over MPI ranks: each rank passes its own boxes of each level and the world (td.AMRDataSet(levels, ratios, world=tc.World(comm))). The hierarchy gathers every rank's boxes when it is made, and its marks, ghost cells, average_down, probes and reductions work across the ranks.

docs.title: Not here
docs.text: Crack-free contouring across levels, periodic domains, tagging and regridding, and conservative interpolation are not part of Tack yet.

docs.title: Octrees
docs.text:
Tree-based AMR codes -- RAMSES and its kind, and CEA's codes, which ParaView reads as VTK's HyperTreeGrid -- refine cell by cell: each cell is split in two along each axis wherever more resolution is needed, into a tree of cells. An OctreeDataSet holds a grid of such trees, laid out for GPUs as a linear octree: every node is three numbers -- its tree, its level, and its Morton key, its integer coordinates in the tree interleaved bit by bit -- and the nodes are sorted so each subtree is one contiguous run. Whether a node is a leaf, and its position and size, come from the keys; nothing about position is stored.

This first pass holds cell data (one value per node, refined ones included, as the codes store them) and is about statistics. Nodes that are not leaves are REFINEDCELL, so reductions count each region once, over the leaves. The leaves are also a dataset of cells, for every filter, and an octree can be probed.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Cells as a RAMSES reader gives them: whole octs, each cell's level and centre.
# One root cell refined to level 2 everywhere, and to level 4 near a blob.
levels, centres = [], []


def refine(lo, size, level):
    mid = lo + size / 2
    if level < 2 or (level < 4 and np.linalg.norm(mid - 0.3) < 0.25):
        for child in range(8):
            offset = np.array([child & 1, (child >> 1) & 1, (child >> 2) & 1]) * size / 2
            refine(lo + offset, size / 2, level + 1)
    else:
        levels.append(level)
        centres.append(mid)


refine(np.zeros(3), 1.0, 0)
centres = np.array(centres)
rho = np.exp(-40 * ((centres - 0.3) ** 2).sum(axis=1))      # a dense blob
roots = td.uniform_grid((2, 2, 2))                           # one root cell, the unit cube
octree = td.OctreeDataSet.from_cells(roots, levels, centres, fields={"rho": rho})
print(octree)

# Leaves differ in size: the plain mean of rho counts a small dense cell like a
# large empty one; the volume-weighted mean is rho's average over the cube.
plain = td.statistics(octree, "rho")
by_volume = td.statistics(octree, "rho", weights="volume")
print(f"mean rho {plain.mean:.4f}, by volume {by_volume.mean:.4f}, mass {by_volume.sum:.4f}")
leaf = octree.is_leaf
volume = octree.measures()[leaf]
assert np.isclose(by_volume.sum, octree.fields["rho"].numpy()[leaf] @ volume)
assert np.isclose(by_volume.weight, 1.0) and plain.mean > by_volume.mean

docs.title: Weights
docs.text: An octree's leaves differ in size by a factor of 8 per level, so the plain mean of a field over the leaves weighs a tiny dense cell like a huge empty one. weights="volume" weighs each cell by its measure, and a field's name (weights="rho") by that field: with a density, the volume-weighted sum is the mass and a mass-weighted mean takes weights= a field of mass per cell. entropy takes the same weights, and so do datasets, pieces and AMR hierarchies, whose levels differ in size too. level= reduces one level's nodes instead of the leaves.

docs.title: From codes and VTK
docs.text:
• OctreeDataSet.from_cells(roots, level, position, fields) takes each cell's level and a position in it, as a RAMSES reader or yt gives them (whole octs), over a grid of root cells (an image or a rectilinear grid); it adds the ancestors no cell gives, their values NaN.
  • vtk_to_dataset takes a vtkHyperTreeGrid (branching factor 2) and dataset_to_vtk gives one back, a mask as HIDDENCELL.

docs.title: Leaves as cells, and probes
docs.text:
octree.leaves() is the leaves as an unstructured DataSet of voxels (pixels in 2D) with every field as cell data: cell c is the c-th leaf in the nodes' order (np.flatnonzero(octree.is_leaf)[c]), and hidden leaves are HIDDENCELL. Corners that coincide are one point, found by sorting their indices on the finest level's lattice, so the cells are connected; corners on a finer neighbour's face stay hanging, as the tree has them. Every filter that reads cell data works on it: threshold, cell_centers, extract_cells, probe.
